meta.source: Code of the Town of North Castle (codified by General Code; ecode360.com/NO0492), legislation through 3-11-2026
meta.methodologyNote: Each chapter was read in full by an AI analyst and rated for clarity, currency, and fitness for purpose. Ratings, scores, and recommendations are AI-generated directional commentary, not legal advice. Peer-town comparisons reflect general professional knowledge of common Westchester County / New York State municipal code practice, not a document-to-document review of other towns' actual code text.

chapters.title: General Provisions
chapters.summary: Chapter 1 is the foundational adoption law for the entire Code of the Town of North Castle, enacted 11-18-2015 by L.L. No. 9-2015. It establishes that Chapters 1 through 355 collectively constitute the 'Code,' continues prior local laws as reaffirmed rather than newly enacted (§1-2), repeals specifically enumerated obsolete chapters such as the former Chapter 108 Fireworks and Chapter 158 Recycling (§1-3B), and preserves categories of rights, fees, and pending actions from repeal (§1-4). It also contains standard severability, code-maintenance, sale, and anti-tampering provisions (§§1-5 through 1-10).
chapters.ratingRationale: This is purely structural, procedural codification boilerplate rather than substantive policy, and it is internally clean and complete: it lists specific repealed predecessor chapters by number and enactment date (§1-3B, e.g., former Chapter 108 Fireworks from 7-11-2007), includes a standard severability clause (§1-5), and assigns ongoing code-maintenance duty to the Town Clerk (§1-8). There is no drafting inconsistency or missing element typical of this chapter type, so a high score and 'Good shape' rating is warranted despite (and because of) its narrow, foundational scope.
strengths: Explicit, itemized table of specifically repealed predecessor local laws with chapter numbers and original enactment dates (§1-3B), giving clear historical traceability

Thorough carve-out of matters saved from repeal — fee amounts, salaries, pension provisions, Zoning Map amendments, and bonded indebtedness (§1-4F, 1-4J, 1-4L, 1-4K) — preventing accidental repeal of unrelated Town obligations
Standard, well-drafted severability clause (§1-5) protecting the remainder of the Code if any single provision is invalidated
Clear, ongoing maintenance duty assigned to the Town Clerk to keep the certified Code copy current (§1-8)
Anti-tampering penalty provision (§1-10) protects the integrity of the public-facing Code itself
concerns: Section 1-11(B) references a 'Schedule A' of substantive amendments/additions made during codification that is not reproduced in or accessible from the chapter text itself, which is a minor transparency gap for a public-facing dashboard

recommendations.suggestion: Ensure the 'Schedule A' referenced in §1-11(B) — which lists the substantive changes made at the time of the 2015 codification — is readily accessible alongside the Code online, since the chapter text itself only references it without including it.

chapters.peerComparison: Chapter 1 is standard General Code codification-service boilerplate (adoption, continuation, repealer, severability, and code-maintenance clauses) used nearly verbatim across hundreds of New York municipalities that codify through the same publisher; it is not a substantive policy chapter and so is not meaningfully comparable to peer-town practice the way Chapters 173, 146, or 263 are. Note this explicitly: this assessment is about internal completeness and clarity, not benchmarking against other towns' discretionary policy choices.

chapters.title: Appearance Tickets
chapters.summary: Chapter 5 authorizes designated Town public servants (Building Inspector, Assistant Building Inspector, Code Enforcement Officer, Town Engineer, police officers, the Fire Inspector, and the Animal Control Officer) to issue and serve appearance tickets for violations of state statutes and local laws within their respective enforcement areas. It defines what an appearance ticket is, specifies how it must be served (personal service, with a Civil Practice Law and Rules §308 alternative for zoning, building, and sanitation code violations), and sets out the consequences of a defendant's failure to appear, including warrant issuance and special rules for corporate defendants. The chapter is purely procedural and administrative, implementing state Criminal Procedure Law appearance-ticket mechanics at the local level.
chapters.ratingRationale: The chapter was rewritten in its entirety in 2015 and is otherwise clean, well-organized, and procedurally sound, authorizing a sensible and current list of enforcement officials (§5-2). However, §5-5B cites 'CPLR § 600.20' for the corporate-defendant appearance rule, when that provision — governing corporate appearance by counsel in criminal matters — properly resides in the Criminal Procedure Law (CPL), not the Civil Practice Law and Rules (CPLR); this is a specific, citable drafting inconsistency that keeps the chapter from being fully clean.
strengths: Authorized-issuer list in §5-2 is specific and role-based (Building Inspector, Fire Inspector for fire prevention/safety, Animal Control Officer for animal control/licensing, police officers), avoiding a vague blanket delegation
Method-of-service provision (§5-4) correctly distinguishes ordinary personal service from the CPLR §308 alternative service methods available for zoning, building, and sanitation code violations
Chapter was amended in its entirety in 2015, so its structure reflects a relatively recent, deliberate redraft rather than a patchwork of old amendments
Defendant's failure-to-appear provision (§5-5) addresses both individual (warrant with bail) and corporate defendant scenarios rather than only the more common individual case
concerns: §5-5B cites 'CPLR § 600.20' for the rule that a corporate defendant must appear by counsel and that failure to do so lets the court enter a guilty plea and impose sentence; that provision is Criminal Procedure Law (CPL) § 600.20, not Civil Practice Law and Rules (CPLR) § 600.20, which is a mismatched statutory citation in a chapter otherwise dealing exclusively in criminal procedure
No definitions section beyond the single definition of 'appearance ticket' in §5-3A, leaving terms like 'public servant' to state-law incorporation without a local cross-reference

recommendations.suggestion: Correct the citation in §5-5B from 'CPLR § 600.20' to 'CPL § 600.20' (Criminal Procedure Law) to avoid confusion for court staff, prosecutors, or defense counsel relying on the local law's cross-reference.

Periodically confirm the §5-2 authorized-issuer list stays current as Town job titles evolve (e.g., if a 'Zoning Enforcement Officer' title is later created distinct from the Code Enforcement Officer), since the list is title-specific rather than function-general.

chapters.peerComparison: Based on general professional knowledge of Westchester municipal codes rather than a document-to-document comparison, North Castle's appearance-ticket chapter is a standard, largely boilerplate implementation of CPL Article 150 issuance authority, and its list of authorized officers (building, code enforcement, fire, animal control, police) mirrors the typical scope granted in comparable towns. The use of CPLR §308 service methods for zoning/building/sanitation violations is also consistent with common local practice for those code-enforcement-style (as opposed to purely criminal) tickets; the apparent CPLR/CPL citation mix-up in §5-5B, however, is a drafting slip not typically seen in cleaner peer-town versions of this same boilerplate chapter.

chapters.title: Boards, Bureaus and Committees
chapters.summary: Chapter 12 establishes and governs five distinct Town bodies in separate articles: a Traffic Violations Bureau dating to 1965 (Article I), the Parks and Recreation Advisory Board dating to 1987 (Article II), the Architectural Review Board created in 2005 with detailed submission procedures (Article III), the Residential Project Review Committee created in 2008 to triage residential permit applications and route only impactful projects to the Planning Board or ARB (Article IV), and a 2022 article authorizing videoconferenced public meetings under Public Officers Law §103-a (Article V). Each article was adopted at a different time and largely stands alone, with membership, quorum, meeting-frequency and appeal rules specific to that body.
chapters.ratingRationale: The chapter is a patchwork of eras: Article V's 2022 videoconferencing authorization and Article IV's 2022 RPRC jurisdiction amendment (§12-22, amended 7-13-2022 by L.L. No. 7-2022) show active recent maintenance, but Article I (Traffic Violations Bureau) is essentially unrevised 1965 text and Article II (Parks and Recreation Advisory Board) shows no amendments at all since its 1987 adoption. The chapter also contains an internal inconsistency in §12-21D, which states the RPRC 'shall schedule meetings at regular intervals no less frequently than once weekly twice monthly' — a self-contradictory frequency requirement that has apparently never been cleaned up.
strengths: Article V (§§12-25 through 12-27) directly implements the 2021 amendment to Public Officers Law §103-a, giving Town boards clear, current authority to meet via videoconference

The Residential Project Review Committee (Article IV) is a genuinely efficient administrative design — it enumerates specific exempt project types (interior alterations, sheds under 144 square feet, generators, most fences per §12-22B) so minor projects skip full Planning Board/ARB review while still requiring RPRC referral for tree removal, wetland or steep-slope permits
The ARB's submission requirements (§12-18) are unusually detailed and itemized by project type, giving applicants clear, predictable expectations rather than vague discretionary standards
Both the ARB (§12-19) and RPRC (§12-23) have explicit, time-bound appeal pathways to a named board (ZBA and Planning Board respectively), giving aggrieved applicants clear due process

Recordkeeping requirements for both ARB and RPRC (§§12-17F, 12-21C) require typewritten minutes showing each member's vote, filed with the Town Clerk within five business days, supporting transparency and public inspection
concerns: Article I (Traffic Violations Bureau) retains 1965-era mechanics — written powers of attorney, in-person answer requirements — with no apparent modernization for e-payment or electronic plea handling, and only its title was touched by the 2015 amendment to §12-1

Article II (Parks and Recreation Advisory Board) has never been amended since 1987 adoption and, unlike Article III and IV, contains no reference to the NYS Open Meetings Law or any conflict-of-interest/ethics cross-reference

Section 12-21D contains contradictory drafting: the RPRC 'shall schedule meetings at regular intervals no less frequently than once weekly twice monthly,' which cannot be satisfied literally as written

The chapter creates an internal inconsistency on transparency: ARB meetings must comply with the NYS Open Meetings Law (§12-17E) while RPRC meetings explicitly do not and 'may be closed to the public' (§12-21D), even though the RPRC has real regulatory power — by majority vote it can compel a property owner into full Planning Board or ARB review (§12-22A)

No article in the chapter cross-references the Town's ethics/conflict-of-interest code for appointed board members, despite Chapter 12 being the natural home for such a cross-reference across all its boards and committees

The Architectural Review Board's five-year reappointment terms (§12-17A) have no stated term limit, unlike the Parks and Recreation Board's staggered three-year terms in §12-11, so the two boards created just 18 years apart follow noticeably different governance models with no explanation for the divergence

recommendations.suggestion: Fix the self-contradictory meeting-frequency language in §12-21D ('no less frequently than once weekly twice monthly') so the RPRC's minimum meeting cadence is unambiguous and enforceable.

Reconcile the Open Meetings Law inconsistency between the ARB (must comply, §12-17E) and the RPRC (explicitly need not comply and may close proceedings, §12-21D), given that the RPRC can unilaterally require an applicant into full board review under §12-22A.

Add a chapter-level or per-article cross-reference to the Town's ethics/financial-disclosure code for members of the Parks and Recreation Board, ARB and RPRC, none of which currently mention recusal or conflict-of-interest obligations anywhere in Chapter 12.

Modernize the Traffic Violations Bureau's 1965-era procedure in §§12-3 and 12-4 (written powers of attorney, in-person answer within a specified time) to reflect how minor traffic tickets are actually processed today, or confirm and note in the code that the state's centralized traffic system has superseded most of this article's practical function.

Consider adding a term limit or periodic-reappointment review to the ARB's five-year terms in §12-17A, paralleling the staggered-term/reappointment recommendation process already built into the Parks and Recreation Board under §12-11B.

chapters.peerComparison: Based on general familiarity with how Westchester towns structure similar chapters, not a document-to-document comparison: it's common for a 'Boards, Bureaus and Committees' chapter to either state or cross-reference a uniform conflict-of-interest/recusal standard for all appointed board members, and North Castle's chapter notably doesn't do that here, leaving ethics coordination to whatever standalone ethics chapter the Town maintains elsewhere. Article V's 2022 videoconferencing authorization tracks the wave of similar local laws many NY municipalities adopted shortly after the state amended Public Officers Law §103-a, so that piece is squarely current. The Residential Project Review Committee model in Article IV is a somewhat more sophisticated administrative streamlining mechanism than what many comparable towns have — plenty of peer municipalities still route every residential building permit through full Planning Board or ARB review rather than triaging low-impact projects out first, so this is a relative strength worth highlighting on a civic-transparency dashboard.

recordEvidence.verdict: No criticism; ARB record effectively absent
recordEvidence.note: Verified structure: 5 articles, §12-1–§12-27 — Art. I Traffic Violations Bureau (§12-1–8), Art. II Parks and Recreation Board (§12-9–15), Art. III Architectural Review Board (§12-16–19: Creation/purpose, Membership and organization, Jurisdiction and submission requirements, Appeals), Art. IV Residential Project Review Committee (§12-20–24), Art. V Videoconferencing for Meetings (§12-25–27). No criticism was retained — but the transcript archive contains only one ARB meeting against 105 Planning Board, 113 Town Board, and 44 Zoning Board of Appeals transcripts, so §§12-16–19 are effectively unobserved rather than confirmed sound. For cross-reference: the Planning Board's authority sits at §355-46 (Zoning Article VIII), not in this chapter; the Zoning Board of Appeals is established as the “Board of Appeals” at §355-77 (appeal procedure §355-78); the Board of Ethics is at §27-19; and no Conservation Board or Conservation Advisory Council chapter exists in the Code as currently codified, notwithstanding the conservation-subdivision provision at §355-31.

chapters.title: Ethics, Code of
chapters.summary: This chapter establishes North Castle's Code of Ethics for all municipal officers and employees, enacted under General Municipal Law §806 and Municipal Home Rule Law §10. It covers disclosure of interests, recusal/abstention rules, conflicts in contracts, investments, private and future employment, nepotism, political solicitation, confidential information, and a detailed gift-acceptance schedule. It also creates a five-member Board of Ethics with staggered terms, advisory-opinion authority, and a defined complaint-investigation-hearing process, plus board-eligibility restrictions tied to political-party leadership roles.
chapters.ratingRationale: The chapter has been actively maintained with substantive amendments in 2019, 2022, and most recently 12-13-2023 (L.L. No. 8-2023, updating §27-7 recusal and §27-19F Board of Ethics removal), and it goes beyond the General Municipal Law Article 18 floor with locally specific mechanisms like the $500 campaign-contribution recusal trigger (§27-6B) and itemized gift-value thresholds (§27-18E). Its main gaps are structural rather than stale: the mandatory annual disclosure/training requirement in §27-6D reaches only elected officials and four named boards, and a 4-of-5 quorum combined with a 4-vote supermajority to find a violation (§27-19L, §27-20F) can make findings difficult if any one member is recused.
strengths: Establishes a five-member Board of Ethics with staggered five-year terms, two alternates, and a political-balance cap of no more than three members from the same party (§27-19B-E).

Defines a detailed, time-bound complaint process: initial reasonable-cause review within 10 business days, written reasonable-cause notice within 20 business days, hearing within 60 days, and a written decision within 30 days of the hearing (§27-20A, E, F).

Codifies specific dollar thresholds for permissible gifts — $25 per instance/$200 aggregate annually for food and beverage, $75 for awards/plaques (§27-18E) — rather than leaving 'nominal value' undefined.

Includes robust revolving-door provisions: a six-month bar on pursuing employment with parties who have pending matters, a two-year bar on representing parties before one's former office, and a permanent bar on matters personally and substantially worked on (§27-11).

Requires annual ethics training and a disclosure statement (Appendix A) for elected officials, Planning Board, Zoning Board of Appeals, Architectural Review Board, and Board of Assessment Review members (§27-6D), kept current through 2019 and 2022 amendments.
concerns: The mandatory annual disclosure statement and ethics-training requirement in §27-6D applies only to elected officials and four named boards, not to all municipal officers and employees or other bodies such as the Conservation Board.
The $500 political-contribution recusal trigger in §27-6B has not been amended since the chapter's original 2016 adoption and is not indexed for inflation.

A Board of Ethics quorum of four (§27-19L) combined with a four-vote supermajority required to find a violation (§27-20F) means a single recusal or absence can make a merits finding effectively unattainable.

The code leans heavily on cross-references to GML §801, §803, and §805-a (§27-9B, §27-10B, §27-14) rather than restating the operative substantive standard, which may be difficult for lay board members to apply without separately consulting state law.
No explicit statute of limitations or filing deadline governs citizen ethics complaints under §27-19J/K, and there is no stated retention period for sealed records of dismissed complaints (§27-20C).

Gift thresholds in §27-18E ($25/$200/$75) and the disclosure filing mechanics in §27-6D rely on the Appendix A form, which is referenced as an attachment but its substantive content (e.g., specific asset/income disclosure categories) is not reproduced within the chapter text itself.

recommendations.suggestion: Reconcile the four-member quorum requirement (§27-19L) with the four-vote supermajority needed to find a violation (§27-20F) — a single absence or recusal currently makes a violation finding structurally very difficult to reach.

Expand the mandatory annual disclosure/training requirement in §27-6D beyond elected officials and the four named boards to cover all municipal officers and employees, consistent with the broader intent of GML Article 18.
Index the $500 campaign-contribution recusal trigger in §27-6B and the $25/$200/$75 gift-value thresholds in §27-18E for inflation, since neither has changed since the code's 2016 enactment.

Add an explicit filing deadline or statute of limitations for citizen complaints under §27-19J/K and clarify the retention/destruction schedule for sealed records of dismissed complaints referenced in §27-20C.

chapters.peerComparison: Based on general professional knowledge of New York municipal ethics codes rather than a document-to-document comparison, North Castle's Code of Ethics is more developed than the bare General Municipal Law Article 18 floor that some small Westchester towns still rely on without a standing local Board of Ethics or codified gift schedule. Its five-member Board of Ethics with staggered terms and a defined complaint-to-hearing timeline (§27-19, §27-20) is more procedurally rigorous than many peer towns' ethics codes, which often lack specific investigation deadlines. The campaign-contribution-triggered recusal rule (§27-6B) and the political-party-leadership eligibility bar for land-use boards (§27-22) are relatively uncommon anti-corruption features that exceed the state-law baseline. Where North Castle's financial-disclosure regime is comparatively narrow is in limiting the mandatory annual disclosure statement (§27-6D) to elected officials and four specific boards rather than requiring broader annual financial disclosure (e.g., outside income or real property interests) from all officers and employees, as some larger Westchester municipalities and NYS Public Officers Law-influenced codes do.

recordEvidence.amendmentTraffic: A 2022 revision cycle ran August 10, September 14, September 28, October 12, and October 26, 2022 (amending §27-2 and §27-6); a further cycle ran December 13, 2023.

chapters.title: Fees
chapters.summary: Chapter 33 establishes the Town Board's authority to impose and collect administrative fees on applications processed by the Planning Department, Zoning Board of Appeals, Sewer and Water Department, Town Board, Building Department, and Police Department. Rather than listing dollar amounts in the chapter itself, it directs the Town Board to set and amend a centralized Master Fee Schedule by resolution (cross-referenced as Chapter A370), broadly defines what counts as an 'administrative cost' recoverable from applicants, and requires payment in advance, with underpayment rendering an application incomplete.
chapters.ratingRationale: Chapter 33 correctly centralizes fee-setting into a Master Fee Schedule adopted and amended by Town Board resolution (SS 33-2, pointing to Ch. A370) instead of hard-coding dollar figures directly into the local law, which is a more flexible, modern approach that avoids needing a full local-law amendment every time a fee changes. The advance-payment rule with a clear consequence for underpayment (SS 33-4, application deemed incomplete) is straightforward and enforceable.
strengths: Centralized Master Fee Schedule model (SS 33-2) that keeps dollar amounts out of the local law text and updatable by simple resolution

Broad, functional definition of 'administrative costs' in SS 33-3 covering ancillary items like hearing notice preparation/publication, affidavits, official record maintenance, photocopies, and vital records
Clear payment-in-advance requirement with a defined consequence (application deemed incomplete) for underpayment (SS 33-4)
Extensive general-references list cross-linking roughly 19 other Town chapters, showing the fee framework is integrated across departments rather than siloed
concerns: The chapter itself contains no actual fee amounts — all figures live in the separate Master Fee Schedule (Ch. A370), so Chapter 33 alone gives residents no visibility into actual costs
No hardship or fee-waiver provision exists in this chapter, unlike the waiver mechanism the Town built into Chapter 114 (SS 114-5)

No stated review cadence (e.g., annual) for keeping the Master Fee Schedule aligned with actual administrative costs, even though SS 33-3 ties fees to 'actual costs of administering and reviewing such applications'
No public notice requirement is specified for when the Town Board amends the Master Fee Schedule by resolution (SS 33-2)

recommendations.suggestion: Since SS 33-2 already defers fee amounts to the Master Fee Schedule (Ch. A370), ensure that schedule is kept current and easily cross-referenced or hyperlinked in the online code, since Chapter 33 itself provides no dollar transparency to the public.

Add a periodic review requirement (e.g., an annual reconciliation against actual administrative costs) to SS 33-2, since SS 33-3 already commits fees to reflect 'actual costs' but no mechanism ensures the schedule keeps pace.

Add a hardship-waiver provision for administrative fees, mirroring the waiver mechanism the Town already built into Chapter 114 (SS 114-5), for consistency and to address cases of financial hardship not currently addressed anywhere in Chapter 33.

chapters.peerComparison: Based on general professional knowledge, not a document-to-document comparison: centralizing fees into a single Master Fee Schedule that the Town Board adopts and amends by resolution (Chapter 33 pointing to Chapter A370) is considered a fiscal best practice relative to towns that still hard-code specific dollar fees inside each individual regulatory chapter (e.g., writing a fixed permit fee directly into a zoning or excavation chapter), which requires a full local-law amendment merely to adjust a number. North Castle's model, adopted in 2013, reflects the more modern, administratively efficient approach that a number of Westchester municipalities have moved toward.

chapters.title: Greenway Compact Plan
chapters.summary: Chapter 39 formally adopts the Westchester County Greenway Compact Plan ('The Greenprint for a Sustainable Future . . . the Westchester Way') pursuant to Environmental Conservation Law §44-0119, making North Castle a participating Greenway community. It establishes a 90-day process for the Town Board to accept or reject amendments proposed by the Hudson River Valley Greenway Communities Council, states a policy that future land use laws should be designed for consistency with the Compact Plan where appropriate, and expressly preserves the Town's home rule authority, including the right to withdraw from the Compact at any time.
chapters.ratingRationale: This short, purely administrative chapter is internally consistent and clearly drafted, with no contradictory provisions: §39-2 gives a concrete 90-day decision window for Compact amendments, and §39-4 carefully and explicitly preserves home rule authority and the Town's unilateral right to withdraw, which is exactly the kind of protective clause this type of intergovernmental compact chapter should contain.
strengths: Sets a concrete, auditable 90-day deadline for the Town Board to act on proposed Compact amendments, rather than leaving the timeline open-ended (§39-2)
Explicitly reserves the Town's home rule authority over land use and zoning decisions and bars any other entity from superseding Town land use laws (§39-4A, §39-4B)
Expressly preserves a unilateral right to withdraw from the Compact at a later date, ensuring participation remains fully voluntary (§39-4C)
Ties consistency review to future amendments and new enactments only ('to the extent the Town amends... or enacts new... laws'), avoiding retroactive disruption of existing zoning (§39-3)
concerns: §39-3's consistency policy uses aspirational, non-mandatory language ('should be designed to be consistent... where appropriate') without a defined review checklist or referenced procedure for how consistency is actually documented in practice

§39-2 sets a 90-day deadline for the Town Board to act on a proposed amendment but does not specify a default consequence (acceptance, rejection, or extension) if the deadline passes without a resolution

recommendations.suggestion: Add a default rule to §39-2 specifying what happens if the Town Board does not act within the 90-day window (e.g., deemed rejection), closing a gap in an otherwise clear procedural timeline.

Strengthen §39-3 by linking the 'consistency with the Compact Plan' policy to a specific review step in the Town's subdivision (Ch. 275) or zoning (Ch. 355) referral process, rather than leaving it as general aspirational policy language.

chapters.peerComparison: Based on general professional knowledge of Hudson Valley and Westchester municipal practice rather than a document-to-document comparison, dozens of Westchester towns participate in the Greenway Compact under Environmental Conservation Law Article 44, and North Castle's chapter follows the standard template used across these participating communities, including the customary home-rule savings clause and reserved withdrawal right in §39-4. This structure and level of detail is typical and unremarkable for a Greenway Compact adoption chapter — most peer towns' versions are similarly brief and procedural, since the substantive commitment is voluntary and largely aspirational by design.

chapters.title: Officers and Employees
chapters.summary: Chapter 60 is a nine-article collection governing Town officers and employees: defense and indemnification for civil rights claims and punitive damages (Article I), mandatory annual training for Planning and Zoning Board members (Article II), the elective Town Clerk's four-year term (Article III), civil service appointment/promotion rules (Article IV), and a series of residency-requirement exemptions allowing the Court Clerk, Building Department titles, Deputy Town Clerk, Town Comptroller, and (appointed) Receiver of Taxes to live anywhere in New York State rather than only within the Town (Articles V-IX).
chapters.ratingRationale: The chapter has been actively maintained, with its most recent amendment (10-23-2024, L.L. No. 6-2024) updating the Building Department residency article, and it addresses a real recruitment problem by letting technical positions such as Building Inspector, Comptroller, and Deputy Town Clerk be filled statewide rather than only by Town residents (§60-16, §60-20, §60-24). The Article I indemnification scheme is detailed, with a specific four-factor Town Board finding required before punitive damages are paid (§60-3A(1)-(4)), and the PZ Board training requirement ties a concrete consequence — ineligibility for reappointment — to noncompliance (§60-5) without disrupting sitting members' voting rights.
strengths: Recently amended (10-23-2024) showing active upkeep rather than stale, decades-old text
Detailed four-part Town Board finding requirement before indemnifying punitive damages, done in executive session for confidentiality (§60-3A-B)

Statewide residency exemptions for hard-to-recruit technical and administrative posts (Building Inspector, Assistant BI, Fire Inspector, Deputy Town Clerk, Comptroller, Receiver of Taxes) widen the Town's hiring pool (§60-16, §60-20, §60-24, §60-29)
PZ Board training noncompliance affects only reappointment eligibility, not current voting authority, balancing accountability with board continuity (§60-5)
Receiver of Taxes conversion from elective to appointive office was carried out properly via mandatory referendum (§60-25, §60-28)
concerns: Five separate, near-identical residency-exemption articles (V through IX) repeat the same Municipal Home Rule Law §10 mechanism for different offices rather than being consolidated into one general residency article
Article IV's civil service provision (§60-11) still cites 'Chapter 104 of the Law of 1936 of the State of New York' verbatim, an archaic citation style not updated in later amendments
§60-15 is marked '(Reserved)' after its 'Title' provision was repealed in 2024, leaving a visible gap in the article numbering
The Planning and Zoning Board training requirement is only four hours per year (§60-4), which is comparatively light and its content approval is left largely to board chairpersons' discretion

recommendations.suggestion: Consolidate the repetitive residency-exemption articles (V, VI, VII, VIII, IX), which all invoke the same Municipal Home Rule Law §10 authority, into a single unified residency article covering all exempted offices.
Modernize the archaic 1936-law citation in §60-11 and confirm the civil service appointment provisions still align with current New York State Civil Service Law.
Clean up the reserved/repealed §60-15 gap and consider renumbering Article VI now that its title was amended in 2024, for code clarity.
Consider whether the four-hour annual PZ Board training minimum in §60-4 should be increased given the complexity of land-use matters these boards decide.

chapters.peerComparison: Based on general familiarity with New York municipal officer/employee chapters rather than a document-to-document comparison, North Castle's pattern of enacting individual Municipal Home Rule Law §10 residency-exemption local laws for specific hard-to-fill titles (Building Inspector, Comptroller, Deputy Clerk, Receiver of Taxes) mirrors what many Westchester towns have done piecemeal over the past two decades as they've struggled to recruit for technical posts under strict Town Law §23/Public Officers Law §3 residency defaults. The 2024 update to the Building Department article suggests North Castle is more current than many peer towns that still have stale, single-title residency laws; the fragmented five-article structure, however, is a common but avoidable drafting inefficiency seen across many town codes of this vintage.

recordEvidence.note: Amended October 23, 2024; no criticism found in the transcript record.

chapters.title: Police Department
chapters.summary: Chapter 68 has two parts: Article I (1989) authorizes the Chief of Police to request or provide mutual aid to and from other Westchester County police agencies under General Municipal Law § 209-m. Article II (2014) establishes the Town Board as the Board of Police Commissioners (chaired by the Supervisor), assigns it the powers of a Board of Police Commissioners under the Westchester County Police Act, and sets out the disciplinary process for department members and the Chief of Police, including the option to use an appointed hearing officer whose findings are advisory only. The chapter explicitly supersedes conflicting provisions of the Westchester County Police Act.
chapters.ratingRationale: The chapter is a functional, internally consistent governance framework — it clearly separates the Chief of Police's day-to-day operational discretion (§ 68-8A) from the Board of Police Commissioners' authority over fundamental policy and discipline (§ 68-8B) — but it is largely administrative in nature and has not been amended since 2014, predating New York's 2020-2021 statewide police reform and reinvention initiative (Executive Order 203), which most Westchester municipalities addressed through adopted collaborative reform plans, though not necessarily through this specific local law.
strengths: Clean separation of authority between the Board of Police Commissioners (fundamental policy, discipline) and the Chief of Police (day-to-day operations) in § 68-8A
Disciplinary process for both rank-and-file members and the Chief of Police himself is spelled out in detail, including who may bring charges and who hears them (§ 68-8B)
Mutual aid authority is grounded in a specific state statute (General Municipal Law § 209-m, § 68-4), giving it clear legal footing
Express supersession clause (§ 68-9) resolves any conflict with the older Westchester County Police Act rather than leaving it ambiguous
concerns: No amendment since 10-22-2014; the chapter does not reference any of the state-mandated police reform/reinvention collaborative planning that followed 2020 (Executive Order 203), civilian complaint review, body-worn camera policy, or use-of-force reporting
The Board of Police Commissioners is entirely composed of the Town Board itself (§ 68-6), with no independent or civilian oversight component built into the chapter

Chapter is very brief (only 10 sections across two articles) and leaves most substantive standards (use of force, records, hiring/civil service) to be governed entirely outside this chapter with only a general catch-all reference (§ 68-10)

recommendations.suggestion: Consider whether the Town's post-2020 police reform/reinvention commitments (if any) should be cross-referenced or incorporated into Chapter 68 itself, rather than living solely in a separate resolution, so the code reflects current departmental accountability practices.
Codify a defined timeline for the disciplinary hearing process in § 68-8B (e.g., time to bring charges, time to hold a hearing) since the current text describes who acts but not by when.

Periodically confirm continued alignment with the Westchester County Police Act (Chapter 104 of the Laws of 1936) referenced throughout § 68-7 through § 68-9, since this chapter relies heavily on incorporation of that 1936 special act by reference.

chapters.peerComparison: Based on general professional knowledge of Westchester County practice (not a document-to-document comparison), it is typical for small-to-mid-sized Westchester towns to keep their police department code chapter narrowly administrative — establishing the Town Board as Board of Police Commissioners, delegating day-to-day authority to the Chief, and setting a disciplinary hearing procedure — while leaving substantive matters like hiring, promotion, and civil service protections to county civil service law and collective bargaining agreements outside the municipal code. North Castle's Chapter 68 is fairly typical in scope and structure for this category of chapter; where it lags some peer towns is in not reflecting any post-2020 police reform/transparency provisions in the code text itself, though many towns handled that reform through a separate adopted plan rather than a code amendment.

chapters.title: Records
chapters.summary: Chapter 77 governs public access to Town records under Article I and internal records management under Article II. It designates the Town Clerk as both Records Access Officer (RAO) and Records Management Officer (RMO), sets FOIL-style response and appeal timelines, caps copying fees, and establishes a Records Advisory Committee and archival/disposition procedures. Both articles were rewritten in their entirety in 2015 to align with then-current state Freedom of Information Law practice.
chapters.ratingRationale: The chapter tracks the state's FOIL procedural framework closely, including the five-business-day acknowledgment and 20-business-day determination windows at Section 77-5C, and the appeal-to-Committee-on-Open-Government transmittal duty at Section 77-7G-H. Fee provisions at Section 77-8C cap photocopies at $0.25 per page, matching the Public Officers Law standard, and Article II builds out a genuine records management infrastructure via the Records Advisory Committee (Section 77-14) rather than leaving retention to ad hoc practice.
strengths: Clear designation of a single Records Access Officer (Town Clerk, 15 Bedford Road) with defined duties at Section 77-2
Response and appeal timelines at Sections 77-5 and 77-7 mirror current state FOIL practice, including the 30-day appeal window and 10-business-day appeal determination
Fee structure at Section 77-8 is state-law-compliant and includes a fee-waiver option
Article II establishes a genuine records management program with a dedicated Records Advisory Committee (Section 77-14) covering appraisal, retention, and grant applications
Section 77-15 clearly separates custody rules for active, inactive, digital (ECMS), and archival records
concerns: Section 77-6 (Subject matter list) is a single cross-reference sentence to NYS Schedule MU-1 with no Town-specific detail or link
No mention of a searchable online request-tracking system beyond noting the FOIL Request Form is submitted via the website (Section 77-5A)
Article II references monitoring of ECMS database backups (Section 77-15C) but includes no cybersecurity, breach-notification, or disaster-recovery standard for digital records
The chapter does not address requests for records in specific electronic formats (e.g., native file/metadata requests), an increasingly common FOIL issue

recommendations.suggestion: Build out an online request-status/tracking feature referenced implicitly at Section 77-5A so requesters can check acknowledgment and determination dates without calling the Town Clerk's office.
Add a data security and breach-notification standard to Section 77-15C, which currently only requires the RMO to monitor 'successful completion of database backups' for the ECMS.
Expand Section 77-6 into an actual proactive-disclosure catalog of commonly requested record types rather than a bare cross-reference to the state MU-1 schedule.

chapters.peerComparison: Based on general professional familiarity with Westchester municipal FOIL practice rather than any document-to-document comparison, North Castle's Chapter 77 is above average for a town of its size: many peer towns still operate under pre-2008 FOIL amendment language with looser response deadlines, whereas North Castle's 2015 rewrite incorporates the acknowledgment/determination-date mechanics that became standard after the 2005-2008 FOIL amendments. Its explicit, functioning Records Advisory Committee under Article II is also somewhat more developed than the bare RAO designation many small towns rely on, though its silence on electronic-format requests and cybersecurity leaves it behind the most current model records-access local laws circulating among Westchester municipal associations.

recordEvidence.note: Cited July 13, 2022 as the source of an appeal process. No criticism retained.

chapters.title: Alarms
chapters.summary: Chapter 109 regulates security and fire alarm devices in North Castle, requiring the Town Clerk (as licensing authority) to issue revocable permits before any alarm system is installed, modified, or operated. It creates an Alarm Review Board (Fire Inspector, Police Chief or designee, and Building Inspector) to hear appeals of permit denials, suspensions, revocations, and false-alarm penalties. It sets technical standards (standby power, audible shutoff timers) and imposes per-day fines for violations and for tampering with alarm equipment.
chapters.ratingRationale: The chapter has a workable permit and appeal structure (§109-3, §109-6) and sound technical standards, such as the four-hour standby power requirement and 15/30-minute shutoff switches in §109-8, but it pushes all actual false-alarm fee amounts out to the separate Master Fee Schedule (Ch. A370) rather than codifying any escalating fee structure in the text itself, and the 'more than four false alarms' threshold in §109-4C(2) has stood unchanged since the 1993 adoption.
strengths: Dedicated Alarm Review Board with a defined appeal process and adjournment rule (§109-3E(3), §109-6)
Concrete technical standards: four-hour standby power supply and defined audible-alarm shutoff windows (§109-8)
Strong Town liability disclaimer and hold-harmless requirement on permit acceptance (§109-4A-B)
Distinguishes intentional false alarms and equipment tampering with separate, stiffer penalty provisions (§109-4C, §109-7C)
concerns: False-alarm fee amounts are entirely deferred to the Master Fee Schedule (Ch. A370) rather than set out or escalated within the chapter itself, so the public cannot see the actual penalty structure from the alarm law text
The 'more than four false alarms' suspension trigger (§109-4C(2)) has not been revisited since the 1993 local law despite three later amendment cycles
No stated permit term or renewal cycle for alarm permits, unlike the six-month renewal cycle in Chapter 161's fill permits
No requirement that alarm users periodically update or verify emergency contact information beyond a general notice-of-changes duty

recommendations.suggestion: Codify a visible escalating false-alarm fee schedule directly in §109-4C (e.g., $0/$50/$100/$150 tiers) rather than leaving all amounts to the Master Fee Schedule, so residents can see the actual cost structure in the alarm chapter.
Add a defined permit term and renewal requirement to §109-3 similar to Chapter 161's six-month renewal cycle, so the Town Clerk's alarm registry stays current.
Consider lowering or tiering the four-false-alarm threshold in §109-4C(2) based on alarm type (residential vs. commercial) to better target chronic false-alarm generators.

chapters.peerComparison: Based on general familiarity with Westchester County alarm local laws rather than any document-to-document comparison, many peer towns build an explicit escalating false-alarm fee schedule (e.g., no charge for the first false alarm, then increasing per-incident fees) directly into the alarm chapter rather than relying entirely on a separate fee schedule, which gives residents clearer notice of consequences. North Castle's four-alarm suspension threshold and its Alarm Review Board appeal structure are broadly typical of the region, but deferring all dollar amounts to Ch. A370 is a somewhat less transparent approach than peer towns that state a two- or three-tier fee escalation in the alarm chapter itself.

chapters.title: Application Processing Restrictions
chapters.summary: Known as the 'Application Processing Restrictive Law' (SS 114-2), this chapter bars any Town board or official from processing or approving a permit, certificate of occupancy, or use approval for a property owner who has outstanding fees owed to the Town or outstanding violations of Town local laws on the subject property. It requires proof of no outstanding fees or violations at the time an application is filed (SS 114-4A), halts an in-process application if a violation surfaces mid-review until it is cured (SS 114-4C), narrowly defines when a 'violation' is deemed to occur for purposes of this chapter (SS 114-4D), and allows the Town Board or, in emergencies, the Building Inspector to grant discretionary waivers (SS 114-5).
chapters.ratingRationale: The law effectively uses application-processing leverage to compel compliance (SS 114-4B), but its definition of 'violation' in SS 114-4D is narrow — a violation only counts for purposes of this chapter once 60 days pass without a variance/appeal being sought, or once a criminal summons issues — meaning a freshly cited, contested, or still-appealable violation may not yet trigger the freeze. The chapter also sets no minimum dollar threshold for 'outstanding fees' in SS 114-4A, so in principle even a trivial unpaid balance could halt an application.
strengths: Clear statement of purpose directly tying fee and violation compliance to eligibility for permit/CO processing (SS 114-1)
Built-in due-process off-ramp: an in-process application resumes once proof the violation was corrected is submitted (SS 114-4C)

Dual waiver mechanism — Town Board for general hardship requests, Building Inspector for emergencies (e.g., water pipe leak, electrical malfunction) — with a requirement that the Building Inspector notify the Town Board of any waiver granted (SS 114-5)
Short title provision (SS 114-2) makes the law easy for residents and applicants to cite and locate
concerns: No minimum dollar threshold or de minimis carve-out for 'outstanding fees' in SS 114-4A, so a trivial unpaid balance could theoretically freeze an application

The definition of 'violation' in SS 114-4D(1)-(2) is narrow (60-day unappealed notice of violation, or issuance of a criminal summons), which could miss a violation still within its appeal window and undercut the chapter's stated purpose
No appeal or dispute process is specified for a property owner who contests the underlying claim that fees are owed or a violation exists, beyond the discretionary hardship waiver in SS 114-5

No explicit cross-reference to Chapter 33 (Fees) even though 'outstanding fees owed to the Town' (SS 114-1, SS 114-4A) is central to this chapter's trigger and is defined and administered under Chapter 33

recommendations.suggestion: Establish a minimum de minimis threshold for 'outstanding fees' in SS 114-4A to avoid disproportionate application freezes triggered by trivial unpaid balances.
Add an explicit cross-reference from SS 114-4A to Chapter 33 (Fees), since 'outstanding fees' is the chapter's central trigger term but is not defined or linked within Chapter 114 itself.

Add an expedited dispute/appeal process for owners who contest an alleged fee or violation, since the only current relief is the discretionary Town Board or Building Inspector waiver under SS 114-5 rather than a right to contest the underlying claim.

chapters.peerComparison: Based on general professional knowledge, not a document-to-document comparison: 'clean hands' or application-freeze provisions that condition permit or certificate-of-occupancy issuance on the absence of outstanding violations or fees are a fairly common enforcement tool that a number of Westchester towns adopted in the 2010s to gain leverage against chronic code violators. North Castle's 2017 law (Chapter 114) is broadly typical in structure — freeze plus a discretionary hardship waiver — though its comparatively narrow, precisely bounded definition of 'violation' (tied only to expiration of a 60-day appeal window or issuance of a criminal summons, per SS 114-4D) is more restrictive than some peer laws that simply reference 'any outstanding violation,' which can leave an enforcement gap during the window before that 60-day period elapses.

recordEvidence.verdict: Criticised as an obstacle, then waived

findings.quote: town code chapter 114 … which prohibits us perhaps from doing as the applicant [requests]. … [Later, in a revision cycle:] in waivers, which is at the bottom, it's 114-5, I think it says we can temporarily waive.
findings.corroboration: A restriction chapter whose practical operation depends on a waiver at its own final section (§114-5), invoked within two years of being criticised as an obstacle — weak by design rather than by drafting. (A separate February 14, 2024 remark about an inconsistent chapter title in a pending local-law document reflects a drafting-quality-control issue generally, not a defect in the operative Code.)

chapters.title: Blasting, Explosives and Chipping
chapters.summary: This chapter regulates blasting/use of explosives (Article II) and mechanical rock chipping (Article III) in North Castle. It requires Building Inspector permits, insurance and a minimum $20,000 performance bond, pre-blast/pre-chipping property inspections, advance notice to neighboring owners, restricted hours of operation, and continuous vibration monitoring, with stop-work authority and per-day fines for violations. Article III (chipping) was added in 2020 and layers on a mandatory dust-mitigation plan and an explicit 1-inch-per-second vibration limit.
chapters.ratingRationale: The chapter was thoughtfully restructured and expanded in 2020 (L.L. No. 6-2020) to add a detailed Chipping article with dust-control and vibration standards (§122-19G, §122-26E), showing active maintenance. However, the blasting article itself lacks a numeric vibration/overpressure standard (unlike chipping's explicit 1 in/sec cap in §122-26E) and its $20,000 minimum bond (§122-6E) has not been revisited since its 1990s/2015 origin.
strengths: Article III (Chipping), added 11-18-2020, requires a Building-Inspector-approved dust mitigation plan with water spray/air suppression, covered trucks, and runoff controls (§122-19G) — a modern environmental provision many peer towns lack.
Objective, evidence-based stop-work trigger: sudden cracks, window damage or excessive vibration is deemed prima facie evidence requiring an immediate stop-work order (§122-8B, §122-21B).
Blasters and chipping contractors are held to an absolute-liability standard 'with or without trespass' (§122-14, §122-27), giving residents a strong civil-liability backstop.

Layered notice requirements scaled to activity: 500-foot notice for blasting served 72 hours to 30 days in advance (§122-12) and 500-foot mailed notice at least 10 days ahead for chipping with certified mailing proof (§122-25).
Mandatory insurance, indemnification, and a minimum $20,000 performance bond before any blasting permit issues (§122-6D, §122-6E).
concerns: No explicit numeric peak particle velocity or air-overpressure limit is set for blasting in Article II; §122-13F merely says vibration must be 'limited to that which is specified within the pre-blast inspection report and/or blasting plan,' leaving the actual standard to case-by-case discretion — unlike chipping's explicit 1 in/sec cap (§122-26E).
The $20,000 minimum performance bond (§122-6E) has not been increased since it was set via the 1993 chapter/2015 amendment, and may be inadequate for large modern rock-removal projects.
Permit fees are entirely deferred to the separate Master Fee Schedule (Ch. A370) with no minimum, maximum, or fee-setting guardrails stated in this chapter (§122-6B, §122-19C).

Blasting permits run 12 months (§122-7) while chipping permits run only 90 days with a possible 90-day extension (§122-20, §122-22B) — the differing durations and renewal pathways (Building Inspector vs. Planning Board appeal) are not explained and add administrative complexity.

Maximum penalty of $1,000/day or up to 15 days imprisonment (§122-17C, §122-28C) is a fairly modest civil/criminal deterrent given the potential for property damage or injury from unauthorized blasting.

No provision addresses air-blast overpressure, seismograph placement standards, or public warning/siren protocols beyond the flag-and-whistle rule in §122-15C, which is a relatively old-fashioned mechanism for warning the public before a blast.

recommendations.suggestion: Add an explicit numeric peak-particle-velocity/air-overpressure standard to §122-15 for blasting (mirroring the 1-inch-per-second limit already codified for chipping in §122-26E) instead of relying solely on ad hoc blasting plans.
Reassess and index the $20,000 minimum performance bond in §122-6E, which has not been revisited in over a decade, to ensure it scales with project size and current construction costs.
Reconcile the differing permit durations for blasting (12 months, §122-7) versus chipping (90 days, §122-20) and align their extension/renewal procedures so applicants face a consistent process.

Revisit the $1,000/day maximum fine in §122-17C and §122-28C, last set by L.L. No. 3-2020, to confirm it remains a sufficient deterrent relative to the potential harm from unauthorized blasting or chipping.

Publish indicative bond/insurance/fee ranges directly within Chapter 122 (or a clear cross-reference summary) rather than requiring applicants to separately consult the Master Fee Schedule (Ch. A370) referenced in §122-6B and §122-19C.

chapters.peerComparison: Based on general professional knowledge of Westchester municipal codes (not a document-to-document comparison), North Castle's blasting-permit regime — requiring insurance, a performance bond, pre-blast surveys within 500 feet, and continuous third-party vibration monitoring — is broadly consistent with practice in other rock-ledge-heavy Westchester towns such as Bedford, New Castle, Somers, and Yorktown. North Castle's 2020 addition of a freestanding Chipping article with its own dust-mitigation and vibration-limit requirements (Article III) is somewhat ahead of many peer towns, which often fold mechanical rock removal into a general excavation or noise ordinance rather than giving it dedicated permit and monitoring standards. Where North Castle lags slightly is in not codifying a specific peak-particle-velocity or air-overpressure ceiling for blasting itself (as some peer codes do by referencing USBM RI 8507-style limits), leaving that standard to be set project-by-project through the blasting-plan review process.

recordEvidence.note: Cited as a compliance standard applicants commit to meeting — “we're going to comply with chapter 122, which deals with the surveying and the monitoring” (Planning Board, March 23, 2026) — and §122-17 was read into the record on December 8, 2025. Functioning as intended on this evidence.

chapters.title: Building Code Administration and Enforcement
chapters.summary: Chapter 127 implements the NYS Uniform Fire Prevention and Building Code and the State Energy Conservation Construction Code locally, creating a Code Enforcement Officer position and setting the full permit-to-occupancy pipeline: building permits (§ 127-4), construction inspections including a remote-inspection option (§ 127-5), stop-work orders (§ 127-6), certificates of occupancy/compliance and temporary certificates (§ 127-7), and operating permits for hazardous or high-occupancy uses such as assembly spaces, tents, mobile food vehicles, and short-term rentals (§ 127-10). It layers in periodic fire-safety/property-maintenance inspections (§ 127-11), a dedicated parking-garage structural condition-assessment regime (§ 127-13), recordkeeping and annual reporting to the Town Board and NYS Secretary of State (§§ 127-15 to 127-16), and enforcement tools (orders to remedy, appearance tickets, fines up to $1,000/day, and injunctive relief) in § 127-17. All actual dollar fees are set separately by Town Board resolution under § 127-18 rather than fixed in the local law text.
chapters.ratingRationale: The chapter was wholesale-readopted in 2022 and has already been amended once more recently (§ 127-10, Operating Permits, amended 3-11-2026 by L.L. No. 2-2026), shows evidence of continuous maintenance, incorporates a post-2019 state-mandated parking garage inspection program (§ 127-13) with phased deadlines by construction date, and builds in modern remote-inspection flexibility (§§ 127-5C, 127-10D, 127-11B). It loses points for a stray '(Reserved)' placeholder left in § 127-10C and for pinning FCNYS/PMCNYS/RCNYS to the 2020 edition by name (§ 127-2) without a mechanism to keep those references current as NYS updates the Uniform Code.
strengths: Comprehensive, current definitions section ties directly into 19 NYCRR references and pins FCNYS, PMCNYS, and RCNYS to their 2020 editions (§ 127-2), giving residents a precise, checkable baseline.

Remote-inspection provisions built into construction inspections, operating permits, and fire-safety/property-maintenance inspections (§§ 127-5C, 127-10D, 127-11B) when a remote check can achieve equivalent quality, reducing friction for applicants.

Dedicated parking garage condition-assessment article (§ 127-13) with phased-in deadlines keyed to a structure's original construction date and mandatory professional-engineer-sealed reports — a proactive public-safety measure many municipalities have not yet codified.
Fees are delegated entirely to a Town Board resolution (§ 127-18) rather than hard-coded into the local law, so the fee schedule can be updated without a full code amendment.

Strong transparency backbone: all code-enforcement records are public and open for inspection (§ 127-15), plus mandatory annual reporting to both the Town Board and the NYS Secretary of State (§ 127-16).
concerns: Section 127-10C is left as a bare '(Reserved)' placeholder with no explanatory text, which reads as an unfinished edit to a public code viewer, likely a residue of the 3-11-2026 amendment to that section.

The Energy Code definition (§ 127-2) is not pinned to a specific edition year the way FCNYS/PMCNYS/RCNYS are, creating inconsistent drafting specificity and risk that the chapter's fixed-year code citations quietly lag as NYS periodically updates the Uniform Code and Energy Code.

No provision addresses electric-vehicle charging make-ready wiring, solar-ready construction, or other green-building overlays; the chapter relies entirely on whatever the state Energy Code separately requires.

Operating-permit duration limits (180 days for tents, 60 days for sugarhouse activities, 3 years, 1 year, under § 127-10F) are hard-coded into the local law rather than delegated to administrative rule, so recalibrating them requires a full local law amendment.

Penalties in § 127-17C are flat statutory maximums ($1,000/day fine or 15 days imprisonment; $1,000/day civil penalty) with no escalation for repeat or willful violations, or scaling between residential and commercial noncompliance.

No permit-review or certificate-of-occupancy turnaround timeframe is specified anywhere in §§ 127-4 or 127-7, leaving applicants without a codified expectation for how long Code Enforcement Officer review should take.

recommendations.suggestion: Resolve the orphaned § 127-10C '(Reserved)' subsection — either restore its substantive content or formally note its repeal — so the publicly posted code doesn't display a dangling placeholder letter.

Pin the Energy Code definition in § 127-2 to a specific edition/year the same way FCNYS, PMCNYS, and RCNYS already are, and consider tying future local law updates to NYS's Uniform Code re-adoption cycle so referenced editions don't go stale unnoticed.

Add an EV-charging readiness / make-ready wiring requirement (and consider solar-ready roof provisions) for new construction under this chapter, coordinated with the Energy Code, mirroring the direction a growing number of Westchester municipalities are taking.

Codify a target review/turnaround window for building permit applications (§ 127-4) and certificate of occupancy issuance (§ 127-7) so applicants have a predictable timeline beyond the existing remote-inspection flexibility.

Given § 127-13's parking-garage condition-assessment model was clearly built from the 2019 state mandate, evaluate extending a similar proactive, schedule-driven structural assessment regime to other structurally vulnerable assembly-occupancy building types, rather than relying only on the complaint- and interval-based inspections in § 127-11A.

chapters.peerComparison: This chapter closely tracks the New York Department of State's model local law for administering the Uniform Code and Energy Code, which most Westchester towns have adopted in near-identical form (definitions, permit/inspection/certificate structure, and enforcement mechanics are boilerplate across the county) — this is general professional knowledge, not a document-to-document comparison. North Castle's inclusion of the parking-garage condition-assessment article and remote-inspection allowances is somewhat ahead of towns that adopted the model law before 2019-2020 and never layered those updates in. Delegating the fee schedule to Town Board resolution (§ 127-18) is standard best practice and generally keeps fees more current than towns that hard-code dollar figures directly into the chapter text. On the other hand, the absence of any EV-charging-readiness or broader green-building overlay in the administration chapter itself is typical rather than a red flag — most towns leave that entirely to the state Energy Code and only a handful have begun adding local supplements, so North Castle is roughly at the peer median on that dimension rather than behind it.

recordEvidence.note: A July 13, 2022 discussion referenced a local law “to replace chapter 127, the administration [chapter]” — a wholesale replacement whose motivating criticism was not captured in the transcript. Flagged here as an unexplained rewrite worth asking the Town about directly rather than a confirmed-clean chapter.

chapters.title: Buildings, Numbering of
chapters.summary: This chapter requires every building owner in North Castle to display an assigned street number, sets standards for the size, placement, and visibility of those numbers (tied to the NYS Uniform Fire Prevention and Building Code), and gives the Building Inspector authority over which buildings on a lot get numbered. It bars display of any number other than the one the Town assigned, spells out a 60-day cure period before noncompliance becomes a violation, and sets penalties for offenders.
chapters.ratingRationale: The chapter directly addresses emergency-responder visibility concerns — requiring numbers legible from the street, unobstructed by trees or porches, positioned near lighting where practicable, and (per SS 131-4D) placed within 15 feet of the road right-of-way when the building itself sits more than 50 feet back. Its penalty provision was modernized in 2020 (up to $1,000/day, L.L. No. 3-2020), showing the chapter is actively maintained rather than frozen at its 1992 origin.
strengths: Concrete setback rule (SS 131-4D) requiring numbers within 15 feet of the road right-of-way when a building is set back more than 50 feet, directly aiding emergency response
Incorporates the NYS Uniform Fire Prevention and Building Code by reference for figure compliance (SS 131-4)
Penalty provision updated in 2020 to a meaningful per-day fine (up to $1,000/day) rather than a stale nominal amount
Clear 60-day cure period and defined notice-service methods before a violation is deemed to occur (SS 131-6)
concerns: No minimum numeral height or reflectivity/retroreflective material requirement is specified in the text itself — it only requires 'sharp contrast' in color and defers to the state code by reference (SS 131-4)
The BUILDING definition (SS 131-1) is circular — it defines 'building' as excluding 'any minor building' without defining what a minor building is
No explicit coordination language with county E911/GIS addressing systems, which many peer municipalities have added post-2000s
Nighttime illumination near the number is only required 'wherever practicable' (SS 131-4C), a discretionary standard with no fallback if impracticable

recommendations.suggestion: Add a specific minimum numeral height (e.g., 4 inches, larger for greater setbacks) directly in SS 131-4 rather than relying solely on incorporation of the NYS Uniform Fire Prevention and Building Code, so responders and residents don't need to consult a separate state code to know the standard.

Clarify the undefined 'minor building' term in SS 131-1 to reduce case-by-case disputes when the Building Inspector exercises discretion under SS 131-2 over which structures on a lot must be numbered.

Convert the discretionary 'wherever practicable' illumination standard in SS 131-4C into a firmer requirement (e.g., reflective numerals) to reduce disputes over what counts as compliant nighttime visibility.

chapters.peerComparison: Based on general professional knowledge of Westchester and NY municipal codes rather than any document-to-document comparison: many towns updated their house-numbering laws in the 2000s-2010s to align explicitly with county E911 addressing/GIS systems and to spell out minimum numeral size and reflective materials directly in the local law. North Castle's Chapter 131, first adopted in 1992 and only lightly amended since (a 2015 display-standard tweak and a 2020 penalty update), is fairly typical of an older-generation numbering law that leans on incorporating the state Uniform Fire Prevention and Building Code by reference rather than spelling out numeral size and reflectivity itself — serviceable, but less prescriptive than some current peer ordinances.

chapters.title: Buildings, Unsafe
chapters.summary: Chapter 135 designates the Building Inspector as the official responsible for inspecting unsafe or collapsed buildings and structures (§135-1, §135-3) and establishes a notice-and-survey procedure: the Town Board directs an inspection, the Building Inspector serves the owner notice of at least 10 days to secure or remove the structure (§135-4), and if the owner fails to comply, a joint survey by Town- and owner-appointed surveyors leads to a Supreme Court application to declare the structure a public nuisance (§135-5). Costs the Town incurs, including repair or removal costs, are assessed against the land (§135-7), and §135-8 defines nine specific engineering and habitability conditions that render a structure 'unsafe or dangerous.'
chapters.ratingRationale: Aside from penalty-amount updates in 1987 and 2020, the chapter's operative procedure has not been substantively revised since its original 1968 adoption, and it still routes contested enforcement through a Supreme Court public-nuisance application (§135-5) rather than a faster administrative process. The penalty section (§135-9) also creates a confusing cross-reference, tying the 10-day compliance clock to 'the report specified in §135-6' (the surveyors' report/posting provision) rather than to the original owner notice in §135-4, which is internally inconsistent drafting.
strengths: Unsafe-condition definitions in §135-8B are unusually specific and quantifiable for a 1968-era code, including a plumb-line/center-of-gravity structural test (§135-8B(1)) and a 33%/50% deterioration threshold (§135-8B(2))
Provides a check on Town discretion by requiring an owner-appointed surveyor alongside the Town's inspector when an owner contests a finding (§135-5)
Clearly assigns enforcement responsibility to a single official, the Building Inspector (§135-1)
Cost-recovery mechanism exists in principle, assessing repair/removal costs against the land (§135-7)
concerns: No emergency provision allows the Building Inspector to order immediate vacating, securing, or demolition of an imminently dangerous structure; every case must proceed through the full notice-survey-court process in §135-4/§135-5
Contested cases require an application to the State Supreme Court, Ninth Judicial District (§135-5) — a slower, costlier route than the administrative hearing/order procedures many towns now use

The penalty provision in §135-9 cites noncompliance with 'the report specified in §135-6' as triggering the fine clock, which does not match §135-4's owner-notice provision — an internally confusing cross-reference
Section 135-7 states costs are 'assessed against the land' but does not specify the lien mechanism, interest, or the Town Law provision under which it is collected

The chapter's substantive process has not been revisited since 1968 apart from penalty amounts, and does not cross-reference how it interacts with the newer Property Maintenance chapter (Ch. 241) or Building Code Administration (Ch. 127) beyond a bare 'General References' listing

recommendations.suggestion: Add an emergency-order provision authorizing the Building Inspector to immediately vacate or secure a structure presenting imminent danger, bypassing the full survey/court process in §135-5 for true emergencies.

Correct the cross-reference in the penalty clause (§135-9), which currently ties the 10-day compliance period to the surveyors' report in §135-6 rather than to the owner notice actually issued under §135-4.

Replace or supplement the Supreme Court public-nuisance application in §135-5 with an administrative hearing process before the Town Board for uncontested or lower-risk cases, consistent with how many towns have modernized unsafe-structure enforcement.

Specify in §135-7 that Town costs assessed against the land are collected as a tax lien with statutory interest, citing the applicable NY Town Law section, to remove ambiguity about the collection mechanism.

chapters.peerComparison: Based on general professional knowledge of unsafe-structure enforcement practice among Westchester and similar NY towns, not a document-to-document comparison: most municipalities have since streamlined this process into an administrative Building Inspector order, followed by a local hearing (before the Town Board or a Board of Appeals) and, if necessary, town-performed abatement with costs recovered via tax lien — without requiring a Supreme Court public-nuisance adjudication as the primary enforcement path. North Castle's Chapter 135 retains its 1968-era reliance on the Supreme Court application in §135-5, making its unsafe-building procedure more cumbersome and slower than what is now typical, even though its underlying engineering definitions of 'unsafe' in §135-8 remain reasonably rigorous by comparison.

chapters.title: Cabarets, Adult Entertainment and E-Cigarette
chapters.summary: Chapter 140 regulates three distinct categories of business: cabarets (Article I, licensing scheme with fingerprinting, public hearings, security and conduct rules), adult entertainment uses such as adult bookstores, adult motels and adult entertainment cabarets (Article II, permit-based siting with buffer distances and a now-lapsed capital-investment amortization schedule for nonconforming uses), and retail sale of e-cigarettes/nicotine delivery products (Article III, added in 2019, permit-based siting, security/surveillance requirements and restricted hours). Each article carries its own definitions, permit/license process and penalty scheme rather than a unified chapter-wide framework.
chapters.ratingRationale: Article III (e-cigarette sales), the chapter's newest and ostensibly most current piece, was added 2-13-2019 by L.L. No. 1-2019 yet contains no age-verification or minimum-purchase-age provision at all, despite New York raising the tobacco/vapor purchase age to 21 later that same year and banning most flavored vapor products in 2020 (Public Health Law Article 13-F) — neither is reflected in §140-37 through §140-40. Article II's amortization schedule in §140-34 lists termination dates of June 1993 through June 1997, meaning that entire provision has been legally spent and inert for roughly three decades yet still occupies the chapter. The chapter also runs two materially different penalty regimes for closely related conduct: §140-30 (Article I, cabarets) allows fines up to $1,000/day and up to 15 days' imprisonment, while §140-35 (Article II, adult entertainment) uses an escalating tiered fine schedule ($350/$700/$1,000) plus up to six months' imprisonment.
strengths: Cabaret licensing (Article I) includes a modern fingerprint/background-check pipeline routed through the North Castle Police Department to NYS DCJS (§140-4C), plus detailed public notice and hearing procedures last updated in 2015 (§140-5)

Adult entertainment and e-cigarette siting rules both use concrete, enforceable buffer distances from sensitive uses like schools, day-care centers, houses of worship and treatment facilities (§140-33D-F; §140-38C-E)

Both Article II and Article III open with detailed legislative findings tying restrictions to documented secondary effects, which supports First Amendment/constitutional defensibility of the siting scheme
E-cigarette retailers are subject to concrete modern security requirements — intrusion alarms and 24/7 recorded video surveillance retained 30 days (§140-39)

Cabaret rules address concrete operational safety details such as maximum occupancy tied to the NYS Uniform Fire Prevention and Building Code (§140-25) and mandatory licensed security staffing ratios (§140-26)
concerns: Article III (e-cigarette sales) has no minimum purchase age or ID-check requirement anywhere in §140-36 through §140-40, an odd omission for a chapter whose stated purpose is protecting adolescents from nicotine products
The Article II amortization schedule in §140-34 sets termination dates entirely in the past (1993-1997), so the provision is dead text that no longer does anything but remains codified

Inconsistent penalty structures across articles within the same chapter: §140-30 (cabarets, up to $1,000/day + 15 days) versus §140-35 (adult entertainment, tiered $350-$1,000 + up to 6 months) versus §140-40 (e-cigarettes, flat $500-$1,000 range)

§140-38G imposes a flat 7:00 p.m.-to-9:00 a.m. closure on e-cigarette retailers with no stated findings or rationale tying that specific window to any documented impact, which is more vulnerable to an arbitrary-and-capricious challenge than the buffer-distance provisions

No cross-reference in Article III to NYS Tax Law Article 20 registration requirements for tobacco/vapor retail dealers, nor to the 2020 flavored-vapor-product restrictions under Public Health Law Article 13-F

The chapter has no provision addressing adult-use cannabis dispensaries or on-site consumption lounges, which became a live siting question for towns after the 2021 MRTA legalized adult-use cannabis in New York

recommendations.suggestion: Add an explicit minimum-age/ID-verification requirement to Article III (§§140-36 through 140-40) that tracks NYS Public Health Law's age-21 purchase restriction, since the current text regulates only where and when nicotine products can be sold, not to whom.
Repeal the spent amortization schedule at §140-34, whose termination dates (1993-1997) have all passed, to remove dead law that only confuses readers of the current code.

Reconcile the three different penalty schemes in §§140-30, 140-35 and 140-40 (flat per-day fine vs. tiered escalating fine vs. flat range) so enforcement officers and courts are applying a consistent framework across the chapter.

Revisit the blanket 7:00 p.m.-9:00 a.m. closure requirement for e-cigarette retailers in §140-38G — either add findings connecting the hours to a specific documented impact or reconsider the restriction, since it currently reads as an outlier compared to the buffer-distance approach used everywhere else in the chapter.

Cross-reference NYS Tax Law Article 20 retail dealer registration in Article III so Town enforcement can coordinate with the state registry rather than running a wholly separate permit system for the same retailers.

chapters.peerComparison: Based on general professional familiarity with Westchester County municipal codes rather than any document-to-document comparison: North Castle's cabaret and adult-entertainment provisions (buffer distances, definitions, secondary-effects findings) are fairly typical of licensing schemes many NY towns adopted in the 1990s-2000s and remain broadly consistent with the Renton line of land-use case law. The e-cigarette article, however, is noticeably behind current practice — many peer towns that touched their tobacco/vapor regulations after 2019-2020 layered in age-21 verification language and referenced the state's flavored-vapor-product restrictions, neither of which appears here despite Article III being the chapter's newest addition. The absence of any cannabis dispensary/consumption-lounge siting framework is also a gap relative to towns that updated their adult-use-adjacent land-use chapters after the 2021 MRTA, though that gap may simply reflect that North Castle addresses cannabis siting in a different chapter not reviewed here.

chapters.title: Dogs
chapters.summary: Chapter 146, the 'Dog Control Law,' requires all dogs to be licensed by four months of age with proof of rabies vaccination, sets differentiated license fees for spayed/neutered versus intact dogs, waives fees for service dogs and senior owners, and bans dogs from being 'at large' outside the Town's dog park (§§146-4, 146-6). It defines and prohibits nuisance behavior such as habitual barking, property damage, and chasing people or vehicles (§146-7), and, following the 11-20-2024 amendment, adds a detailed rules-and-regulations section for the North Castle Dog Park covering hours, leashing, aggressive dogs, and per-owner dog limits (§146-9).
chapters.ratingRationale: The chapter is current — it was substantively updated as recently as 11-20-2024 to add the dog-at-large exception and a full dog-park rules section (§146-9) — and its licensing/fee structure is specific and internally consistent (e.g., senior and service-dog fee waivers in §146-4C(6)-(7), precise 'habitual barking' timing thresholds of 20/45 minutes in §146-7A).
