It loses points because the general penalty section (§146-8), last amended in 2020, predates the 2024 addition of §146-9 and does not clearly state that dog-park rule violations are punishable offenses.
strengths: Recently modernized: the dog park exception to the at-large ban and the full dog-park rules section were added by the 11-20-2024 amendment (§§146-6A, 146-9)
Specific, objective nuisance-barking standard (20 minutes continual or 45 minutes intermittent) in §146-7A avoids vague 'excessive noise' language
Equity-minded fee structure: fee waivers for service dogs (§146-4C(6)) and seniors 65+ (§146-4C(8))
Clear chain of custody for at-large dogs, including a 5-day redemption window before forfeiture/adoption or euthanasia (§146-6B)
Detailed, practical dog park operating rules (hours, adult supervision age 18+, three-dog-per-owner limit, size segregation) in §146-9
concerns: §146-8 (Penalties for offenses), last amended 4-29-2020, predates the 2024 addition of the dog park rules in §146-9 and does not explicitly reference §146-9, leaving the enforceability/penalty basis for dog park rule violations ambiguous

No local 'dangerous dog' or 'vicious dog' declaration/hearing procedure is included, relying entirely on the general reference to NYS Agriculture and Markets Law Article 7 in §146-2, unlike many peer towns that add a supplemental local process
The dog park rules in §146-9 use non-binding phrasing ('should,' 'be cautious') for some items (e.g., 'Be cautious with dog toys'), which is difficult to enforce as a violation
No maximum leash length or muzzle requirement is specified anywhere in the chapter despite detailed 'under restraint' and nuisance definitions

recommendations.suggestion: Amend §146-8 to explicitly cross-reference §146-9 so that dog park rule violations have a clear, unambiguous penalty basis rather than relying on inference from a section adopted four years after the general penalty provision.

Add a local dangerous/vicious dog designation and hearing procedure to supplement the general reference to NYS Agriculture and Markets Law Article 7 in §146-2, giving the Animal Control Authority defined local tools for escalating cases.
Convert advisory language in the dog park rules (e.g., 'Be cautious with dog toys' in §146-9) into enforceable requirements or remove it, since ambiguous phrasing undermines consistent enforcement.

chapters.peerComparison: Based on general professional knowledge of Westchester/NY municipal practice rather than any document comparison: North Castle's licensing, fee-waiver, and at-large/nuisance framework tracks standard NY Agriculture and Markets Law requirements closely and is typical of Westchester towns. The 2024 addition of a dedicated, detailed dog park rules section is a relatively modern feature many peer towns have only added in the last several years as municipal dog parks became more common. Where the chapter is thinner than some peer codes is on locally defined dangerous/vicious dog procedures — many nearby municipalities layer a local hearing and restriction process on top of the state Article 7 framework, which North Castle has not done here.

chapters.title: Electrical Installations
chapters.summary: Chapter 152 gives the Building Inspector authority to issue electrical permits to licensed contractors and to deputize electrical inspectors for individual jobs (§152-1, §152-2), and lets the Building or Fire Department disconnect current found dangerous to life or property (§152-3). Permits are required for essentially all wiring, device, or equipment work except lamp/fuse replacement or portable-device connections (§152-4), must be posted on-site (§152-5), and are issued only to registered, licensed electrical contractors (§152-7). Completed and concealed work must be inspected and certified before connection or concealment (§152-8 through §152-11), with all installations required to conform to the National Electrical Code and National Electric Safety Code 'as amended from time to time' (§152-12), and penalties reach $1,000/day or 15 days' imprisonment (§152-14).
chapters.ratingRationale: The chapter's dynamic incorporation of the National Electrical Code and National Electric Safety Code 'as amended from time to time' (§152-12) is a forward-looking drafting choice that keeps technical standards current without requiring local amendment. However, the chapter contains no fee provision at all (unlike Chapter 202's explicit tie to the Master Fee Schedule), relies on ad hoc, uncompensated 'deputized' inspectors rather than a named inspection agency (§152-2), and its adoption HISTORY line states it was 'Adopted by the Town Board of the Town of New Castle' rather than North Castle, an apparent uncorrected drafting/transcription error.
strengths: Adopts the National Electrical Code and National Electric Safety Code 'as amended from time to time' (§152-12), automatically keeping technical standards current
Requires a certificate of approval before any connection to electric service, including after a disconnection or discontinuance order (§152-11)
Distinguishes temporary and preliminary certificates, both revocable at the Building Inspector's discretion, for phased or ongoing construction (§152-9)
Clear liability disclaimer preserving contractor/owner responsibility for defects despite Town inspection or certification (§152-13)
concerns: No fee section exists anywhere in the chapter; unlike Chapter 202 (§202-10), there is no cross-reference to the Master Fee Schedule for electrical permit fees
Inspections may be performed by an inspector the Building Inspector 'deputizes' ad hoc 'without compensation from the Town' (§152-2), rather than a named, credentialed third-party inspection agency
No stated permit validity period, expiration, or renewal process for open electrical permits

The chapter's own adoption HISTORY line reads 'Adopted by the Town Board of the Town of New Castle 4-14-2004,' apparently a drafting or transcription error given every other chapter attributes adoption to the Town of North Castle
Section 152-7 requires contractors to be 'registered' and hold 'an appropriate license' without specifying which licensing authority or registry governs that qualification

recommendations.suggestion: Add an explicit fee provision cross-referencing the Master Fee Schedule (Ch. A370) for electrical permits and inspections, mirroring the approach already used in Chapter 202 §202-10.
Replace the ad hoc 'deputized' volunteer inspector model in §152-2 with a requirement to use a specific, state-recognized third-party electrical inspection agency, ensuring consistent credentialing.
Correct the apparent 'Town of New Castle' error in the chapter's adoption HISTORY note to avoid any interpretive ambiguity about which municipality's Town Board adopted the law.
Clarify the contractor registration/licensing standard referenced in §152-7 and add a defined permit validity/expiration period so contractors know how long an issued permit remains active.

chapters.peerComparison: Based on general professional knowledge of electrical-permitting practice in Westchester County and similar NY municipalities, rather than a document-to-document comparison: most towns require electrical work to be inspected either by the Building Department's own licensed electrical inspector or by a specific, state-recognized third-party inspection agency, with permit fees set out in a master fee schedule that the local code cross-references. North Castle's Chapter 152 instead relies on an ad hoc 'deputized' inspector model (§152-2) and is silent on fees entirely, which is less structured than typical current practice, even though its choice to incorporate the National Electrical Code 'as amended from time to time' (§152-12) matches common and well-regarded regional practice.

chapters.title: Filling and Grading
chapters.summary: Chapter 161 (Article I, adopted 1999) regulates the delivery of fill onto land in North Castle, requiring landowners to obtain a Building Department permit, provide signed trucking manifests documenting fill origin and 6 NYCRR Part 360 compliance, and — for larger jobs — retain an independent engineer, soil scientist, or testing lab to certify compliance. It requires liability insurance, allows the Building Department to demand a surety bond or letter of credit for remediation, restricts delivery hours (7:30 a.m.-5:00 p.m., no Sundays or federal holidays), and sets out a lien-based cost-recovery and enforcement scheme, including a small-quantity exemption and six-month permit terms.
chapters.ratingRationale: The chapter is unusually thorough for a fill-and-grading law, tying compliance directly to state solid-waste regulation (6 NYCRR Part 360) and backing enforcement with a surety-bond and lien mechanism (§161-1D, §161-4E), which gives the Town real financial recourse against noncompliant fill. However, permits are valid for only six months and must be renewed 'as if the application was brought anew' (§161-8), which is a fairly short and administratively heavy cycle for phased construction projects, and the small-quantity exemption thresholds in §161-7 (50 cubic yards / 250 cubic yards) have not been revisited since the article's 1999 origin despite four later amendment cycles touching other sections.
strengths: Manifest-and-certification system ties directly to state solid waste rules under 6 NYCRR Part 360 (§161-1A(1),(3))
Surety bond/letter of credit requirement gives the Town a funded remedy to remediate contaminated fill and repair roadway damage (§161-1D)
Defined delivery-hour restriction (7:30 a.m.-5:00 p.m., no Sundays or federal holidays) directly protects neighborhood quality of life (§161-2)
Clear lien-based cost recovery scheme for Town-performed remediation when an owner fails to comply (§161-4E)
Small-quantity exemption avoids over-regulating minor, common construction deliveries (§161-7)
concerns: Permits run only six months with renewal treated as a brand-new application (§161-8), which can be an administrative burden for longer-duration or phased grading projects
The 50-cubic-yard and 250-cubic-yard exemption thresholds in §161-7 have not been adjusted since the article's 1999 adoption despite several later amendments to other sections
Delivery-hour restriction only exempts 'federal holidays,' not state or local observances, leaving some ambiguity
Testing/monitoring cost provisions (§161-1C) give the Building Department broad discretion without an explicit cap or standard for what is 'reasonable'

recommendations.suggestion: Replace the six-month, start-over permit renewal in §161-8 with a streamlined administrative extension process for active, in-compliance projects.
Revisit the 50/250-cubic-yard exemption thresholds in §161-7, which have not changed since 1999, to ensure they still appropriately balance minor deliveries against cumulative development impact.
Add a defined methodology or cap for 'reasonable' testing and monitoring cost assessments under §161-1C so applicants can better anticipate project costs.
Extend the delivery-hour holiday exemption in §161-2 beyond 'federal holidays' to include state-recognized and local observed holidays for consistency.

chapters.peerComparison: Based on general knowledge of Westchester County fill and grading local laws rather than any document-to-document comparison, North Castle's approach — manifest-based tracking, mandatory 6 NYCRR Part 360 certification, and a surety-bond backstop for remediation — is fairly typical of, and in some respects more rigorous than, comparable local laws in similarly situated towns. The six-month permit renewal cycle is on the shorter/more restrictive end compared to some peer towns that issue annual or project-duration fill permits, and the unchanged 1999-era cubic-yard exemption thresholds are consistent with, rather than ahead of, typical regional practice.

chapters.title: Filming and Photography
chapters.summary: Chapter 165 requires a permit for most commercial, promotional, entertainment, public-service, or student filming and photography on public or private property in North Castle, with two tiers of review: a Town Clerk-issued permit for smaller productions (Section 165-3A) and a Town Board-issued permit for larger, longer, or off-hours productions (Section 165-3B). It requires insurance and indemnification naming the Town, adjacent-property-owner notice, and caps recurring filming at a location to 12 days per 12-month period, with escalating enforcement including permit forfeiture and an 18-month debarment for repeat violators.
chapters.ratingRationale: The chapter uses concrete, objective thresholds (cast/crew size, hours, duration) to route applications to either the Town Clerk (Section 165-3A) or the Town Board (Section 165-3B), which is a more sophisticated tiered-review structure than many small-town filming ordinances use. It also bakes in resident-protective mechanics rare in bare-bones permit schemes: mandatory adjacent-property-owner notice at Sections 165-3A(5) and 165-4D, and a hard 18-month debarment for prior violators at Section 165-8.
strengths: Objective, size/duration-based tiering between administrative (Town Clerk) and legislative (Town Board) review at Section 165-3A and 165-3B
Required notification of contiguous/adjacent property owners at Sections 165-3A(5) and 165-4D protects residential quality of life
Insurance and indemnification requirements naming the Town as additional insured, at Sections 165-3A(3) and 165-3B(4)
Clear carve-outs for casual/tourist photography and credentialed news media at Section 165-3C(1), avoiding overreach into ordinary personal or press activity
Meaningful deterrent structure: permit forfeiture for violations (Section 165-7C) plus an 18-month debarment on repeat offenders (Section 165-8)
concerns: The 12-cumulative-day-per-12-months cap on filming at a single location (Section 165-6A) has no defined administrative renewal path short of a full Town Board resolution, which could burden recurring or episodic productions
No provision addresses drone/UAV-based filming, a medium that has become common since the chapter's last full rewrite in 2015
Fee amounts are not stated in the chapter itself and are entirely deferred to the Master Fee Schedule (Sections 165-4B and 165-5)
No specific standard or minimum lead time is set for the adjacent-property-owner notice required by Section 165-4D, leaving 'notify' undefined in practice

Categories of filming in Section 165-2 (commercial/promotional/entertainment/public service/student) do not clearly address independent social-media or influencer content creation, an increasingly common activity

recommendations.suggestion: Add an administrative renewal path for productions that would otherwise hit the 12-day/12-month cap in Section 165-6A, rather than requiring a full Town Board resolution each time.
Add explicit drone/UAV filming standards (FAA coordination, altitude and privacy limits) since Chapter 165 is currently silent on this now-common filming medium.
Specify a minimum advance-notice period for the adjacent-property-owner notification required at Section 165-4D, which is currently open-ended.
Publish indicative permit fee tiers alongside the Section 165-4B and 165-5 cross-references to the Master Fee Schedule for applicant transparency.

chapters.peerComparison: Based on general professional knowledge of Westchester/NY commercial-filming permit practice rather than a document-to-document comparison, North Castle's Chapter 165 is above average in structure: the tiered Town Clerk/Town Board thresholds, mandatory insurance naming the municipality as additional insured, and required neighbor notice all match or exceed the norms seen in comparable Westchester filming ordinances, many of which rely on a single undifferentiated permit process. Where it lags current practice is on production formats that have grown common since the 2015 rewrite - most notably the absence of any drone/UAV-specific standard, an area a number of municipalities have since added given the FAA's expanded commercial drone rules and resident privacy concerns.

chapters.title: Fire Prevention
chapters.summary: As provided, Chapter 169 consists of Article I, Key Boxes, which requires certain buildings and gated driveways to install a lockbox ('key box') that gives first responders emergency access. It covers findings, definitions of 'emergency service provider' and 'key box,' the buildings and driveways subject to the requirement (new commercial and multifamily buildings, gated commercial and residential driveways, and existing commercial buildings that generate three false alarms), an exception for buildings with round-the-clock security, and a clause making the article's requirements prevail over conflicting Code or Town Law provisions. No other fire-prevention topics (e.g., open burning, brush burning, fire lanes) appear in the reviewed text.
chapters.ratingRationale: The article is well-organized and was substantively updated as recently as 2020 (§169-3, amended by L.L. No. 3-2020), with a clear, objective trigger — three false alarms under the same ownership — for requiring retrofits on existing commercial buildings (§169-3B), a sensible 24-hour-security exception (§169-4), and a precedence clause resolving conflicts with other Code or Town Law provisions (§169-5).
strengths: Existing-building retrofit trigger is an objective, auditable standard — three false alarms while under the same owner's control (§169-3B) — rather than a vague discretionary standard
24-hour-security exception (§169-4) sensibly avoids requiring a key box where a building already has an equivalent access solution
§169-5's precedence clause explicitly resolves conflicts with other Code or state Town Law provisions, reducing the risk of contradictory interpretation
Requirement is tiered by building type/risk (mandatory for new commercial/multifamily and gated driveways, optional for one- and two-family homes), reflecting a proportionate approach (§169-3D)
concerns: No specific key box brand or technical standard (e.g., a Knox-Box-type standard) is named in §169-3; it only requires a type 'approved by the Building Department,' which could allow inconsistent equipment across the Town over time
'Gated communities' is used in §169-3C without further definition, leaving scope (e.g., HOA-private streets vs. Town-maintained roads) unclear
The reviewed text contains no penalty provision specific to this chapter, so it is unclear from Chapter 169 alone what enforcement mechanism or fine applies to noncompliance

The chapter as provided contains only the Key Boxes article; if 'Fire Prevention' as a whole omits brush/open-burning and fire-lane-obstruction provisions from the local code (leaving them solely to state Uniform Fire Code adoption), that gap is worth confirming against the full Code.

recommendations.suggestion: Specify an approved key box make/standard in §169-3 so that all emergency service providers in Town can rely on a single compatible master-key system rather than a Building Department case-by-case approval.
Add an explicit penalty or enforcement cross-reference within Chapter 169 itself, since the reviewed text relies on outside enforcement (e.g., Ch. 5 appearance tickets) without stating so.
Define 'gated communities' and the verification process for the three-false-alarm trigger in §169-3B/C to reduce disputes between fire chiefs and property owners over when the mandate is triggered.

chapters.peerComparison: Based on general professional knowledge of Westchester fire-prevention codes rather than a document-to-document comparison, a local key-box (commonly 'Knox-Box') ordinance like North Castle's Article I is standard practice among comparable towns, and the three-false-alarm retrofit trigger and 24-hour-security exception used here are consistent with typical peer-town thresholds. Many neighboring municipalities' fire-prevention chapters also include separate articles on brush and open burning permits and fire-lane/obstruction enforcement — those topics do not appear in the Chapter 169 text reviewed here, so it cannot be confirmed whether North Castle addresses them elsewhere in its Code or relies on the state Uniform Fire Prevention and Building Code by reference.

chapters.title: Fireworks
chapters.summary: Chapter 173 regulates the storage and public display of fireworks in North Castle, requiring a permit from the Fire Prevention Officer (the 'permitting authority') for any fireworks storage or display and banning indoor displays entirely (§173-3). It sets detailed application requirements including operator certifications, a 30-day advance filing deadline, and a minimum $1,000,000 bond or equivalent insurance (§173-4). It also imposes on-site safety measures such as minimum viewing distances, fire extinguishers, a 200-foot no-smoking zone around stored materials, and civil/criminal penalties for violations (§§173-5, 173-7, 173-8).
chapters.ratingRationale: The permit and safety framework for professional pyrotechnic displays is detailed and internally consistent (30-day filing and $1,000,000 bond requirement in §173-4, vertical-discharge and 200-foot no-smoking rules in §173-7), and enforcement authority was clarified in the 4-29-2020 amendment to §173-8. However, the chapter addresses only professional public displays and never mentions consumer sparklers or 'novelty' devices that NYS General Business Law has permitted municipalities to allow/regulate since 2015 — the same year this chapter was last substantively adopted — leaving that increasingly common local question unaddressed.
strengths: Detailed, document-driven permit application (§173-4A) requiring DOT hazmat, ATF explosives, and NYS Labor Department certifications before any display is approved
Firm financial-responsibility backstop: a minimum $1,000,000 bond or equivalent indemnity insurance naming the Town as additional insured (§173-4B)
Concrete on-site safety mandates — vertical-discharge requirement, two on-duty operators, two fire extinguishers, and a 200-foot no-smoking perimeter (§173-7)
Explicit non-transferability of permits with automatic revocation on attempted transfer (§173-3D)
2020 amendment (§173-8) clearly assigned civil-penalty enforcement to the Building Inspector alongside other authorized agencies
concerns: No provision addresses consumer sparklers or 'novelty' devices, which NYS General Business Law has allowed localities to permit/regulate since 2015 — the chapter is silent on retail sale, possession, or use of these lower-risk items

§173-6 (revocation) describes no appeal process for a sponsor whose permit is denied or revoked, unlike Chapter 263's special-event chapter which expressly notes permit decisions are 'subject to review by provisions of law' (§263-6)
The two-family/multiunit dwelling ban in §173-3B is not clearly linked to zoning district definitions used elsewhere in the Code, risking inconsistent application
No maximum or minimum distance figures are specified for the 'minimum safe viewing distance' in §173-5, leaving a purely case-by-case, potentially inconsistent standard

recommendations.suggestion: Add a subsection addressing sale, possession, and use of NYS-legal sparklers/novelty devices (per GBL and Penal Law §270), since §173-1 acknowledges the 2015 Penal Law change but the operative sections only regulate professional displays.
Add an explicit appeal procedure to §173-6 for permit denial or revocation, comparable to the judicial-review language in Chapter 263 §263-6, to reduce due-process exposure.
Establish objective minimum viewing-distance benchmarks (e.g., by shell size/class) in §173-5 rather than leaving the standard entirely to case-by-case approval, to speed review and reduce disputes.

chapters.peerComparison: Based on general professional knowledge of Westchester/NY municipal practice rather than any document comparison: North Castle's fireworks chapter is a fairly typical 2015-era 'display permit' ordinance (bond/insurance, certified-operator, and Fire Marshal-consultation requirements) that mirrors the state General Business Law/Penal Law framework for professional displays. Where it diverges from an increasing number of peer Westchester towns is in not separately addressing the sparkler/novelty-device carve-out that NYS law created around the same time — many municipalities have since added specific hours-of-use, age, or retail provisions for those items, which this chapter omits entirely.

chapters.title: Flood Damage Prevention
chapters.summary: This chapter implements the Town's participation in the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) by regulating all development within FEMA-designated areas of special flood hazard. It establishes a floodplain development permit process administered by the Building Inspector as 'local administrator' (§ 177-11, § 177-12), sets elevation and floodproofing standards for residential, nonresidential, manufactured-home, and accessory structures requiring the lowest floor to sit at least two feet above base flood elevation (§ 177-17, § 177-18, § 177-19, § 177-20), and bars new critical facilities from special flood hazard areas and 500-year flood zones (§ 177-21). A Zoning Board of Appeals variance procedure (Article VI) and enforcement/penalty provisions (§ 177-9) round out the chapter, which was readopted in its entirety in 2022 to conform to the current FEMA/NYSDEC model local law.
chapters.ratingRationale: The Town readopted this chapter in its entirety on 10-12-2022 (L.L. No. 9-2022), aligning it with the modern FEMA/NYSDEC model floodplain law, and it requires two feet of freeboard above base flood elevation for both residential and nonresidential structures (§ 177-17A(1), § 177-18A(1)) — exceeding the NFIP statutory minimum of bare BFE compliance. It also bars new critical facilities from flood hazard areas (§ 177-21) and includes compensatory storage/encroachment analysis requirements (§ 177-15B(4)), all hallmarks of a well-drafted, current ordinance. The main drag on the rating is a stale, low-dollar penalty clause and an escrow cap that may not reflect real review costs.
strengths: Requires 2 feet of freeboard above base flood elevation for both residential and nonresidential lowest floors (§ 177-17A(1), § 177-18A(1)), exceeding bare NFIP minimums
Prohibits siting new critical facilities in special flood hazard areas or 500-year (shaded X/B zone) floodplains (§ 177-21)
Requires compensatory (balanced) excavation for any fill placed below base flood elevation, not just anchoring (§ 177-15B(4))
Comprehensive, FEMA-model-consistent Article II definitions covering manufactured homes, substantial damage/improvement, and cumulative substantial improvement (§ 177-4)
Was readopted in its entirety in 2022, incorporating a 2022 Letter of Map Revision for FIRM panel 36119C0276F (§ 177-6A(3))
concerns: Underlying Flood Insurance Study and most FIRM panels still carry a September 28, 2007 effective date (§ 177-6A(1)-(2)); only one panel has a 2022 LOMR update, so most of the community's mapped flood risk is based on 19-year-old hydrology
Maximum penalty is capped at a $250 fine or 15 days imprisonment per offense (§ 177-9), a low deterrent by current standards for repeat or willful noncompliance
The local administrator's cost-recovery escrow for permit review is capped at $500 (§ 177-12B), which may not cover engineering/FEMA review costs on complex applications
No explicit sea-level-rise, climate-resilience, or supplemental freeboard provision beyond the standard 2-foot NFIP-plus freeboard, despite increasing peer-town adoption of such measures

Chapter still incorporates NFIP revisions only 'through October 27, 1997' by its own text (§ 177-7), an internal cross-reference that reads as stale even though the chapter itself was substantively updated in 2022

recommendations.suggestion: Increase the § 177-9 penalty ceiling (currently $250/15 days per offense) to a level with real deterrent value and consistent with other Town Code enforcement chapters, since underenforcement of floodplain violations can jeopardize the Town's NFIP participation.
Reassess the $500 escrow cap in § 177-12B against actual engineering/FEMA review costs for complex encroachment or LOMR applications, so the Town isn't subsidizing developer-driven technical review.

Given most FIRM panels still date to 2007 (§ 177-6A(1)), the Town should track FEMA's Westchester County remapping schedule and consider adding a supplemental climate-resilience freeboard standard for critical or high-occupancy structures beyond the current 2-foot minimum in § 177-17/§ 177-18.

Clean up the outdated internal reference in § 177-7 stating the chapter incorporates NFIP revisions only 'through October 27, 1997,' which is inconsistent with the chapter's 2022 wholesale readoption and could confuse both staff and the public reviewing the code online.

chapters.peerComparison: Based on general professional knowledge of Westchester County and NY floodplain ordinances rather than a document-to-document comparison: this chapter's structure, definitions, and Article-by-Article organization track very closely with the FEMA Region II / NYSDEC model local floodplain management law that most Westchester towns (e.g., Bedford, Mount Kisco, New Castle) adopted or readopted around 2021-2022 after DEC guidance updates. The two-foot freeboard requirement is now fairly common among updated Westchester ordinances and exceeds the bare NFIP minimum (BFE only), putting North Castle in the more protective tier rather than merely minimum-compliant. Referencing a September 28, 2007 FIS/FIRM effective date is typical for Westchester municipalities, since FEMA has not completed a countywide remap for many of these communities — so this is less a North Castle-specific deficiency and more a shared regional condition, though it is still worth monitoring given 19 years of watershed and climate change since that study. The low $250 penalty ceiling is somewhat below what some peer towns have moved to in recent updates, and the absence of any explicit climate-adaptation or sea-level-rise freeboard add-on (which a handful of more progressive Hudson Valley municipalities have begun incorporating) is a modest area where North Castle could differentiate itself further.

recordEvidence.note: Amended September 14 and October 12, 2022 expressly to comply with the National Flood Insurance Program's floodplain management requirements — an externally compelled update; this chapter's currency is maintained by federal condition rather than local initiative.

chapters.title: Games of Chance
chapters.summary: Chapter 186, the town's 'Games of Chance Licensing Ordinance,' authorizes charitable, educational, scientific, health, religious, and patriotic organizations to raise funds through licensed games of chance, adopted pursuant to Article 9-A of the General Municipal Law (§§ 185 through 195-k). Rather than setting independent local standards, the chapter incorporates the state statute by reference for regulation and supervision (§ 186-3), conduct restrictions (§ 186-4), and licensing procedure (§ 186-5), with a locally-added provision in § 186-6 permitting Sunday games between noon and midnight. Section 186-7 sweeps in the remainder of GML §§ 191-195-k for any additional rules.
chapters.ratingRationale: Section 186-3 designates the 'New York State Racing and Wagering Board' as the governing regulatory body, but that agency was abolished and folded into the New York State Gaming Commission by state legislation in 2012 — meaning this chapter has referenced a defunct agency for over a decade. Combined with the fact that the chapter's substantive text has not been amended since 1996 (the Sunday-hours addition), this is a clear stale-reference problem in an otherwise simply-drafted, reference-heavy chapter.
strengths: Efficiently incorporates NY General Municipal Law Article 9-A (§§ 185-195-k) by reference in § 186-2, avoiding duplicative or conflicting local drafting
Clearly limits the licensing purpose to bona fide charitable, educational, scientific, health, religious, and patriotic causes (§ 186-1), matching the state's public-interest rationale
Section 186-6's Sunday-hours provision is specific and unambiguous (noon to midnight, only if included in the license)
concerns: Section 186-3 names the 'New York State Racing and Wagering Board' as the supervising authority, an agency abolished and merged into the New York State Gaming Commission in 2012 — a stale, factually incorrect reference that has gone uncorrected for well over a decade

The chapter has not been substantively amended since 1996 (nearly 30 years), despite significant subsequent changes in state gaming law (commercial casino gaming, sports wagering) that could warrant a local review even if incorporation-by-reference technically still functions
Section 186-6 contains lettered subitems (A. through E.) with no visible text, suggesting either an incomplete codification or a formatting artifact that should be cleaned up in the official code

The chapter never explicitly designates which town official or body (e.g., Town Clerk vs. Town Board) serves as the 'licensing authority' referenced in § 186-6, leaving that role to be inferred entirely from the incorporated state statute

recommendations.suggestion: Correct § 186-3 to reference the New York State Gaming Commission rather than the defunct Racing and Wagering Board, which was abolished by state legislation in 2012.

Add a clarifying provision naming the specific town official or board that functions as the 'licensing authority' under § 186-6, rather than leaving that role implicit in the incorporated GML sections.

Conduct a review of the incorporation-by-reference sections (§§ 186-2, 186-4, 186-5, 186-7) against the current numbering and text of GML Article 9-A, since state statutes are periodically renumbered and the chapter has not been revisited since 1996.

chapters.peerComparison: Based on general professional knowledge rather than document-to-document comparison, most Westchester towns adopted nearly identical 'Games of Chance Licensing Ordinances' in the 1970s under GML Article 9-A, and the incorporation-by-reference structure North Castle uses is standard practice statewide. However, the reference to the defunct Racing and Wagering Board is a common legacy defect across many older municipal codes that have not been swept for post-2012 agency-name updates, and North Castle's chapter appears to be a typical example of that unaddressed drift rather than an outlier.

chapters.title: Landmarks Preservation
chapters.summary: Chapter 195 establishes the Town's nine-member Landmarks Preservation Committee (LPC), empowered to designate individual landmarks and historic districts and to review exterior alterations, demolition, and new construction affecting them through a certificate-of-appropriateness process. It sets out the designation procedure (LPC investigation and report, Town Board public hearing and decision), certificate-of-appropriateness criteria and application steps, a hardship/economic-return variance mechanism for denied demolition or alteration applications, an anti-demolition-by-neglect maintenance obligation, and an appeals path to the Town Board.
chapters.ratingRationale: The chapter has been actively maintained, with substantive amendments in 2015 (L.L. Nos. 2-2015 and 9-2015), 2020 (L.L. No. 3-2020), and as recently as January 2024 (L.L. No. 1-2024, updating the meeting-notice requirements in §195-4B), and it includes a real anti-demolition-by-neglect provision (§195-24B) plus a standard, case-law-grounded hardship test (§195-22B: property "incapable of earning a reasonable return"). It falls short of "excellent" because it contains no reference to coordinating landmark designation with state/federal historic tax credit programs or a local property-tax incentive, an omission common in older ordinances of this type.
strengths: Recently amended notice/meeting provisions (§195-4B, amended 1-24-2024) show the chapter is still being actively updated, not left to go stale.

Anti-demolition-by-neglect clause (§195-24B) with specific examples of prohibited deterioration (exterior walls, roofs, chimneys, stucco/mortar, waterproofing) gives real teeth against owners who might otherwise let a landmark decay to justify demolition.

Hardship exception (§195-22) requires proof the property cannot earn a reasonable return and that good-faith efforts to sell for preservation have failed — the classic, court-tested formulation rather than a vaguer standard.
LPC composition requirement (at least one architect, civil engineer, historian, and realtor, §195-3) builds relevant expertise directly into the reviewing body.
Clear, bounded timelines throughout (60-day hearing, 45-day designation decision, 60-day certificate review, 30-day appeal window) reduce uncertainty for applicants.
concerns: No mention of coordinating landmark designation with the New York State/National Register nomination process or state/federal historic rehabilitation tax credits, despite the LPC's power to recommend funding sources (§195-4A(8)).

No fee schedule referenced for certificate-of-appropriateness or designation applications (unlike Chapter 308's explicit Master Fee Schedule cross-references), leaving cost recovery for LPC review unclear.

The chapter does not require a publicly accessible register or map of currently designated landmarks and districts, relying instead on an internal "current list" the Building Inspector must consult (§195-18B(2)).
Certificates of appropriateness expire after 24 months (§195-18C(4)) with no explicit renewal or extension procedure if a project is delayed past that window.

recommendations.suggestion: Add explicit coordination language directing the LPC to advise designated owners on available NYS/federal historic rehabilitation tax credits and any local tax abatement, building on the funding-recommendation power already in §195-4A(8).

Require the Town to publish and maintain a public online list/map of designated landmarks and historic districts rather than relying solely on the Building Inspector's internal list referenced in §195-18B(2).

Add a defined renewal or extension process for certificates of appropriateness nearing their 24-month expiration (§195-18C(4)) to avoid forcing re-application for projects with routine permitting delays.

Publish a fee schedule for certificate-of-appropriateness and designation-related applications, mirroring the Master Fee Schedule cross-references used elsewhere in the Town Code (e.g., Chapter 308), so applicants have upfront cost certainty.

chapters.peerComparison: Drawing on general knowledge of Westchester and downstate NY municipal practice rather than a document comparison, North Castle's designation and certificate-of-appropriateness process (LPC investigation, Town Board hearing and designation, then LPC-issued certificates of appropriateness) tracks the standard structure used by many Westchester towns and villages with local landmarks laws. Where North Castle's chapter is comparatively thin is on tax-incentive coordination: peer communities with more mature preservation programs and National Register historic districts more explicitly tie local designation to the New York State/National Park Service historic rehabilitation tax credit and, in some cases, a local partial tax abatement, which encourages owners to pursue and maintain designation rather than experience it purely as a regulatory burden.

recordEvidence.note: §195-4 (Powers and duties) was the subject of a public hearing on January 24 and 25, 2024. Spoken citation only — no criticism retained.

chapters.title: Markets
chapters.summary: Chapter 202 regulates 'merchandise or public markets,' commonly known as farmers' markets, along with outdoor auctions and hawking/peddling. It requires a Town Board-issued license, insurance and a $10,000 surety bond (§202-8), and imposes detailed operating conditions covering hours, parking, sanitation, rubbish removal, noise, and supervision by a designated market manager (§202-9). Markets are restricted to nonresidential properties or districts (§202-6), and the Town Board retains authority to waive requirements (§202-11) or revoke a license after a public hearing for nuisance or noncompliance (§202-13).
chapters.ratingRationale: The chapter was substantively modernized by L.L. No. 9-2015 (adding the market manager requirement, license application details, and revocation procedure) and penalties were updated in 2020, giving it reasonably current enforcement teeth. However, several operating conditions are stale or oddly rigid, such as the flat prohibition on any sales-area lighting (§202-9B) and a $10,000 bond amount fixed since 1983 (§202-8) with no inflation adjustment mechanism.
strengths: Clear, itemized license application requirements including a required market manager name and mobile number (§202-7)
Detailed day-to-day operating conditions covering sanitation, rubbish deadlines, parking, and noise (§202-9)
Fee-setting is delegated to the Master Fee Schedule (§202-10) rather than hard-coded, allowing administrative updates
Explicit license revocation process tied to a public hearing (§202-13) protects due process while giving the Town real enforcement leverage
concerns: The $10,000 surety bond amount (§202-8) has not been adjusted since 1983 and is not indexed to inflation or market scale
The blanket ban on 'any lighting of the sales area' (§202-9B) is unusually restrictive and dated, potentially conflicting with markets that run into early evening
The 5:00 p.m. sales cutoff / 9:30 p.m. work-stoppage rule (§202-9A) is rigid and delegates day/frequency decisions to the Town Board without stated criteria
No mention of modern farmers'-market features such as SNAP/EBT acceptance, food-truck-specific rules, or cottage food law interplay

recommendations.suggestion: Index the $10,000 surety bond requirement in §202-8 to inflation or scale it to market size/duration so it keeps pace with actual risk exposure decades after its 1983 setting.
Revisit the fixed 5:00 p.m. sales cutoff in §202-9A to allow seasonal evening markets (a growing regional trend), rather than requiring case-by-case Town Board discretion for hours.
Reconsider the categorical lighting ban in §202-9B; permit limited, shielded task lighting for safety during shoulder-season markets instead of a blanket prohibition.

Add stated criteria (e.g., traffic capacity, prior compliance history) the Town Board must weigh under §202-9A when setting permitted market days, to make licensing decisions more predictable for applicants.

chapters.peerComparison: Based on general professional knowledge of Westchester County practice rather than a document-to-document comparison: many peer towns handle farmers'/public markets through an administrative permit issued by the Building Department or Town Clerk with a simpler application, whereas North Castle routes every license through a full Town Board sworn-statement application (§202-7) and reserves revocation to a Town Board public hearing (§202-13) — a more governance-heavy model than typical. The chapter's coordination requirements with the County Board of Health for food concessions (§202-9F) and sanitary facilities (§202-9E) are consistent with standard regional practice.

chapters.title: Noise
chapters.summary: Chapter 210, the 'Town of North Castle Noise Control Law,' prohibits 'loud, unnecessary or unusual noise' that disturbs the peace or safety of others (§210-4), then enumerates specific violations without limiting that general standard: vehicle horns, sound equipment audible at night, commercial sound advertising, yelling in public, excessive animal noise, unmuffled engine exhaust, lawn/garden equipment and construction work outside set hours, unresolved alarms, and noisy container/material handling and tire-squealing (§210-5). Enforcement rests with the Police Department (§210-6), penalties reach $1,000/day or 15 days' imprisonment with a juvenile-violator provision (§210-7), and Highway Department vehicles and fuel-delivery trucks are exempt (§210-8).
chapters.ratingRationale: The chapter's core prohibition in §210-4 and most of its enumerated violations in §210-5 rely entirely on subjective standards ('unnecessary,' 'annoys, disturbs,' 'unreasonably annoying') rather than an objective, measurable decibel (dBA) limit. The only quasi-objective test in the entire chapter is the 50-foot 'distinctly audible' threshold for sound equipment in §210-5B, and even the animal-noise provision (§210-5D) relies on a duration-based audibility test rather than a sound-level measurement, making enforcement more vulnerable to subjective dispute and legal challenge than a decibel-based ordinance would be.
strengths: Specific, enumerated time windows for noisy activities, e.g., lawn equipment (8:00 p.m.-7:30 a.m. weekdays, §210-5G) and construction work (7:00 p.m.-7:30 a.m. weekdays, §210-5H)
Includes a bright-line 50-foot distance/audibility test for sound equipment at night as prima facie evidence of violation (§210-5B)
Addresses modern nuisance sources such as unresolved vehicle/home alarms (§210-5I) and tire-squealing (§210-5K)
Explicit First Amendment savings clause (§210-3) and carve-outs for Highway Department equipment and fuel trucks (§210-8) reduce overbreadth litigation risk
Distinct juvenile-violator classification for offenders under 16 (§210-7)
concerns: No objective decibel (dBA) standard exists anywhere in the chapter; the general prohibition in §210-4 and most of §210-5 depend on subjective terms like 'unnecessary,' 'unusual,' or 'annoys'
The enumerated list in §210-5 is expressly stated to be 'not exclusive,' which combined with the subjective general standard in §210-4 increases vagueness/void-for-vagueness litigation exposure
The animal-noise threshold (continuously audible 20 minutes or intermittently audible 45 minutes, §210-5D) is difficult for a complainant or officer to document evidentiarily in real time
No provision allows property owners to obtain a permit or variance for construction outside the hours fixed in §210-5H (e.g., for emergency repairs)
Enforcement is limited to the Police Department or its designated agent (§210-6), with no code-enforcement-officer alternative

recommendations.suggestion: Add an objective decibel (dBA) limit measured at the property line to supplement the subjective 'loud, unnecessary or unusual noise' standard in §210-4, reducing vagueness challenges and giving officers a defensible enforcement tool.
Create a limited emergency/permit exception to the construction-hours restriction in §210-5H so utility or structural emergency repairs are not automatically noncompliant.
Authorize designated code enforcement officers, not just Police, to enforce the chapter under §210-6, easing the burden on patrol staffing for routine daytime noise complaints.
Replace the duration-based animal-noise test in §210-5D with clearer, more objectively documentable criteria (e.g., a log/affidavit requirement) to make enforcement more consistent.

chapters.peerComparison: Based on general professional knowledge of noise-ordinance practice in Westchester and similar NY municipalities, rather than any document-to-document comparison: many peer towns have moved toward pairing a subjective nuisance standard with an objective decibel-based limit (commonly 60-65 dBA daytime / lower at night, measured at the receiving property line) precisely because purely subjective 'plainly audible' or 'unreasonable annoyance' language is harder to enforce and more susceptible to challenge. North Castle's Chapter 210 uses the more traditional subjective/distance-based model (its main objective element being the 50-foot audibility test in §210-5B) without a companion decibel standard, which places it behind the curve relative to towns that have modernized their noise codes with sound-level-meter enforcement.

recordEvidence.verdict: Noted as split across two provisions
recordEvidence.note: A Planning Board speaker (July 11, 2022) observed the subject is split across two places in the code: “We have chapter 210 noise, which is your general [standard]” — distinct from the zoning performance standards at Chapter 355 Article X, Performance Standards (§§355-60–355-64). A structural observation, not a criticism, but relevant to whether performance standards are coherently located.

chapters.title: Outdoor Dining
chapters.summary: Chapter 218 establishes a Building Inspector-issued, annually renewable license for outdoor dining areas accessory to restaurants, carry-out restaurants, accessory cafes, or retail food stores, on sidewalks or private property. It sets detailed operational standards covering furnishings, signage, barriers, aisle widths, alcohol service, noise/lighting, and requires insurance and indemnification. It was adopted in 2010 and last substantively amended in 2021, but retains a seasonal closure window (January 2 through March 31) even after that amendment.
chapters.ratingRationale: Section 218-3B(4) still bars outdoor dining operation between January 2 and March 31 even though the subsection was itself amended in 2021 by L.L. No. 3-2021, meaning the Town revisited this exact provision post-pandemic and chose to keep the seasonal shutdown rather than move toward the year-round or expanded outdoor-dining models many municipalities made permanent after 2020-2021. The chapter is otherwise procedurally solid, with clear licensing, appeal, suspension, and insurance mechanics, keeping it out of 'Needs work' territory.
strengths: Clear annual licensing and renewal process with a Town Board appeal right on non-renewal, at Section 218-3B(1)
Due-process protections on suspension/revocation, including a hearing with counsel, at Section 218-5
Detailed, streetscape-protective furnishing, signage, and barrier standards at Section 218-3B(3) through (9)
Insurance and indemnification requirements naming the Town, at Sections 218-7 and 218-8
Explicit ban on live/mechanical music at outdoor dining areas protects neighboring residential uses (Section 218-3B(11))
concerns: Seasonal closure from January 2 to March 31 (Section 218-3B(4)) survived a 2021 amendment to the same subsection, unlike many municipalities that eliminated seasonal caps or created year-round programs post-COVID
No provision allowing use of parking spaces or 'parklets' for expanded outdoor dining; the definition in Section 218-2 is limited to sidewalks or the restaurant's own property
Allows 'seasonal heating' furnishings at Section 218-3B(3) without cross-referencing any propane/electric heater fire-code safety standard
All fee and deposit amounts are entirely deferred to the Master Fee Schedule (Section 218-10) with no amount, cap, or fee category specified in the chapter itself
No ADA/accessibility standard beyond the four-foot walking-aisle requirement at Section 218-3B(13) and (14)

recommendations.suggestion: Reconsider or narrow the January 2 - March 31 seasonal shutdown at Section 218-3B(4) to allow winter outdoor dining with weatherproofed/heated setups, following the post-COVID trend toward year-round outdoor dining programs.

Add a fire-code cross-reference for the 'seasonal heating' furnishings permitted at Section 218-3B(3), given propane and electric heaters carry distinct safety requirements not otherwise addressed in this chapter.
Publish indicative fee/deposit ranges alongside the Section 218-10 cross-reference to the Master Fee Schedule so applicants and residents can see cost expectations directly in the chapter.

Retain the no live/mechanical music rule in Section 218-3B(11) but consider pairing it with an explicit decibel or hours-based noise standard to make enforcement of 'disturb the peace and comfort' more objective.

chapters.peerComparison: Based on general professional knowledge of Westchester/NY outdoor-dining regulation rather than a document-to-document comparison, North Castle's Chapter 218 sits in the middle of the pack post-pandemic. Many municipalities used 2020-2021 emergency outdoor-dining expansions (parklets, parking-lane dining, extended seasons) as the basis for permanent code changes broadening where and when outdoor dining can operate; North Castle's 2021 amendment touched hours, furnishings, and noise but left the pre-pandemic seasonal shutdown window intact and did not add any parking-lane or parklet option, making it more conservative than the trend line even though the chapter is not stale in the sense of being an untouched, purely emergency-era rule.

chapters.title: Cannabis Retail Dispensaries and On-Site Consumption
chapters.summary: Chapter 219 is the Town's opt-out of allowing cannabis retail dispensaries and on-site cannabis consumption sites under NYS Cannabis Law Article 4, adopted in June 2021 pursuant to Cannabis Law § 131. Section 219-3 states the opt-out directly, and § 219-5 confirms the local law was subject to a permissive referendum under Municipal Home Rule Law § 24, with an editor's note confirming no petition was ever filed to force a public vote. The chapter includes a standard severability clause (§ 219-4) and took effect upon filing with the Secretary of State (§ 219-6).
chapters.ratingRationale: Section 219-3's blanket opt-out has not been revisited in the roughly five years since adoption despite substantial evolution of the state's adult-use cannabis regulatory framework (finalized Office of Cannabis Management adult-use rules, on-site consumption lounge regulations, and delivery licensing all emerged after this chapter's June 2021 passage), and the chapter is entirely silent on cannabis-adjacent issues within local control — such as home cultivation nuisances or delivery services — that the opt-out in § 219-1 does not itself reach.
strengths: Correctly grounds the opt-out in the specific statutory authority, Cannabis Law § 131, and properly follows the Municipal Home Rule Law § 24 permissive referendum procedure (§§ 219-2, 219-5)
Includes a standard, well-drafted severability clause (§ 219-4) protecting the balance of the chapter if any provision is invalidated
The editor's note under § 219-5 documents that no referendum petition was filed, giving a clear procedural record that the opt-out was never subject to a public vote challenge
concerns: The chapter has not been amended or reconsidered since its June 2021 adoption, despite the Office of Cannabis Management finalizing substantial adult-use regulations, on-site consumption lounge rules, and delivery licensing categories in the years since

Section 219-1's opt-out reaches only retail dispensaries and on-site consumption sites under Cannabis Law Article 4; the chapter says nothing about cannabis delivery services or adult-use home cultivation, both of which fall outside the opt-out and remain otherwise unaddressed anywhere in the town code
There is no mechanism in the chapter for periodic Town Board review of the opt-out decision in light of the local cannabis excise tax revenue the Town forgoes by remaining opted out
No accompanying zoning definitions or time/place/manner framework exists in case the Town Board later opts back in, meaning reversal would require building a licensing structure from scratch

recommendations.suggestion: Have the Town Board periodically reassess the opt-out in § 219-3 against the local cannabis excise tax revenue being forgone, particularly as neighboring opt-in municipalities begin realizing dispensary tax revenue.

Supplement the chapter with provisions addressing cannabis delivery services and adult-use home cultivation nuisances (odor, noise), since § 219-1's opt-out does not reach either activity and neither is addressed elsewhere in the code.

Confirm the chapter remains aligned with the current NYS Cannabis Law Article 4 and Office of Cannabis Management adult-use regulations, which have been substantially built out through rulemaking since this chapter's 2021 adoption.

If the Town Board ever revisits § 219-3, consider replacing a blanket prohibition with defined time/place/manner zoning standards and buffer distances, as several peer municipalities have adopted to allow controlled dispensary siting rather than outright exclusion.

chapters.peerComparison: Based on general professional knowledge of the Westchester County cannabis-opt-out landscape rather than comparison to other specific municipal documents, a large share of Westchester towns opted out of retail dispensaries and on-site consumption in 2021 during the same statutory window North Castle used, but a number of those municipalities have since revisited the decision and opted back in via subsequent local law to capture licensing and tax revenue as the state's adult-use market matured. North Castle's Chapter 219 is a fairly standard example of the original 2021 opt-out wave, but its lack of any subsequent update leaves it comparatively behind peer towns that have since layered in buffer-distance zoning or reconsidered opt-in status as Office of Cannabis Management regulations have matured.

chapters.title: Parkland Reservations
chapters.summary: Chapter 225 requires multifamily developments (condominiums/cooperatives) that need only site plan approval — not subdivision approval — to set aside on-site recreation area or, alternatively, pay a recreation fee to a Town trust fund used exclusively for neighborhood parks, playgrounds, and recreation land acquisition. It sets a minimum recreation area size (12% of site or one acre, whichever is greater, excluding wetlands/steep slopes) and a per-unit fee schedule with a reduced rate for assisted-living, middle-income, and AFFH units. It also credits any parkland already dedicated or fees already paid under the Town's subdivision regulations (Ch. 275) against this chapter's requirement.
chapters.ratingRationale: The core recreation fee in § 225-5B ($3,000/unit, $1,000/unit for assisted living, AFFH, or middle-income units) has not been adjusted since the 2011 and 2014 amendments — twelve years of inflation and Westchester land-value appreciation have likely eroded its real value as a substitute for actual parkland. There is also no indexing or escalation mechanism, and the chapter's applicability is narrow (only multifamily needing site-plan approval only), leaving standard subdivisions to a separate, unreviewed chapter (275).
strengths: Clearly excludes wetlands and steep slopes from counting toward the minimum recreation-area percentage (§ 225-4A), preventing developers from satisfying the requirement with unusable land
Built-in credit/anti-double-fee provision in § 225-7 for parkland or fees already provided under subdivision regulations
Reduced $1,000/unit fee for assisted-living, middle-income, and AFFH units (§ 225-5B, C) ties the fee structure to the Town's affordable-housing goals
Findings section (§ 225-3) gives a clear, legally defensible rationale connecting multifamily density to added recreational burden
concerns: Flat per-unit recreation fee ($3,000 standard / $1,000 reduced) has not been updated since the 5-14-2014 amendment to § 225-5C, over a decade of inflation and rising Westchester land costs
No inflation-indexing or periodic-review mechanism is built into the fee schedule
Applies only to multifamily development requiring site plan approval only (§ 225-6), creating a gap relative to subdivision-based residential development handled separately under Ch. 275
The standard for when the Planning Board may accept a fee instead of land is fairly open-ended ("not practical," § 225-5A) with no objective criteria or formula tied to appraised land value

recommendations.suggestion: Adjust the § 225-5B/C per-unit recreation fees for inflation since 2014 (e.g., via CPI indexing or a fresh land-value appraisal), since $3,000/unit is unlikely to buy meaningful parkland or improvements in the current Westchester real estate market.

Add an automatic periodic review clause (e.g., every 3-5 years) so the Town Board revisits the § 225-5 fee schedule without needing a standalone local law each time, similar to how many peer towns handle recreation and park fees.

Consider clarifying in § 225-5C the exact definition/cross-reference for 'middle-income unit' and 'AFFH unit' within this chapter itself (rather than relying on definitions housed elsewhere), to reduce ambiguity for developers computing fees.

chapters.peerComparison: Based on general professional knowledge of Westchester County practice (not a document-to-document comparison), most towns tie parkland dedication and fee-in-lieu requirements to Town Law §§ 274-a and 277 for both subdivision and site-plan-only multifamily development, often using a formula based on a percentage of appraised fair market land value per unit or per acre rather than a static flat dollar figure — which keeps the fee current without requiring a new local law every few years. North Castle's approach of a flat $3,000/$1,000 per-unit fee, last set in 2014, is a more common structure for older or smaller-town codes, but it is more likely to fall behind land values over time than a value-based or CPI-indexed formula used by comparably situated Westchester towns.

recordEvidence.note: §225-5 identified as the source of a recreation fee provision (Town Board, March 22, 2023). No criticism retained.

chapters.title: Parks and Public Lands
chapters.summary: Chapter 229 governs conduct on all Town-owned parks and public lands, establishing a list of prohibited acts (vandalism, littering, unauthorized fires, weapons, engine-powered devices, unpermitted swimming, alcohol without a permit, camping without a permit, illegal substances) and setting park hours to one hour after sunrise until one hour after sunset. It sets a 10 mph vehicle speed limit and a flat penalty structure for violations. The chapter cross-references the Town's Noise chapter (Ch. 210) and Master Fee Schedule (Ch. A370) for alcohol-permit fees.
chapters.ratingRationale: The chapter is adequate and was updated as recently as 2020 to raise penalties (§229-4, up to $1,000/day or 15 days' imprisonment, amended by L.L. No. 3-2020), but the substantive prohibited-conduct list in §229-2 has not been meaningfully modernized since its 1987 origin and 2015 alcohol-permit amendment, leaving newer recreational-use conflicts (e.g., e-bikes/scooters, drones, off-leash dogs) unaddressed.
strengths: Penalty provision was actively updated in 2020 to a meaningful per-day fine ($1,000) and jail exposure, with each day of continuing violation treated as a separate offense (§229-4)

Alcohol use is not blanket-prohibited but channeled through a permit process routed to the Superintendent of Recreation and Parks and Town Board approval, tied to the Master Fee Schedule (§229-2, amended 2015)
Cross-references the Noise chapter (Ch. 210) rather than duplicating noise standards, keeping the code internally consistent (§229-2)
Clear, objective hours-of-operation rule tied to sunrise/sunset rather than a fixed clock time that would need seasonal adjustment (§229-3)
concerns: "Engine-powered devices" are banned from park lands except maintenance, police and emergency vehicles, but the term is undefined, leaving ambiguity over increasingly common e-bikes, e-scooters, and other motorized personal mobility devices (§229-2)
No definitions section exists in the chapter at all — terms like 'park,' 'vehicle,' and 'designated areas' are used repeatedly without definition
No leash, pet-waste, or drone/UAV provisions, which are common additions in comparable park-conduct chapters
Swimming and camping are addressed only by a one-line permit reference with no cross-reference to where those permit standards or fees actually live
The 10 mph park speed limit (§229-2) has no stated enforcement mechanism or cross-reference to the Vehicle and Traffic chapter

recommendations.suggestion: Add a definition of 'engine-powered devices' in §229-2 that explicitly addresses e-bikes and motorized scooters, rather than leaving that judgment call to on-site enforcement.
Add a leash-law and pet-waste-removal requirement to §229-2, which is conspicuously absent from the current prohibited-acts list.

Cross-reference the specific permit application/fee sections for swimming and camping (currently only 'designated' or 'by permit only' in §229-2) so enforcement officers and residents aren't left guessing which office issues them.

Consolidate the alcohol-permit reference in §229-2 with an explicit citation to the current Master Fee Schedule section number rather than only the editor's note, to keep the two documents synchronized as fees change.

chapters.peerComparison: Based on general professional knowledge of Westchester County municipal park codes rather than a document-to-document comparison, North Castle's approach — dawn/dusk-adjacent hours, permit-only alcohol and camping, and a per-day monetary penalty topping out at $1,000 — is squarely in line with typical practice among comparable towns (e.g., Bedford, Mount Pleasant, New Castle), several of which use similar sunrise/sunset hour language and permit-based carve-outs for alcohol. Where North Castle lags common current practice is in rules-of-conduct granularity: many peer towns have added explicit leash-law, drone, and e-mobility-device provisions in the last five to ten years, while North Castle's §229-2 prohibited-acts list still reads largely as it did in 1987 apart from the alcohol-permit and penalty updates.

chapters.title: Peddling and Soliciting
chapters.summary: Chapter 233 regulates peddlers, solicitors and canvassers operating in the Town, requiring a fingerprint-backed permit for commercial peddling and soliciting (§§233-3 to 233-9) and a separate registration process for canvassers (§233-12), which by definition includes political petitioning, fundraising and membership drives. It sets hours-of-operation, location and conduct restrictions (§233-13), lists exemptions for groups such as local businesses, minors in scouting-type organizations, political candidates, charities and interstate commerce (§§233-16, 233-17), and establishes bonding, insurance, revocation and appeal procedures enforced by the Police Department and Town Clerk.
chapters.ratingRationale: The chapter's canvasser registration requirement in §233-12 — applied to anyone who goes door-to-door to 'seek contributions, fund-raise, petition, seek membership or disseminate information' per the §233-2 definition of 'canvass' — closely resembles the municipal registration mandate for door-to-door religious and political advocacy that the U.S. Supreme Court struck down in Watchtower Bible & Tract Society v. Village of Stratton (2002); it demands SSN, date of birth, photo ID and is subject to denial for a prior conviction (§233-12C(3)). Separately, §233-5B mandates permanent, non-individualized denial of a peddler/solicitor permit for 'any criminal offense,' with no nexus, recency or rehabilitation standard. These are real legal-exposure gaps rather than stylistic ones, even though the chapter does carve out useful exemptions for candidates, minors and charities (§233-16).
strengths: Explicit exemptions for political candidates and referendum campaigners (§233-16A(5)), minors soliciting for scouting or school-sponsored organizations (§233-16A(2)), and charitable/not-for-profit organizations (§233-16A(6)) show real drafting attention to constitutionally sensitive categories
§233-17 exempts interstate-commerce solicitation from permit fees entirely, respecting the Commerce Clause
A due-process structure exists throughout: written notice before permit denial (§233-5F), a hearing before revocation (§233-22B-D), and a right of appeal to the Town Board within 15 days (§233-24)

Canvassers are distinguished from commercial peddlers/solicitors by being subject to registration rather than a fee-bearing permit, and are not required to submit fingerprints under §233-12 the way commercial peddlers are under §233-4C
Veterans holding a Westchester County hawker's permit are exempted from the local permit fee (§233-15), aligning with state law
concerns: §233-12's canvasser registration requirement — covering political petitioning, fundraising, and membership drives per the §233-2 definition of 'canvass' — requires SSN, date of birth, and 10-day advance notice, and is deniable for a prior conviction (§233-12C(3)); this closely tracks the fact pattern invalidated in Watchtower Bible & Tract Society v. Village of Stratton (2002) for noncommercial door-to-door advocacy

§233-5B requires permanent denial of a peddler/solicitor permit for a conviction of 'any criminal offense, including but not limited to violent crimes, sexual assault, possession of a controlled substance, theft, fraud or burglary,' with no individualized assessment of recency, rehabilitation, or nexus to the licensed activity

Permit/registration denial is also triggered by 'two or more complaints' within the prior year (§233-5D, §233-12C is silent on this but §233-22A(5) revokes on the same basis) without any requirement that the complaints be adjudicated or substantiated before triggering denial or revocation

The $15,000 surety bond figure in §233-20 is written directly into the local law rather than tied to the Master Fee Schedule mechanism used for permit fees in §233-6, so it cannot be adjusted for inflation without a local law amendment

Fingerprinting is required of every peddler/solicitor and 'each assistant and employee' (§233-4C) before an application will even be processed by the Town Clerk (§233-4D), a significant administrative burden for small or seasonal commercial operations

The blanket 10:00 a.m.-to-8:00 p.m., no-Sunday/no-federal-holiday window in §233-13A applies to canvassing 'with a permit or without,' meaning it constrains even wholly noncommercial door-to-door political or religious speech

recommendations.suggestion: Reconsider the §233-12 canvasser registration mandate in light of Watchtower Bible & Tract Society v. Village of Stratton (2002); at minimum, exempt purely political, religious, or charitable canvassing that is currently only carved out from fees (§233-16A(5)-(6)) but not from the registration/SSN/background-review requirement itself.

Replace the mandatory lifetime disqualification for 'any criminal offense' in §233-5B with an individualized standard weighing offense type, recency, and rehabilitation, consistent with NY Correction Law Article 23-A's fair-chance licensing framework.

Move the fixed $15,000 bond amount in §233-20 into the Master Fee Schedule mechanism already used for permit fees under §233-6, so it can be periodically adjusted by Town Board resolution rather than requiring a local law amendment.

Streamline the fingerprinting requirement in §233-4C for low-risk categories (e.g., seasonal farm-produce sellers already exempted under §233-16A(7), or registered charitable organizations under §233-16A(6)) rather than applying it uniformly to every assistant and employee.

chapters.peerComparison: Based on general familiarity with New York municipal peddling/soliciting codes rather than any direct document comparison: many towns still carry forward permit-plus-police-background-check structures adopted before Watchtower Bible & Tract Society v. Village of Stratton (2002) reshaped the constitutional landscape for door-to-door canvassing, and this chapter — last substantively restructured in 2009 with piecemeal amendments through 2020 — shows some but not complete modernization. Its exemptions for political candidates, minors in scouting organizations, and registered charities (§233-16) are a positive step that many older ordinances lack entirely. However, requiring canvassers to register with the Town Clerk (name, SSN, DOB, 10-day advance notice, denial for a prior conviction) rather than treating registration as purely voluntary or eliminating it for noncommercial speech is more restrictive than what many towns have since adopted post-Watchtower. On permit fee mechanics, tying fees to a Master Fee Schedule (§233-6) rather than hard-coding dollar amounts is standard modern practice; the fixed $15,000 bond in §233-20 is an exception to that otherwise-updated approach.

chapters.title: Property Maintenance
chapters.summary: Chapter 241 combines two separately adopted articles: Article I (1971, amended through 2020) regulates landfilling, dumping, littering, junked vehicles, and general blight conditions on any premises, while Article II (2014) creates a Building Inspector-driven notice-hearing-removal-lien process specifically for vacant lots, improved property, and public lands, incorporating the NYS Property Maintenance Code by reference. Together they cover weed height, refuse storage, junked vehicles, and Town-performed cleanup with cost recovery via property lien. The two articles carry different, non-aligned penalty schedules for overlapping conduct.
chapters.ratingRationale: The chapter lacks any proactive vacant/abandoned or bank-owned property registration requirement; Section 241-12 only authorizes Building Inspector action after a complaint-driven notice-and-hearing process, unlike the registry-with-fee model many NY towns adopted following the 2016 'zombie property' law. It also carries an internal inconsistency: Article I's penalty at Section 241-6 (flat fine up to $1,000 or 15 days, last amended 1991) does not align with Article II's escalating $500-to-$7,500 repeat-offender schedule at Section 241-10, even though both articles reach overlapping litter/blight conduct.
strengths: Article II provides a concrete inspection-notice-hearing-lien pathway for abandoned properties at Sections 241-9 through 241-12
Escalating penalty schedule for repeat offenders under Section 241-10 (up to $7,500 for a fourth offense within 18 months) is a meaningful deterrent
Incorporates the NYS Property Maintenance Code (2010) by reference at Section 241-8, avoiding duplicative drafting
Specific, enforceable weed-height standard (10 inches) at Section 241-4E
Town-performed removal costs are recoverable as a real property lien under Sections 241-11B and 241-12C
concerns: No proactive vacant/abandoned property registry or mortgagee registration requirement; enforcement under Section 241-12 is entirely complaint- or inspection-triggered after the fact

Article I's flat penalty (Section 241-6: up to $1,000 fine/15 days, unchanged since the 1991 amendment) is inconsistent with Article II's graduated $500-$7,500 scheme (Section 241-10) for materially overlapping conduct
Definitions in Section 241-2 (e.g., 'junked vehicle,' 'infestation') largely retain 1971-era drafting with only piecemeal amendments layered on in 1987, 1991, and 2020
No rental-property registration or periodic inspection program tied to maintenance compliance
Article I and Article II were adopted 43 years apart and are not cross-referenced to clarify which governs a given violation

recommendations.suggestion: Harmonize the penalty provisions between Section 241-6 (Article I, flat fine) and Section 241-10 (Article II, escalating fine) so enforcement outcomes do not depend on which article a violation is charged under.

Adopt a formal vacant/abandoned property registry (with an owner or mortgagee registration fee) to make Section 241-12's currently reactive process proactive, consistent with post-2016 NY zombie-property practice.

Cross-reference Article I and Article II explicitly, or consolidate them, since both currently regulate blight/litter/debris conditions through different officials (Town Board generally vs. Building Inspector under Section 241-9) without a clear jurisdictional line.
Consider funding vacant-lot cleanup costs upfront through a registration fee rather than relying solely on after-the-fact lien recovery under Sections 241-11B and 241-12C.

chapters.peerComparison: Based on general professional knowledge of Westchester property-maintenance practice rather than a document-to-document comparison, North Castle's reliance on a purely complaint-driven, notice-and-lien model in Article II is now somewhat behind the curve: many peer Westchester towns adopted dedicated vacant and abandoned property registries (often requiring mortgagee/bank registration with an annual fee) in the years following the 2008 foreclosure crisis and New York's 2016 RPAPL Section 1962 zombie-property legislation, giving code enforcement earlier notice of at-risk properties rather than waiting for visible blight to trigger action. The chapter's bifurcated, differently-penalized structure (a 1971-era Article I bolted alongside a 2014 Article II) is also a common artifact of incremental small-town codification that better-maintained codes typically resolve through a comprehensive rewrite rather than leaving as two overlapping regimes.

recordEvidence.verdict: Single but concrete conflict with Town policy

findings.quote: [A pollinator garden] flies against our code … [on] lawn height or violation. If [the] board agrees … [and wants to] embrace [it], [we should] modify [the] code.
findings.corroboration: An amendment cycle followed on the same provision — September 14, September 28 (‘to amend Chapter 241, Section 3E’), and October 26, 2022, described as clarifying maintenance — supporting this as an accepted defect rather than an isolated view. A blight-control lawn-height standard captured a land-cover practice (pollinator gardens) the Town wants to encourage.

chapters.title: Sewers
chapters.summary: Chapter 250 is organized into four Parts, each governing one of the Town's sanitary sewer districts: District No. 1 (original 1941 gravity system), District No. 1b (2009 low-pressure/grinder-pump system), District No. 2 (1983), and District No. 3 (1992). Each Part sets connection requirements (mandatory hookup when a public sewer is within 100 feet), construction/material standards for building sewers, prohibited and controlled discharges (flammables, high-temperature or corrosive wastes, grease, industrial pollutants), permit and inspection procedures, and civil/criminal penalties. Districts No. 2 and No. 3 additionally include unit-based use-charge rate schedules and ad valorem/unit-based capital cost assessment formulas, with a mandated biennial rate review. Enforcement authority rests with the Director of Water and Sewer Operations, with entry/inspection rights also extended to Westchester County Health Department, NYSDEC, and EPA officials for industrial dischargers.
chapters.ratingRationale: The chapter is functional but shows its age and patchwork drafting: Article VI/VII (Sewer District No. 3, §§ 250-102 through 250-147) is an almost verbatim copy of Article III/IV (Sewer District No. 2, §§ 250-52 through 250-101) rather than a consolidated ordinance, and District No. 1's construction specs (§ 250-19, § 250-21) still mandate 1941-era cast-iron pipe with oakum/lead-caulked joints without the SDR-35 PVC alternative that later districts allow. The $5,000 contractor indemnity bond (§ 250-4, § 250-50) and several rate/discharge provisions have not been revisited in decades despite a biennial-review mandate (§ 250-96, § 250-146).
strengths: Each sewer district's use regulations are self-contained with clear definitions matching current federal/state terminology (BOD, slug, significant industrial user) in § 250-52 and § 250-102

Grants explicit inspection and entry rights to the Town, Westchester County Health Department, NYSDEC, and USEPA for industrial dischargers (§ 250-84, § 250-134), supporting a defensible pretreatment enforcement posture
Mandatory biennial review of use charges to keep O&M cost recovery proportionate to actual users and costs (§ 250-96, § 250-146)
