Grease/oil/sand interceptor requirements include owner recordkeeping and licensed-hauler obligations (§ 250-73, § 250-123), consistent with modern FOG control practice

District No. 1b (2009) ties code requirements to specific stamped engineering designs for the Orchard Drive Sewer Extension (§ 250-66B, § 250-66C), showing the Town links code compliance to as-built engineering records
concerns: Sewer District No. 3's entire use-ordinance article (§§ 250-102 through 250-147) duplicates Sewer District No. 2's article (§§ 250-52 through 250-101) almost word-for-word instead of being consolidated, creating drift risk (e.g., District 2's health-spa unit rate is 'each 25 members' in § 250-93 while District 3's is 'each 5 members' in § 250-143, with no explanation for the difference)
District No. 3's use-charge schedule (§ 250-143) carries no amendment note since the article's 1992 adoption despite the biennial review mandate in § 250-146

Numeric pollutant limits are frequently left entirely to the Director's discretion (§ 250-71E, § 250-121E) rather than codified in a published local-limits table, unlike many EPA-approved industrial pretreatment programs

'Significant industrial users' are categorically barred from connecting to Districts No. 2 and No. 3 (§ 250-80, § 250-130) rather than routed into a conditional pretreatment-permit program under CWA § 307
The $5,000 indemnity bond required of contractors (§ 250-4, § 250-50) has apparently gone unchanged since the 1941 original adoption, with no inflation adjustment mechanism
District No. 1 still specifies antiquated cast-iron/oakum/molten-lead joint construction (§ 250-19, § 250-21) without the SDR-35 PVC alternative offered under District No. 1b (§ 250-42D)

recommendations.suggestion: Consolidate the near-duplicate Sewer District No. 2 and No. 3 use ordinances (§§ 250-52–250-101 and §§ 250-102–250-147) into a single chapter-wide sewer use ordinance with district-specific rate tables, cutting roughly 45 redundant sections and reducing the risk that future amendments update one district's language but not the other's.

Conduct and document the overdue biennial review of the District No. 3 use-charge schedule (§ 250-143), which shows no amendment since 1992, to confirm O&M cost recovery still matches actual treatment plant costs as required by § 250-146.

Replace discretion-only pollutant restrictions (§ 250-71E, § 250-121E) with a published numeric local-limits table for metals, oil/grease, and pH consistent with an EPA-approved industrial pretreatment program, giving dischargers clear compliance targets rather than case-by-case Director judgment.

Replace the blanket prohibition on 'significant industrial users' connecting to Districts No. 2 and No. 3 (§ 250-80, § 250-130) with a conditional industrial pretreatment permit pathway under Clean Water Act § 307, so legitimate industrial users have a compliance route instead of an outright bar.

Increase or index the $5,000 contractor indemnity bond (§ 250-4, § 250-50), unrevised since the 1941 original adoption, to reflect present-day repair and liability costs before the Town accepts it as adequate security.

chapters.peerComparison: Based on general professional familiarity with Westchester County town sewer codes rather than a document-to-document comparison, North Castle's Chapter 250 follows the common pattern for small Westchester sewer districts: unit-based (EDU-style) use charges rather than metered billing, ad valorem/unit hybrid capital assessment formulas, and district-by-district codification reflecting how each district was separately created and financed over time (here, 1941, 1983, 1992, and 2009). Many peer towns with multiple legacy districts (e.g., Bedford, Mount Pleasant, Yorktown) show similar redundancy where each district's use ordinance was adopted or amended independently rather than unified, though best-practice codes increasingly consolidate shared provisions (definitions, discharge prohibitions, enforcement) into one district-agnostic sewer use ordinance with only rates and capital charges varying by district. On I&I control, North Castle's blanket prohibitions on roof/foundation drain connections (§ 250-33, § 250-65, § 250-115) are standard, but it lacks the more modern smoke-testing, dye-testing, or private lateral inspection-upon-sale programs some peer municipalities have adopted to actively find and correct infiltration sources. On industrial pretreatment, an outright ban on significant industrial users (rather than a conditional discharge permit under an EPA-approved local pretreatment program) is less common among peer towns with formal treatment plants and suggests the Town's plants were sized without expecting industrial-scale users, consistent with North Castle's largely residential/commercial character.

chapters.title: Sewer Systems, Private
chapters.summary: Chapter 254 requires owners of parcels within the New York City Croton or Kensico Reservoir Watersheds that rely on a separate sewage disposal/on-site wastewater treatment system (e.g., septic tanks) to have that system inspected at least once every five years, beginning May 1, 2011, and to retain inspection records for at least six years. It implements a specific New York State DEC SPDES general permit requirement (Part IX.A.3.b of Permit GP-0-10-002) governing municipal stormwater systems, and designates the Building Inspector as the appeals authority, who may extend (but never waive) compliance deadlines by up to 180 days. Violations are enforced with a written notice, a 30-day cure period, and escalating fines up to $1,000 per violation per day (or up to 15 days' imprisonment).
chapters.ratingRationale: The chapter directly implements a specific, named state permit obligation (SPDES GP-0-10-002, § 254-1B) with clear defined terms tied to the Westchester County Sanitary Code (§ 254-2), and its enforcement provision was updated as recently as 2020 (§ 254-5C). The five-year inspection cycle and six-year recordkeeping requirement are concrete and enforceable, though the chapter's geographic scope is narrowly limited to reservoir watershed parcels only.
strengths: Ties the inspection mandate to a specific, named DEC permit and MS4 stormwater program (§ 254-1B), giving it clear legal grounding beyond generic home-rule authority
Clear, objective five-year inspection interval and six-year record-retention requirement (§ 254-3A, B)
Enforcement mechanism was updated as recently as 2020 (§ 254-5C amendment) with an escalating fine structure and a mandatory 30-day cure notice before penalties attach

Explicitly limits the appeals authority's discretion — it can extend time (up to 180 days) but cannot waive or exempt compliance (§ 254-4), preventing case-by-case erosion of the watershed protection goal
concerns: Geographic scope is limited to parcels in the NYC Croton or Kensico Reservoir Watersheds (§ 254-3A); parcels outside those watersheds with septic systems are not covered by this chapter at all

No provision addresses what happens if an inspection reveals a failing or noncompliant system — the chapter mandates inspection and recordkeeping but does not itself require repair, pump-out, or rehabilitation upon a failed result

Relies on specific numbered sections of the Westchester County Sanitary Code (e.g., §§ 873.721, 873.722, 873.724, 873.726 in § 254-2) that could be renumbered or superseded by the County without a corresponding update to this chapter
No fee schedule or Town cost-recovery mechanism is specified for administering the inspection-verification/appeals process

recommendations.suggestion: Add an explicit remediation trigger requiring repair or pump-out within a set timeframe when an inspection under § 254-3 reveals a failing system, rather than relying solely on the inspection-and-recordkeeping requirement.

Consider Town-wide applicability (or a mechanism to expand it) rather than limiting § 254-3A to the Croton/Kensico watersheds only, so septic maintenance oversight isn't dependent on a parcel's specific watershed location.

Periodically verify that the Westchester County Sanitary Code section citations in § 254-2 (§§ 873.721 et seq.) remain current, since a County renumbering could create ambiguity about which provisions this chapter incorporates by reference.

chapters.peerComparison: Based on general professional knowledge of Westchester County practice (not a document-to-document comparison), septic/private sewage maintenance chapters tied to the NYC Croton and Kensico Reservoir Watersheds are common among neighboring towns (e.g., Bedford, New Castle, Yorktown, Somers) because they share the same DEC SPDES MS4 permit obligation and the same County Sanitary Code inspection/licensing regime for septage collectors. North Castle's five-year inspection interval, Building Inspector appeals role, and escalating penalty structure are consistent with the typical peer-town approach; where North Castle is somewhat lighter than some peers is in not specifying a mandatory remediation/repair trigger following a failed inspection, which some neighboring watershed-town codes address more explicitly.

chapters.title: Solar Infrastructure Siting
chapters.summary: Chapter 258 governs the siting of solar energy systems, distinguishing rooftop/BIPV systems (permitted in all zoning districts) from small- and large-scale ground-mounted/freestanding systems (barred from residential districts and subject to Planning Board site plan approval or Town Board special use permit in nonresidential districts). It sets setback, height (8-foot max tilt), screening, and safety standards, requires operation and maintenance plans and fire department coordination for large-scale installations, and establishes a removal process — including a Town Board public hearing and cost-lien mechanism — for solar collectors that stop functioning for over 12 months.
chapters.ratingRationale: The chapter has a reasonably clear removal/hearing process for nonperforming installations (§258-5G) but, unlike Chapter 161's fill law which requires a surety bond or letter of credit up front (§161-1D), it imposes no decommissioning bond or financial security requirement for large-scale ground-mounted solar before installation, leaving the Town to rely on after-the-fact enforcement and cost assessment if an operator disappears. It also flatly bars all ground-mounted and freestanding solar in residential districts (§258-4H), which is a blunt restriction not updated since the 2016 adoption despite a decade of solar-technology and state-policy change.
strengths: Tiered permitting structure by system type and scale, with rooftop and BIPV systems permitted as-of-right in all zoning districts (§258-4C-D)
Concrete safety provisions requiring qualified-installer work, Building Inspector and utility inspection sign-off, and Uniform Fire Code compliance (§258-5A-E)
Defined removal process for nonperforming installations with public hearing, notice, and a cost-lien mechanism against the property (§258-5G)
Requires large-scale installations to share project summaries, electrical schematics, and site plans with the Fire Chief and designate a public-inquiry contact (§258-5I)
concerns: No decommissioning bond, letter of credit, or other financial security is required before construction of large-scale ground-mounted arrays, unlike the surety-bond requirement in Chapter 161's fill law

Ground-mounted and freestanding solar collectors of any scale are entirely prohibited in residential zoning districts (§258-4H), which can block solar access for homes without adequate roof orientation
Adopted in 2016 with no amendments noted since, predating New York's 2019 Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act and subsequent updates to NYSERDA's model solar law guidance
No glare/glint study requirement despite view-blockage language in §258-4K(4)
Height limit for ground-mounted systems is capped at 8 feet with no separate large-scale array standard beyond the special-permit carve-out for vehicle canopies (§258-4K(3))

recommendations.suggestion: Add a decommissioning bond or letter-of-credit requirement for large-scale ground-mounted installations in §258-4J/K, consistent with NYSERDA's model solar energy law, so the Town isn't exposed if an operator abandons the site.

Revisit the blanket ban on small-scale ground-mounted/freestanding solar in residential districts (§258-4H) to allow accessory ground arrays under conditions (setback, screening) for homes with poor roof solar access.
Clarify the timeline and criteria for the Town Board special use permit process referenced for large-scale ground-mounted systems in §258-4J, since no processing timeframe is specified.
Update the chapter to reference current NYSERDA/CLCPA guidance and consider a formal glare/glint assessment requirement alongside the existing view-blockage standard in §258-4K(4).

chapters.peerComparison: Drawing on general familiarity with NYSERDA's Unified Solar Permit and model solar energy law rather than a document-to-document comparison, many Westchester municipalities that updated their solar codes after 2016 added decommissioning security requirements for large-scale ground-mounted arrays and permitted small accessory ground-mounted systems in residential districts under setback and screening conditions. North Castle's outright residential ground-mount ban and its absence of any decommissioning bond are both more restrictive/less protective, respectively, than what has become fairly standard peer-town practice in the years since this chapter's 2016 adoption.

recordEvidence.verdict: Criticised for what it does not contain

findings.quote: There are no guidelines [for battery energy storage systems]. … [The Town should] create special use/local law … regs.
findings.attribution: Adam Kaufman, Town Planner (same statement indexed under Chapter 355, §355-40)
findings.corroboration: This chapter regulates solar collector systems and their storage batteries at §258-5.F, but has no counterpart addressing freestanding battery energy storage systems (BESS) as their own use — the gap the Town Planner flagged. Still unremedied as of the March 11, 2026 code date.

chapters.title: Solid Waste and Recycling
chapters.summary: Chapter 259, adopted in 2015, governs residential and commercial solid waste and recyclables collection in North Castle, tying the Town's program to the 1974 Westchester County solid waste management plan and the State's 2010 "Beyond Waste" strategy. It covers curbside preparation and container standards, single-stream recycling definitions, brush and yard waste collection by the Highway Department, hauler licensing (administered by the Highway Department, expiring each March 31), and enforcement/penalties for unlawful scavenging or improper mixing of waste streams.
chapters.ratingRationale: The chapter explicitly treats food and other organic waste as ordinary "solid waste" "until such time as outlets for composting or otherwise processing or recycling them become available" (§259-3, definition of NON-YARD ORGANIC WASTES) — meaning as of the current text there is still no operating curbside organics/food-scrap diversion program, a gap increasingly closed by peer NY municipalities. The chapter's substantive collection and recycling provisions have not been amended since original 2015 adoption (only the penalty amounts were updated in 2020 per L.L. No. 3-2020), so it predates and does not reference New York's statewide plastic bag ban (effective 2020) or expanded polystyrene foam ban (effective 2022).
strengths: Clear source-separation mandate with real enforcement teeth: recyclables set at curbside vest in the Town, and unauthorized removal ("scavenging") is a violation (§259-4E, §259-9A).

Detailed, practical container and placement rules (32-gallon/60-lb limits, curbside timing windows, front-yard setback restriction on dumpster/bunker placement in §259-5G) reduce ambiguity for residents and enforcement staff alike.

Hauler licensing regime requires proof of good standing with the Westchester County Solid Waste Commission, insurance certificates, and a Highway Department vehicle inspection (§259-16), giving the Town real leverage over service quality.
Ties municipal goals to an explicit external framework (NYSDEC's "Beyond Waste" strategy) rather than operating in a policy vacuum (§259-2).
concerns: Non-yard organic/food waste is explicitly deferred rather than mandated for diversion — the code itself states these materials remain "solid waste" pending future composting infrastructure (§259-3), so there is no curbside food-scrap or organics program.
No numeric diversion-rate or waste-reduction target is set; §259-2 only lists "incremental steps" and references a 2010 state report without adopting a measurable local goal.

Adopted in 2015 and never substantively revised since (only the penalty section, §259-12, was amended in 2020), the chapter predates and does not address New York State's 2020 single-use plastic bag ban or 2022 expanded polystyrene foam ban.

Penalty levels ($100 first offense/$250 subsequent for haulers under §259-17; up to $1,000/day for general violations under §259-12) are internally inconsistent and markedly lower than the $1,000/day penalties in Chapters 308 and 195, suggesting the solid waste penalty structure has not been harmonized with the rest of the Town Code.

Construction and demolition waste is carved out of the "solid waste" definition (§259-3) and left to private arrangement between resident and hauler (§259-15A(1)) with no Town-level diversion or recycling requirement for C&D materials.

recommendations.suggestion: Establish a curbside food-scrap/organics collection pilot or drop-off program and update the NON-YARD ORGANIC WASTES definition in §259-3, which currently defers organics diversion indefinitely pending unspecified future infrastructure.

Amend the chapter to reference and align local practice with New York's statewide plastic bag ban (2020) and expanded polystyrene foam ban (2022), neither of which is mentioned despite both predating the chapter's last substantive review.

Adopt a specific, measurable waste-diversion or recycling-rate target (e.g., a percentage goal by a target year) rather than the open-ended "incremental steps" language in §259-2, to make use of the hauler-report data collection already required in §259-2A.
Harmonize the hauler penalty schedule in §259-17 ($100/$250 flat fines) with the $1,000-per-day general penalty in §259-12 so licensed haulers face proportionate consequences for repeated violations.

chapters.peerComparison: Based on general professional knowledge of Westchester County solid waste practice rather than a document-to-document comparison, North Castle's private-hauler licensing model (Highway Department administered, tied to Westchester County Solid Waste Commission standing) is typical of the county's smaller towns, many of which rely on licensed private carters rather than municipal collection crews. Where North Castle lags increasingly common peer practice is on organics: a growing number of Westchester municipalities and the county itself have introduced food-scrap drop-off or curbside collection programs in the years since 2015, and New York's statewide food donation/recycling law (effective 2022) requires large generators to divert food waste — developments this chapter, last substantively written in 2015, does not reflect.

chapters.title: Special Events
chapters.summary: Chapter 263 requires a Town Clerk/Town Board-issued permit for special events such as bazaars, carnivals, circuses, fairs, and similar outdoor amusements, and mandates applicant-funded fire watch and police security/traffic control (§263-3). Applications must include event plans, proof of insurance, a $500 cleanup bond, structural safety certifications for temporary structures, and mailed notice to neighbors within 250 feet (§263-4). The chapter exempts charitable/religious/school events on their own premises, non-commercial private-residence gatherings, government-sponsored events, and events at purpose-built venues (§263-8), restricts operating hours to 10:00 a.m.-midnight (§263-7B), and gives the Town Board broad authority to waive or modify requirements (§263-10, most recently amended 10-22-2025).
chapters.ratingRationale: The chapter has been actively maintained, with its permit-requirement and application sections both amended as recently as 10-22-2025 (§§263-3, 263-4), and it pairs a thorough multi-agency application process (fire watch, police detail, insurance, structural certification) with sensible, clearly enumerated exemptions in §263-8 that avoid overregulating private and charitable gatherings. It falls short of the top tier because the $500 cleanup bond in §263-4(I) is a flat figure not tied to the Master Fee Schedule (unlike the chapter's own application fee), and the Town Board's waiver authority in §263-10 is granted without any stated standards.
strengths: Actively maintained: the core permit requirement (§263-3) and application procedure (§263-4) were both amended within the last year (10-22-2025)

Comprehensive multi-agency application requirements — fire watch, police security, insurance with Town as additional insured, and engineer/architect-certified structural integrity for temporary structures (§263-4E, 263-4K)
Well-scoped exemptions (§263-8) that keep the permit burden off private residences, charitable/religious/school events on their own premises, and government-sponsored events
Concrete numeric safety guardrails — 250-foot residential setback (§263-3C), 8 amusement rides per acre, 10-day duration cap (§263-3E)
Neighbor notice requirement by first-class mail within 250 feet before the event (§263-4L) builds in a measure of community transparency
concerns: The $500 cash cleanup bond (§263-4I) is a flat, non-indexed figure — unlike the application fee, it is not tied to the Master Fee Schedule and has apparently not been revisited since the chapter's 2009 adoption

§263-10's Town Board waiver/modification authority ('if the Town Board determines that the goals of this chapter are better served thereby') provides no enumerated standards or criteria, creating a risk of inconsistent or arbitrary application
No minimum advance-filing deadline is specified for special event applications in §263-4, unlike the 30-day requirement for fireworks permits in Chapter 173 §173-4B(2)

The chapter cross-references the Building Code (Ch. 127) in its General References but not the Noise chapter (Ch. 210), despite carnivals, outdoor entertainment, and amusement rides being an obvious noise source

Fixed 10:00 a.m.-midnight operating hours (§263-7B) apply uniformly regardless of proximity to residences beyond the 250-foot setback, without a mechanism for stricter hours in more sensitive locations

recommendations.suggestion: Add enumerated standards or criteria to §263-10 to guide the Town Board's discretion in waiving or modifying chapter requirements, reducing exposure to arbitrary-and-capricious challenges.
Add a minimum advance-filing deadline to §263-4, comparable to the 30-day requirement in Chapter 173 §173-4B(2) for fireworks permits, so the Town Board has adequate lead time to review applications.

Tie the flat $500 cleanup bond in §263-4(I) to the Master Fee Schedule or scale it to event size/attendance so it keeps pace with actual cleanup costs, similar to how the application fee is already indexed.
Cross-reference the Noise chapter (Ch. 210) in §263-7 or add specific sound-level standards, given that carnivals and outdoor entertainment covered by this chapter are common noise-complaint sources.

chapters.peerComparison: Based on general professional knowledge of Westchester/NY municipal practice rather than any document comparison: North Castle's insurance-certificate, indemnification, and applicant-funded police/fire-watch cost recovery requirements are consistent with standard special-event permitting practice across Westchester towns. The flat $500 cleanup bond is on the low end and has not been updated in step with the fee schedule, which peer towns more commonly index or scale to event size. The broad, standardless Town Board waiver provision in §263-10 is also more discretionary than many peer codes, which tend to enumerate specific denial/waiver criteria directly in the ordinance rather than leaving it to board discretion alone.

chapters.title: Stormwater Management
chapters.summary: Chapter 267 is North Castle's Stormwater Management, Erosion and Sediment Control and Illicit Discharge law, adopted in 2007 to implement the NYSDEC MS4 general permit's Minimum Control Measures 4 and 5. Article I (§§ 267-1 to 267-8) requires a Stormwater Pollution Prevention Plan (SWPPP) for land development activities disturbing 5,000+ square feet, sets detailed SWPPP content and post-construction green infrastructure requirements, and creates a maintenance-agreement, performance-guarantee, and inspection regime enforced by a designated Stormwater Management Officer (SMO). Article II (§§ 267-9 to 267-25) prohibits illicit discharges and connections to the municipal separate storm sewer system (MS4), authorizes SMO access/monitoring, and lays out a graduated enforcement toolkit including notices of violation, stop-work orders, MS4 access suspension, injunctive relief, alternative remedies, and public-nuisance declarations. The chapter has been amended three times (2013, 2015, 2020) to update fees, definitions, and penalties, mostly to conform to revised NYSDEC SPDES general permit numbers.
chapters.ratingRationale: The chapter is thorough and structurally sound — it embeds SWPPP content standards, green infrastructure references, maintenance easements/agreements (§ 267-7D), and performance/maintenance guarantees (§ 267-8B) that go beyond a bare-bones ordinance. However, the Article I penalty schedule in § 267-8D(4) ($350/$700/$1,000 tiers) has not been updated since original 2007 adoption even though Article II's penalty (§ 267-19B) was raised in 2020, and the chapter cites specific NYSDEC permit numbers (GP-15-002, GP-15-003, GP-0-12-001) that have since been reissued, giving it a moderately dated feel typical of adequate-but-unremarkable local stormwater laws.
strengths: Detailed SWPPP content requirements in § 267-5D covering site maps, phasing (no more than five disturbed acres at a time per § 267-5D(1)(d)), pollution prevention measures, and a full post-construction stormwater management practice component with O&M plans and maintenance easements

Layered financial enforcement tools: construction completion performance guarantees and separate maintenance guarantees/letters of credit (§ 267-8B(1)-(2)), plus recorded maintenance agreements running with the land as deed restrictions (§ 267-7D)

Graduated, restorative enforcement option in § 267-23 ("Alternative remedies") allowing compliance workshops, storm drain stenciling, or stream cleanup in lieu of civil penalties for minor, cooperative first-time violations — uncommon in many peer codes
Explicit incorporation of green infrastructure practices and the NYS Stormwater Management Design Manual's Chapter 5 (§ 267-4 definition; § 267-5D(2)(a))
Clear right-of-entry, inspection frequency (every seven days for qualified inspectors on 1+ acre sites, § 267-7A(5)), and appeal process (§ 267-20) giving both enforcement teeth and due process
concerns: Article I penalties in § 267-8D(4) ($350/$700/$1,000 fine tiers) remain unchanged since 2007 adoption despite two later amendments to the chapter, while Article II's penalty was updated to $1,000/15 days in 2020 (§ 267-19B) — an inconsistent and dated deterrent for large land-development violations

The chapter's core permit citations (GP-15-002 for construction activity, GP-15-003 for MS4s, GP-0-12-001 for industrial activity) reflect NYSDEC's 2015-era permit numbering and have not been refreshed even though those permits have since been reissued

No locally created green infrastructure incentive (e.g., stormwater fee credit, density bonus, or expedited SWPPP review) — the chapter defers entirely to the state Design Manual's Chapter 5 rather than adding a town-specific incentive

Fee amounts for SWPPP review, inspections, and SMP maintenance are entirely deferred to the separate Master Fee Schedule (Ch. A370) via § 267-8E, so the chapter itself gives no visibility into actual applicant costs

No cross-reference in the SWPPP/phasing provisions (§ 267-5D(1)(d)) to North Castle's steep-slope, excavation, or filling/grading chapters (Ch. 157, Ch. 161), despite the town's hilly terrain increasing erosion risk on any given disturbed-acreage cap

recommendations.suggestion: Raise the Article I penalty tiers in § 267-8D(4) (unchanged $350/$700/$1,000 fines from 2007) to at least match the 2020-updated Article II penalty in § 267-19B, so land-development violations carry a deterrent proportional to today's construction and remediation costs.

Add a locally defined green infrastructure incentive (stormwater fee credit, expedited review, or similar) to § 267-5D(2)(a) rather than relying solely on the reference to Design Manual Chapter 5, to actively encourage green infrastructure adoption rather than merely permitting it.

Refresh the NYSDEC permit citations in § 267-3B(1)-(2) and the definitions of GP-15-002/GP-15-003/GP-0-12-001 in § 267-4 to reference the current reissued general permits, reducing ambiguity for applicants and reviewers relying on the plain text.

Publish or hyperlink the Master Fee Schedule (Ch. A370) fee amounts referenced in § 267-8E directly alongside Chapter 267 on the public code site so applicants can find SWPPP review/inspection costs without a separate lookup.

Cross-reference the five-acre active-disturbance cap in § 267-5D(1)(d) with the Town's excavation (Ch. 157) and filling/grading (Ch. 161) chapters for sites on steep slopes, since erosion risk from a fixed acreage cap varies significantly with terrain.

chapters.peerComparison: Based on general professional familiarity with Westchester County and NYSDEC MS4 general permit compliance (not a document-to-document comparison), Chapter 267 is a fairly typical "Phase II MS4 community" stormwater law: it mirrors the standard template many NYSDEC-regulated municipalities adopted around 2007-2008 and updated after the 2015 MS4 permit reissuance (GP-15-003), covering the same core elements — SWPPP requirements, illicit discharge prohibitions, maintenance agreements, and enforcement. Its use of recorded maintenance easements/agreements, performance and maintenance guarantees, and a formal alternative-remedies program place it on the more complete end of peer ordinances, many of which omit graduated remedies or long-term maintenance bonding altogether. Where it lags typical current practice is on green infrastructure incentives: several Westchester towns have begun layering local density bonuses, fee credits, or expedited review for green infrastructure and low-impact development on top of the state Design Manual reference, which North Castle has not done here. The unrefreshed permit numbers and the unequal treatment of penalty amounts between Articles I and II are common but fixable drafting artifacts seen across many towns that have not done a comprehensive stormwater chapter overhaul since their last MS4 permit cycle.

recordEvidence.note: A second, targeted pass built specifically to find criticism of stormwater provisions produced 16 candidates, all application-specific — no criticism retained. As with Trees, this reflects an absence of testing in board proceedings rather than a confirmed clean bill of health.

chapters.title: Streets and Sidewalks
chapters.summary: Chapter 271 sets the rules governing the Town's streets, highways, bridges, culverts and sidewalks. Article I establishes New York's standard 'prior written notice' liability shield for defects and snow/ice conditions. Article II bars physical obstructions on sidewalks and public ways. Articles III and IV, both added in 2020, create permit systems for street excavations/openings and for driveway entrances, complete with fees, security deposits, insurance and indemnification requirements.
chapters.ratingRationale: The chapter is internally consistent and was substantively modernized in 2020 (L.L. No. 3-2020), which added a detailed, ISO-form-referenced insurance and indemnification regime (§271-16) and a full driveway permitting article (Article IV) that did not previously exist. The core prior-notice liability provisions (§§271-1 through 271-5) track well-settled New York municipal law. The main gaps are the absence of any ADA/accessibility or stormwater standard for sidewalks and driveway aprons.
strengths: Article I's prior-written-notice scheme (§§271-1 to 271-5) closely tracks established NY municipal liability law and gives the Town Clerk a concrete, auditable index-record duty (§271-4) with a 5-year retention requirement

The 2020 insurance article (§271-16) is unusually sophisticated for a small-town code, specifying ISO CG 00 01 form language, a minimum A-VII Best rating, additional-insured endorsements, and waiver-of-subrogation clauses

Permit fees and deposit amounts are pegged to the externally-updatable Master Fee Schedule (Ch. A370) rather than hard-coded dollar figures in §§271-15 and 271-23, letting the Town Board adjust costs by resolution without amending the local law
§271-19B requires Planning Board approval before a second driveway curb-cut is permitted on a parcel that already has one, curbing proliferation of highway access points
The permit system caps street-opening permits at 300 contiguous feet of frontage (§271-14C), giving inspectors a concrete, non-discretionary unit to manage large linear projects
concerns: No ADA/PROWAG-style accessibility standard appears anywhere in the sidewalk or driveway provisions — the chapter addresses liability for sidewalk defects (§271-2) but sets no construction or curb-ramp standard for new or repaired sidewalks

Excavation work hours in residence districts (§271-13) are capped at 7:00 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. on weekdays only, with no Saturday work permitted — a narrower window than many peer Westchester towns allow for utility and contractor work, which can extend project timelines and cost

The $10,000 minimum bond figures in §271-10 (public utilities) and §271-20 (driveway contractors) are fixed dollar amounts written directly into the local law rather than tied to the Master Fee Schedule, so they cannot be inflation-adjusted without a full local law amendment
No stormwater or permeable-surface standard is imposed on driveway aprons or excavation restoration in §271-21C beyond a general instruction to 'minimize' drainage damage
Article IV cross-references the Zoning Code (§355-59F) for driveway standards, requiring readers to consult two separate chapters to understand the full permitting picture
Security deposits go unclaimed and become Town property after 18 months (§§271-15C, 271-23B) with no specified notice-to-permittee requirement before forfeiture

recommendations.suggestion: Add a permeable-surface or stormwater-mitigation standard to the driveway permit conditions in §271-21C, which currently only requires that grade and drainage 'minimize any possible damage,' rather than meeting an affirmative runoff standard.

Peg the $10,000 bond minimums in §271-10 and §271-20 to the Master Fee Schedule (as is already done for permit fees in §§271-15 and 271-23) so they can be periodically updated by resolution instead of requiring a local law amendment.

Consider adding an explicit ADA-compliance or PROWAG reference to the sidewalk and driveway construction standards, since the chapter otherwise only addresses the Town's tort liability exposure (§271-2) rather than accessibility of new construction.
Revisit the 7:00 a.m.-3:30 p.m., weekdays-only excavation window in §271-13, which is more restrictive than many neighboring towns and may extend the duration of disruptive street work for residents.

chapters.peerComparison: Based on general familiarity with Westchester County municipal codes rather than any direct document comparison: the prior-written-notice liability provisions in Article I are essentially boilerplate shared across most NY towns and follow the same template driven by Town Law and case law requiring actual written notice before tort liability attaches for highway and sidewalk defects. The Article III/IV excavation and driveway permitting scheme, including the detailed ISO-form insurance and indemnification language, is more thorough than many small-town codes of similar vintage — some peer towns still rely on a one- or two-paragraph insurance clause rather than the multi-page ISO-referenced text here, reflecting a 2020 risk-management-driven rewrite. Where this chapter lags typical current practice is the absence of any ADA/PROWAG sidewalk-accessibility standard and stormwater/green-infrastructure conditions on driveway and excavation permits, both of which a growing number of Westchester towns have begun folding into their streets and driveway chapters.

chapters.title: Subdivision of Land
chapters.summary: This chapter gives the Planning Board authority to review and approve subdivision plats (§ 275-1) through a three-step process of sketch plat conference, preliminary plat, and final plat review (§ 275-12), with timelines and public hearing procedures coordinated with SEQRA environmental review at each stage (§§ 275-15, 275-16). Article IV sets detailed design standards for streets, drainage, lots, and easements, including a private-street option for large-lot districts (§ 275-25B) and specific road geometry tables. Article III requires completion or bonding of public improvements (streets, utilities, sidewalks, drainage) before plat signing, with escrow accounts for consultant review costs (§§ 275-17, 275-36). Article VII's fee schedule largely defers dollar amounts to the Town's separately maintained Master Fee Schedule (Ch. A370) rather than fixing figures in the chapter text.
chapters.ratingRationale: The chapter is procedurally thorough and has been amended periodically as recently as 11-13-2024 (§ 275-15), with solid SEQRA integration and an unusual anti-piecemeal-subdivision look-back rule (§ 275-15F). However, it contains a genuine internal cross-reference conflict on stormwater management -- citing 'Ch. 267' in § 275-24C, 'Chapter 276' in §§ 275-32 and 275-35, and 'Ch. 340' in the chapter's own general references list at the top -- and it offers no conservation/cluster subdivision design option, a feature common in comparable Westchester towns.
strengths: Preliminary and final plat review timelines are explicitly coordinated with SEQRA lead-agency status, EIS filing, and public hearing procedures (§ 275-15G-L, § 275-16F-G), reducing legal exposure on state environmental review compliance.

A 'look-back' provision caps subdivision of a parent parcel lacking central sewer/water at 49 lots within any 10-year period to prevent evasion of infrastructure requirements through sequential minor subdivisions (§ 275-15F).
Design standards explicitly direct new streets toward an east-west axis and lot arrangements that maximize solar access, a sustainability-minded provision added in 2012 (§ 275-24H, § 275-26A).

Nearly all fee provisions point to a separately maintained Master Fee Schedule (Ch. A370) rather than embedding dollar figures in the chapter, easing periodic fee updates without code amendments (§§ 275-36 through 275-39).
Recreation (park-in-lieu) fees are reduced for middle-income and 'affirmatively furthering fair housing' (AFFH) units, tying subdivision exactions to the Town's affordable-housing goals (§ 275-37B).
concerns: Three different chapter numbers are cited for 'Stormwater Management' within this single chapter: the general references list cites Ch. 340 (which is otherwise defined as Wetlands and Watercourse Protection), § 275-24C cites 'Chapter 267, Stormwater Management,' and §§ 275-32 and 275-35 cite 'Chapter 276, Stormwater Management' -- an unresolved renumbering conflict that could confuse applicants and reviewers about which chapter's SWPPP standards actually govern.

Article IV offers no conservation/cluster/open-space subdivision option; the only density-neutral design alternative is the private-street standard in § 275-25B, which by its own terms cannot be used to increase yield beyond conventional subdivision.

Drainage design is keyed only to 25-year and 100-year storm-frequency thresholds by watershed size (§ 275-25C) with no reference to green infrastructure or low-impact-development (LID) site design practices in the chapter's own design standards.

Section 275-9 vests the Planning Board with authority to adopt amendments to 'these regulations' subject to Town Board approval, which is inconsistent with the chapter's actual amendment history -- every amendment since at least 1988 has been enacted directly by the Town Board as a local law.

The final plat fee provision (§ 275-16A) refers only to a fee 'as set by the Town Board,' while nearly every other application fee section (§§ 275-12, 275-13, 275-14, 275-15) expressly cross-references the Master Fee Schedule (Ch. A370), creating ambiguity about which schedule governs final plat submission.

The definitions article still carries multiple editor's notes documenting repealed terms (Town Environmental Quality Review Act, Wetlands and Drainage Law, Zoning Ordinance) rather than a fully cleaned-up defined-terms list (§ 275-29).

recommendations.suggestion: Correct the stormwater chapter cross-references so that § 275-24C, §§ 275-32/275-35, and the chapter's own general references list all cite the same, current stormwater management chapter number, eliminating the present three-way conflict between Ch. 267, Ch. 276, and Ch. 340.

Add an explicit conservation/open-space subdivision option to Article IV -- alongside the existing private-street standard in § 275-25B -- allowing lot-size averaging or clustering in exchange for permanent open-space dedication, consistent with Town Law § 278 authority already referenced elsewhere in the chapter (§ 275-8).

Revise § 275-9 to reflect actual practice by having the Town Board, rather than the Planning Board, adopt amendments to this chapter, since every amendment on record since 1988 has in fact been enacted as a Town Board local law.

Reconcile § 275-16's final-plat fee language ('fee as set by the Town Board') with the Master Fee Schedule cross-references used throughout §§ 275-12 through 275-15, so applicants have one clear, consistently referenced source for every subdivision-related fee.

Revisit the § 275-15F look-back threshold (49 lots per 10 years) and the § 275-27C park-fee-in-lieu mechanism to confirm the recreation trust fund is adequately capitalized against current land and recreational-facility costs, since neither figure appears to have been reexamined since adoption.

chapters.peerComparison: Based on general professional familiarity with Westchester County subdivision regulations rather than a document-to-document comparison: North Castle's chapter is fairly typical in structure (sketch/preliminary/final plat sequence, SEQRA-coordinated hearings, bonded improvements, Master Fee Schedule cross-references) and is comparably detailed on street geometry and drainage design. Where it lags many peer towns (e.g., Bedford, New Castle, Pound Ridge, Somers) is in the absence of a codified conservation/cluster subdivision or 'open development area' option under Town Law §§ 278/281, which those towns commonly use to incentivize open-space preservation in exchange for flexible lot design, and in the lack of explicit low-impact-development/green-infrastructure standards within the subdivision design article itself (as opposed to leaving all stormwater quality design to a separately cross-referenced, and here inconsistently cited, stormwater chapter).

recordEvidence.verdict: Cited once, in a variance recitation
recordEvidence.note: §275-23 cited once, alongside §355-21, in a Zoning Board of Appeals variance recitation (February 1, 2024). Eight articles, §275-1–§275-40, with no criticism and almost no traffic in this corpus.

chapters.title: Tattooing
chapters.summary: Chapter 284 imposes an outright ban on tattooing for pay anywhere in the Town of North Castle, with a narrow exception for medical purposes performed by a physician or osteopath licensed under the Education Law. Section 284-1's findings explain the ban as a response to the Town's inability to enforce Penal Law § 260.21 (prohibiting tattooing minors) and its lack of resources to license and inspect tattoo establishments for health risks like serum hepatitis. Section 284-3 sets the penalty at up to a $1,000 fine and/or 15 days imprisonment, deemed a misdemeanor for jurisdictional purposes, with each day of violation a separate offense.
chapters.ratingRationale: The chapter's core rationale in § 284-1 is that the Town 'lacks the resources to implement and staff an effective regulatory scheme of licensing and inspection,' a 1998-era judgment that has been overtaken by New York's now-comprehensive statewide Body Art sanitary code framework administered through county health departments, meaning a categorical ban on a lawful trade rather than a licensing/inspection regime leaves the chapter's stated justification stale and potentially exposed to legal challenge. Only the penalty clause was updated (2020); the substantive ban and findings have not been revisited since 1998.
strengths: Section 284-1 provides a clearly articulated legislative rationale grounded in a specific Penal Law citation (§ 260.21) and a named public health concern (serum hepatitis)
The medical-purposes exception in § 284-2 is narrowly and clearly drafted, tying the carve-out to licensure under the Education Law
Penalty structure in § 284-3 mirrors other town chapters (e.g., Ch. 312), giving consistent enforcement treatment across the code
concerns: Section 284-1's stated rationale — that the Town cannot staff a licensing/inspection scheme — predates New York's now-established statewide Body Art regulatory framework administered through county health departments, undermining the ban's original justification

Section 284-2 imposes a total prohibition on a legal commercial activity rather than a health-based licensing or permitting scheme, which is a substantially different (and more restrictive) approach than most peer municipalities take

The chapter has not been substantively revisited since 1998 (only the penalty section was amended, in 2020), despite significant intervening changes in how New York State regulates body art establishments
No coordination language referencing the Westchester County Department of Health, which is the entity that would normally administer any body-art licensing under the state framework
No mention of related practices such as permanent cosmetic makeup or piercing, leaving ambiguity about the ban's exact scope

recommendations.suggestion: Direct the Town Board to review § 284-1's findings and § 284-2's outright ban against New York's current statewide Body Art sanitary code framework, since a blanket municipal prohibition premised on the Town's inability to regulate may no longer hold up now that a state/county licensing structure exists.

Consider replacing the categorical ban in § 284-2 with a licensing/registration requirement coordinated with the Westchester County Department of Health, consistent with how most peer municipalities regulate tattoo establishments today.
Update the 1998-era findings in § 284-1 to reflect the current health regulatory landscape rather than relying on a 27-year-old resource-constraint justification.

chapters.peerComparison: Based on general professional knowledge rather than comparison to other specific municipal codes, most Westchester and downstate NY municipalities do not ban tattooing outright; instead they regulate tattoo and body-art establishments through health-permit/licensing coordination with the county health department under the state's Body Art sanitary code provisions. North Castle's Chapter 284 is unusual among peer towns in imposing a categorical ban rather than a licensing scheme, and that gap has widened as the state's regulatory infrastructure for body art has matured since this chapter's 1998 adoption.

chapters.title: Taxation
chapters.summary: Chapter 288 assembles ten articles of local real property tax exemptions and tax-collection procedures: the Alternative Veterans exemption (§ 288-1–288-2, RPTL § 458-a), a Senior Citizens/Persons-with-Disabilities sliding-scale income exemption (§ 288-3–288-4, RPTL §§ 467 and 459-c), a second, separately adopted Disabled Persons exemption (§ 288-6–288-9, also RPTL § 459-c), the STAR exemption (§ 288-10–288-11), a Volunteer Firefighters/Ambulance Workers exemption (§ 288-12–288-15), a Cold War Veterans exemption (§ 288-16–288-20), a Historic Property alteration/rehabilitation exemption (§ 288-21–288-23), an installment-payment plan for delinquent taxes (§ 288-24–288-29), a detailed 3% Room Occupancy (hotel/motel) Tax with full collection, refund, penalty and confidentiality machinery (§ 288-30–288-48), and rules for assessing converted condominiums (§ 288-49–288-50). It does not include a business investment (RPTL 485-b) or renewable-energy (RPTL 487) exemption.
chapters.ratingRationale: The Town properly overhauled the senior/disabled income schedule in § 288-4 on 2-14-2024 to the current statutory ceiling (up to $58,399.99 for a 5% exemption), but the separate Article III disability exemption in § 288-7 — implementing the identical RPTL § 459-c authority — still runs on the 2010/2011 'Schedule A' income table topping out at $37,399.99 and was never reconciled with the 2024 update, leaving two conflicting income ceilings on the books for the same exemption category.
strengths: Article II's senior/disabled income schedule (§ 288-3, § 288-4) was amended in its entirety on 2-14-2024 to the higher, current sliding-scale thresholds (up to $58,399.99), keeping pace with the state's 2022 RPTL income-cap increase
Cold War Veterans exemption (§ 288-19) was amended in 2018 to remove the ten-year sunset, correctly implementing Chapter 290 of the Laws of 2017
Alternative Veterans exemption (§ 288-2) layers basic, combat, and disability components per § 458-a and was last recalibrated in 2022 (dollar caps of $75,000/$50,000/$250,000)

Room Occupancy Tax article (§ 288-30–§ 288-48) is unusually thorough, with definitions, registration/certificate-of-authority procedures, recordkeeping, refunds, Article 78 review rights, penalties, and a confidentiality provision
Installment plan for delinquent taxes (§ 288-24–288-29) gives taxpayers a defined 24-month structured payment option tied to the Town's normal collection cycles under RPTL § 1184
concerns: Article III's disabled-persons exemption (§ 288-7, RPTL § 459-c) still cites the 2010 assessment-roll 'Schedule A' income table (max $37,399.99) while Article II's § 288-4 — the same statutory exemption — was updated in 2024 to a ceiling of $58,399.99; the chapter never repealed or harmonized the older article, so two different income thresholds coexist for what appears to be the same relief
§ 288-7E cross-references 'Chapter 470 of the Laws of Westchester County' alongside Article II without clarifying which schedule controls when both provisions purport to implement § 459-c

No Business Investment Exemption (RPTL § 485-b) or renewable-energy systems exemption (RPTL § 487) appears anywhere in the chapter, despite these being increasingly common local options for commercial/solar investment

The Room Occupancy Tax article's definitions of 'hotel' and 'operator' (§ 288-30) are framed around traditional lodging establishments and do not explicitly address short-term rental marketplace platforms
Historic Property exemption (§ 288-21) has not been amended since its 2011 adoption, so its interplay with any later updates to Chapter 195 (Landmarks) has not been revisited in this chapter

recommendations.suggestion: Reconcile or repeal Article III's § 288-7 disability-exemption schedule so it matches the current sliding-scale table adopted in § 288-4 (2-14-2024); maintaining two different RPTL § 459-c income ceilings in the same chapter risks inconsistent assessor administration and potential Article 78 challenges from residents denied under the stale table.

Add a Business Investment Exemption (RPTL § 485-b) and/or a renewable-energy systems exemption (RPTL § 487) to Chapter 288, since neither currently exists, leaving commercial and solar/wind investment tax treatment undefined at the local level.

Amend the Room Occupancy Tax's 'hotel' and 'operator' definitions in § 288-30 to expressly reach short-term rental marketplace platforms, mirroring how many Westchester municipalities have updated hotel-tax chapters for Airbnb/Vrbo-type bookings.

Build in a recurring (e.g., biennial) review clause for the fixed dollar caps in § 288-2 (veterans, $75,000/$50,000/$250,000) and § 288-18 (Cold War veterans, $12,000/$40,000) so these amounts are revisited on a schedule rather than only through ad hoc local law amendments.

Clarify in § 288-4/§ 288-7 which article a disabled applicant should file under, or consolidate the two disability-exemption articles into one, so residents and the Assessor's office are not left guessing which income schedule applies.

chapters.peerComparison: Based on general familiarity with Westchester and Hudson Valley town tax codes rather than a document-to-document comparison: North Castle's 2024 update of the senior/disabled income ceiling to roughly $58,400 for a full sliding scale is in line with, or slightly ahead of, many peer towns that were slower to adopt the state's 2022 RPTL increase raising the maximum local option above the old $37,400 cap. Its adoption of the Cold War Veterans exemption (Article VI) and the volunteer firefighter/ambulance worker exemption (Article V) matches common practice among Westchester towns, most of which adopted these optional exemptions in the 2000s. Where North Castle looks behind the curve is the absence of a Business Investment Exemption (RPTL 485-b) and a renewable-energy systems exemption (RPTL 487), both of which a growing number of Westchester and Putnam towns have added in the last decade to address solar installations and light commercial/industrial investment; and the unreconciled duplicate disability-exemption schedule (Article II vs. Article III) is the kind of legacy-code drafting artifact that peer towns typically clean up during a codification refresh but that persists here.

recordEvidence.note: Senior-citizen and disability exemption amendments only, following a January 18, 2024 memo from Town Assessor George Ann Richardson, moving through Town Board January 25 and February 14, 2024, with earlier cycles February 16, 2022 and February 8, 2023 — routine, externally driven by New York State exemption changes rather than local initiative.

chapters.title: Telecommunication Facilities
chapters.summary: Chapter 292 is North Castle's Wireless Communications Facilities Law, adopted in 2021 to replace a 1997 predecessor. It sets out separate, parallel regimes for tower-based facilities (§292-4, special permit from the Town Board, allowed in most business/industrial districts and, by special permit, in every residential district), non-tower building/structure-mounted facilities (§292-5, Planning Board review with residential building attachment barred), and small wireless facilities in the public rights-of-way (§292-6, Planning Board approval with 60/90-day shot clocks). All three tracks include a streamlined "eligible facilities request" building-permit path for modifications that don't substantially change a structure's dimensions, plus detailed siting setbacks, historic/environmental buffers, collocation-first requirements, bonding, annual RF-emissions certification, and abandonment/removal rules. A separate article (§292-8) imposes extensive insurance and indemnification obligations, and §292-7/292-9 cover Town-property use, penalties, and severability.
chapters.ratingRationale: The chapter is comprehensive and its timing provisions largely track the FCC's presumptively-reasonable shot clocks (150 days for new towers, 90 days for non-tower/collocation, and 60/90 days for small WCF collocation vs. new-structure applications in §292-6A(3)), which is good current practice. But it also carries clear signs of an unlocalized template: §292-7B sets penalties before a "magisterial district judge," a Pennsylvania court title with no New York equivalent, and §292-5(15)/§292-6(10) direct RF-compliance filings to a "Municipal Secretary" that appears nowhere else in the Town's Code (elsewhere it is the Town Clerk).
strengths: Detailed, well-organized siting standards for towers including 150-foot height cap, 90-foot separation rule, and buffers from historic districts (100 feet, §292-4A(12)), open space/conserved land, and endangered-species habitat (500 feet, §292-4A(9))
Collocation-first policy with a documented good-faith-effort requirement before a new tower may be approved (§292-4A(5))
Robust removal/abandonment provisions (six months for towers, three months for non-tower facilities) with municipal self-help and lien rights if the owner fails to remove (§292-4A(21), §292-5(20))
Extensive insurance, bonding ($75,000 plus removal-cost estimate), and indemnification requirements protecting the Town from liability (§292-4A(30), §292-8)
Includes a small wireless facilities article with FCC-aligned 60/90-day shot clocks and a reference to a separate Small WCF Design Manual (§292-6(15))
concerns: §292-7B's penalty clause refers to a "magisterial district judge" — a Pennsylvania judicial office not used in New York — indicating boilerplate carried over from an out-of-state model ordinance without being localized
§292-5(15) and §292-6(10) direct RF-emissions compliance filings to a "Municipal Secretary," inconsistent with the "Town Clerk" designation used throughout the rest of the chapter

The eligible facilities request provisions (§292-4A(24), §292-5(8), §292-6(4)) use only the vague phrase "does not substantially change the dimensions" and never cross-reference the FCC's specific quantitative substantial-change thresholds in 47 C.F.R. §1.6100, leaving room for Section 6409(a) disputes
Flat $500-per-offense penalty cap (§292-7B) is very low relative to the scale of wireless infrastructure being regulated

Tower-based WCF are permitted by special permit in nearly every single-family residential district in town (R-4A through R-5, plus R-2F and R-MF) per §292-4A(2)(a)[2], a notably broad allowance for residential character

Small WCF fee and annual ROW compensation provisions (§292-6(6), §292-6(20)) do not reference the FCC's 2018 Small Cell Order fee-safe-harbor amounts, creating some preemption risk if the Master Fee Schedule sets fees above federal limits

recommendations.suggestion: Correct §292-7B's reference to a "magisterial district judge" to the appropriate New York forum (e.g., Town of North Castle Justice Court) so the penalty provision is actually enforceable.
Replace "Municipal Secretary" with "Town Clerk" in §292-5(15) and §292-6(10) to match the officer designated everywhere else in the chapter and avoid confusion for applicants and staff.

Amend the eligible facilities request sections (§292-4A(24), §292-5(8), §292-6(4)) to expressly incorporate the quantitative "substantial change" criteria from 47 C.F.R. §1.6100 (e.g., 10%/20-foot height increase, equipment-compound expansion limits) to reduce Section 6409(a) litigation exposure.
Cross-reference the FCC's small-cell fee safe harbors in §292-6(6) and §292-6(20) so the Master Fee Schedule amounts for small WCF applications and ROW use stay within federally defensible limits.

Revisit allowing tower-based WCF by special permit in nearly all single-family residential zoning districts (§292-4A(2)(a)[2]) or add residential-specific design/screening conditions beyond the general stealth-technology standard.
Reconsider the flat $500-per-offense penalty ceiling in §292-7B, which has not been indexed and is low compared to the cost of wireless infrastructure noncompliance.

chapters.peerComparison: Based on general familiarity with Westchester-area wireless siting ordinances (not a document-to-document comparison): North Castle's 2021 chapter is on the more thorough end for insurance, bonding, indemnification, and abandonment/removal detail, and its 150-day tower / 90-day collocation / 60-90-day small-cell timelines correctly mirror the FCC's presumptively-reasonable shot clocks from the 2009 Declaratory Ruling and 2018 Small Cell Order — many peer towns' older ordinances still lack the small-WCF article altogether. Where it lags typical current-generation peer ordinances is in Eligible Facilities Request precision: most modern Westchester/Hudson Valley wireless laws explicitly cite 47 C.F.R. §1.6100 and spell out the FCC's quantitative substantial-change thresholds, while North Castle's chapter uses only generic "does not substantially change the dimensions" language, leaving more room for dispute under Section 6409(a). The leftover "magisterial district judge" and "Municipal Secretary" references are a strong indicator the law was adapted from a national or Pennsylvania-based model ordinance template without full localization — a pattern seen in a number of municipal telecom codes drafted this way, and worth a clean-up amendment even though it does not undermine the chapter's substantive siting and safety standards.

chapters.title: Towing
chapters.summary: Chapter 300 sets the requirements a tow company must meet to be placed on the North Castle Police Department's official tow list, including 24/7 availability, target response times (25 minutes for light-duty, 50 minutes for heavy-duty towing), a 24-hour business phone line, business recordkeeping, a storage yard within three miles of the Town's boundaries, and detailed insurance/indemnification requirements naming the Town as an additional insured or providing contractual liability coverage. It requires towing rates to be 'fair and equitable... not excessive,' to be assessed via a countywide survey if a dispute arises, and requires the Town's Risk Manager to review and approve insurance policies, with the Chief of Police's office as the point of contact.
chapters.ratingRationale: Section 300-1G's rate standard — 'fair and equitable... not excessive,' assessed by 'a random countywide survey should the need arise' (§ 300-1G) — sets no actual maximum dollar rate, drop fee, mileage fee, or storage fee, leaving consumers with no published ceiling to check a bill against. The chapter also has no stated consumer-facing provisions (e.g., accepted payment methods, itemized invoice requirements, or a complaint/dispute process) and no explicit procedure in the text for removing a noncompliant company from the tow list, despite otherwise-detailed operational and insurance requirements.
strengths: Concrete, measurable response-time targets for light-duty (25 minutes) and heavy-duty (50 minutes) towing (§ 300-1B)
Storage yard proximity requirement (within three miles of Town boundaries, § 300-1H) protects vehicle owners from having to travel far to redeem impounded vehicles
Detailed, itemized insurance and indemnification requirements including specific coverage types and a 30-day cancellation-notice requirement (§ 300-1L, M)
Requires Police Department verification of tow operators' driver's licenses and vehicle registration/insurance (§ 300-1O, P), adding an accountability check beyond the tow company's own records
concerns: No defined maximum towing or storage rate — § 300-1G's 'fair and equitable... not excessive' standard, backed only by a survey conducted 'should the need arise,' gives consumers no published rate ceiling to rely on
No consumer protection provisions addressing accepted payment methods (e.g., credit cards), itemized receipts, or a formal complaint/dispute resolution process for vehicle owners
No explicit removal/revocation procedure in the chapter text for a tow company found to violate these requirements — only listing requirements are specified

Substantive requirements (response times, rates, storage-yard distance) have not been revisited since the 2006 entire-chapter rewrite; the only amendment since then (11-18-2015) touched insurance provisions only (§ 300-1L, M)
No towing license fee or renewal/inspection cadence is specified for staying on the tow list

recommendations.suggestion: Replace the vague 'fair and equitable... not excessive' rate standard in § 300-1G with an actual published maximum rate schedule (updated periodically via countywide survey), so residents whose vehicles are towed have a concrete rate to check their bill against.

Add an explicit tow-list removal/suspension procedure for companies that violate § 300-1's requirements, since the chapter currently only describes qualification criteria, not consequences for noncompliance.

Clarify in § 300-1F what specific 'special request' triggers after-hours personnel obligations and how tow companies are compensated for that added availability, to reduce ambiguity for companies seeking to join the tow list.
Formalize the 'random countywide survey should the need arise' language in § 300-1G into a defined periodic review cycle (e.g., every 2-3 years) rather than an ad hoc, undefined trigger.

chapters.peerComparison: Based on general professional knowledge of New York municipal and Westchester County practice (not a document-to-document comparison), many municipalities' towing ordinances specify concrete maximum rates or rate caps, mandatory credit-card acceptance, itemized invoice requirements, and a defined complaint or hearing process for consumers disputing a tow — features aimed squarely at preventing predatory towing. North Castle's Chapter 300 is comparatively thin on these consumer-facing protections: its rate-fairness standard in § 300-1G is aspirational rather than a defined cap, and the chapter reads more as an operational qualification checklist for the Police Department's own tow list than as a consumer protection ordinance, which is a narrower approach than some peer municipalities have adopted.

chapters.title: Trapping
chapters.summary: This short chapter restricts trapping methods to protect children and companion animals: it bans steel-jaw leghold traps, conibear traps, and harmful snares within 500 feet of any residential building (including dwellings located outside the Town), and prohibits trapping altogether on Town-owned property, though nonlethal animal removal is still permitted there. It exempts private landowners (and those with the landowner's written permission) acting entirely on their own property, and layers Town penalties on top of the licensing and seasonal restrictions already imposed by NYS Environmental Conservation Law Article 11. Penalties escalate from a violation on a first offense to a misdemeanor for a repeat offense within 10 years.
chapters.ratingRationale: The chapter is narrowly scoped and has not been amended since its 2007 adoption. It accomplishes its core purpose with a clear numeric buffer — a 500-foot no-trapping zone around residential buildings (SS 304-3) and a flat ban on Town-owned property (SS 304-4) — but it leaves out details common in more developed local trapping laws, such as trap-check frequency or a Town permit/notification system, relying instead on a general cross-reference to state ECL Article 11 licensing (SS 304-1C).
strengths: Clear, enforceable numeric buffer of 500 feet from residential buildings, explicitly extended to dwellings located outside the Town (SS 304-3)
Outright ban on trapping on Town-owned property while still allowing nonlethal removal methods to address public health and welfare (SS 304-4)
Tiered penalty structure that escalates a repeat offense within 10 years from a violation to a misdemeanor (SS 304-6A)
Private-landowner exception requires the permission-holder to carry written proof and exhibit it to law enforcement on request (SS 304-5B), giving the exemption some enforceability
concerns: No Town permit or registration requirement for trappers, unlike some peer local trapping laws
No definition of how the 500-foot distance is measured (from property line, structure wall, or trap location), inviting disputes
No trap-check or trap-tending frequency requirement, a common companion provision elsewhere meant to limit the duration an animal can be caught before suffering or death
Enforcement is assigned to the Building Inspector (SS 304-6B), which is an unusual fit for wildlife/trapping enforcement compared to police or animal control in many peer towns
The private-property exception (SS 304-5A) requires only that prohibited activity not 'cross onto the lands of another owner,' without any notice-to-Town or record-keeping requirement

recommendations.suggestion: Add a mandatory trap-check frequency (e.g., inspection at least once every 24 hours) to reduce the risk to companion animals and wildlife caught in traps for extended periods, since the current chapter (SS 304-3, SS 304-5) is silent on tending frequency.

Explicitly cross-reference NYS ECL Article 11 licensing requirements within the substantive sections (not just the general SS 304-1C reference) so Town enforcement can verify state license status as part of any complaint investigation.
Define the measurement methodology for the 500-foot buffer in SS 304-3 (e.g., nearest point of the residential structure to the trap location) to prevent line-drawing disputes during enforcement.

chapters.peerComparison: Based on general professional knowledge, not a document-to-document comparison: NYS Environmental Conservation Law Article 11 sets statewide trapping licensure, methods, and seasons, and it is common for suburban Westchester towns to layer a local overlay restricting trap types or imposing setbacks from dwellings in response to companion-animal safety complaints. North Castle's 500-foot residential buffer and Town-property ban (SS 304-3, SS 304-4) are a fairly standard version of this kind of local law, but it sits on the lighter end of the spectrum compared to peer ordinances that also require a local trapping permit/notification system and impose a trap-check frequency requirement, both of which are absent here.

chapters.title: Trees
chapters.summary: Chapter 308 governs the planting, maintenance, and preservation of trees in North Castle. Article I (adopted 1987) establishes a five-member Tree Board, an official street tree species list (Appendix A), planting/spacing/utility-clearance standards, and rules for pruning, topping, and removal of public trees. Article II (adopted 2002) creates a tree-removal permit system for private property, defining "significant trees" (24-inch DBH or greater), regulated setback zones by zoning district, and clearing/thinning thresholds, backed by a mitigation bank/fee-in-lieu and a diameter-based replacement requirement.
chapters.ratingRationale: The chapter pairs a detailed permit process (§308-15 through §308-24) with a concrete enforcement mechanism — aggregate-diameter tree replacement plus a Tree Mitigation Bank fee-in-lieu option (§308-25C) — that many neighboring towns lack, and penalties were updated as recently as 2020 (L.L. No. 3-2020). It loses points because the base "tree" threshold (8-inch DBH, §308-12) is on the permissive end and the chapter sets no town-wide canopy-cover goal.
strengths: Regulated setback zone table tied to zoning district (25 feet in R-4A down to 5 feet in denser districts) gives clear, district-specific protection (§308-12).
Replacement is tied to the aggregate diameter of trees removed, not just tree count, with a Tree Mitigation Bank fee-in-lieu option dedicated to planting or invasive removal (§308-25C).
Clear procedural due process: a stop-work order triggers a mandatory hearing within 10 days of request (§308-19), with an appeal path to the Conservation Board (§308-22).
Explicit exemptions for NYS RPTL §480-a forest management and licensed cemetery associations (§308-14) avoid overreach into legitimate land uses.
concerns: "Tree" is defined at only 8 inches DBH (§308-12), a relatively low threshold that pulls many ordinary landscape trees into the permit system.
No town-wide tree canopy percentage or numeric replacement-ratio target — replacement is diameter-based only (§308-25C(2)), where peer towns often also require a per-tree ratio.

Article I (planting, 1987) and Article II (removal, 2002) were adopted 15 years apart, and "tree" is left undefined in Article I while only defined with an 8-inch DBH threshold in Article II (§308-12), creating minor internal inconsistency.

Penalty provisions were last touched in 2020 only to raise fines (§308-10, §308-25); the underlying permit thresholds and the Appendix A species list have not been revisited since 2002 and 1987, respectively.

recommendations.suggestion: Consider adding a numeric town-wide tree-canopy or per-tree replacement-ratio target (e.g., minimum two replacement trees per significant tree removed) to complement the aggregate-diameter formula in §308-25C(2).

Reconcile the undefined "tree" in Article I with the 8-inch DBH definition adopted for Article II in §308-12 to avoid ambiguity over which trees the Town's pruning/removal rights in §308-6 and §308-8 actually reach.
Update the Appendix A recommended street tree species list, unchanged since 1987, to reflect current climate-resilient and native species guidance.
For minor projects already streamlined under §308-15B, consider a categorical fee reduction or a review timeline shorter than the general 14-day determination window in §308-16E.

chapters.peerComparison: Based on general knowledge of Westchester County practice rather than a document-to-document comparison, North Castle's tree-removal permit threshold (any significant tree of 24-inch DBH, or clearing of more than five 8-inch-plus trees per quarter acre) is roughly in line with comparable Westchester towns such as Bedford, New Castle, and Mount Kisco, several of which use similar DBH-based significant-tree thresholds. North Castle's diameter-based replacement formula plus a dedicated Tree Mitigation Bank is a somewhat more sophisticated enforcement tool than the flat per-tree replacement fees used in some peer codes, though towns with more aggressive climate/canopy goals increasingly pair such permits with an explicit percentage tree-canopy retention target that North Castle's chapter does not include.

recordEvidence.note: A second, targeted pass built specifically to find criticism of tree provisions produced 9 candidates, all application-specific or procedural — no criticism retained. §308-25(C)(4) provides a fee-in-lieu/replacement mechanism and the chapter includes a 2002 preservation article, so this plausibly is a well-functioning chapter — but the transcript record is too thin to say so with confidence. This is silence from lack of testing, not the confirmed adequacy Chapter 340 demonstrates.

chapters.title: Trespassing
chapters.summary: Chapter 312 lets landowners protect their property from trespass by posting statutorily-specified notices and, alternatively, by personal service of a written no-trespass notice. Section 312-3 dictates exact notice dimensions, spacing (no more than 20 rods apart, one per side and corner), required warning text, and provides that filing a posting affidavit with the Town Clerk is presumptive proof of compliance. Section 312-4 sets the penalty at up to a $1,000 fine and/or 15 days imprisonment, with each continuing day treated as a separate offense.
chapters.ratingRationale: The chapter is short, internally consistent, and its penalty clause was updated as recently as 2020 (L.L. No. 3-2020), but the core posting mechanics in § 312-3 still use archaic units ('20 rods') and predate New York's 2022 amendment authorizing purple-paint markings as an alternative to signage, which the chapter does not reference at all.
strengths: Section 312-3 gives objective, measurable posting requirements (11-inch minimum sign size, spacing, corner placement) that reduce disputes over adequate notice
The affidavit-filing mechanism in § 312-3 (filed with the Town Clerk) creates an efficient, low-cost way for owners to establish presumptive proof of compliance
Penalty provision in § 312-4 was refreshed in 2020, keeping fine/imprisonment levels current
concerns: Section 312-3 measures spacing in 'rods' (a unit of roughly 16.5 feet), which is confusing to modern landowners and enforcement officers and has no cross-reference to feet
No reference anywhere in the chapter to New York's purple-paint marking option now recognized as an alternative to signage for posted land
The chapter does not cross-reference Penal Law Article 140 trespass degrees, leaving the relationship between this local violation and state criminal trespass charges unstated
Section 312-1 speaks only to 'owners' and persons with a 'right to possession,' without addressing modern issues like drone overflight or short-term posting for special events

recommendations.suggestion: Amend § 312-3 to recognize purple-paint tree/post marking as an alternative to physical signage, consistent with the state provision New York adopted for posted-property notice, so the local code doesn't leave landowners relying on an incomplete option set.
Convert the '20 rods apart' spacing requirement in § 312-3 into feet (approximately 330 feet) to eliminate ambiguity for code enforcement and residents unfamiliar with the rod as a unit of measure.
Add a cross-reference in § 312-4 clarifying how this local violation interacts with Penal Law Article 140 criminal trespass charges so police have clear guidance on which charge to pursue.

chapters.peerComparison: Based on general knowledge of Westchester County municipal codes rather than any comparison to other specific documents, a locally-adopted posted-property/trespass-notice chapter modeled on the same boilerplate (minimum sign size, spacing measured in rods, Town Clerk affidavit filing) is extremely common among towns of North Castle's era and size, many of which trace back to similar 1960s-1980s local laws. North Castle's version is fairly typical for the region and is neither noticeably more protective nor more lax than peer towns, though like many of those peer codes it has not been updated to reference the state's newer purple-paint marking alternative.

chapters.title: Vehicles and Traffic
chapters.summary: Chapter 325 governs traffic control, vehicle dimensions/weights, stopping/standing/parking, snow-emergency parking bans, and vehicle removal and impoundment in North Castle, with the Town Board and Police Department as the principal enforcing authorities. Article VII implements a 23-schedule system (§§ 325-43 through 325-65) that lists the specific streets, intersections, and hours to which each substantive regulation (stop signs, one-way streets, no-parking zones, time-limited parking, handicapped spaces, crosswalks, etc.) applies. The schedules are street-by-street and are amended piecemeal by local law whenever the Town adds or removes a sign or restriction, with entries dating from the chapter's 1987 adoption through late 2025. Several enabling sections (e.g., through highways, U-turns, lane designations, loading zones, angle parking, bus stops, taxi stands) have corresponding schedules that are entirely "(Reserved)" — no locations have ever been entered even though the underlying regulatory sections remain in force.
