chapters.ratingRationale: The schedule system is genuinely kept alive — Schedule IIA/III got a new Cross Road North entry on 12-10-2025 and Schedule XIII got Old Mount Kisco Road entries on 6-11-2025, showing recent, real maintenance activity. But several core schedules the chapter's own sections point to — Schedule VI (Through Highways, § 325-48), Schedule XI (Lane Designations, § 325-53), and Schedules XVIII-XXI (Loading Zones, Angle Parking, Bus Stops, Taxi Stands, §§ 325-60 through 325-63) — are marked "(Reserved)" with zero entries, and Schedule XXII (Handicapped Parking, § 325-64) lists only a single space on Kent Place, which is thin for a full town.
strengths: Schedule system (Article VII, §§ 325-43 to 325-65) is actively amended into 2025, e.g. Cross Road North turn/one-way entries added 12-10-2025 and Old Mount Kisco Road no-parking zones added 6-11-2025 by L.L. No. 3-2025
Vehicle dimension and weight limits (§ 325-16) closely track NYS formulas (including the axle-weight formula W = 500((L x N)/(N-1) + (12 x N) + 36)), reducing conflict with state law
Layered, escalating penalty structure for repeat offenses in § 325-4 and detailed graduated fine schedules by excess weight in § 325-16B

Dedicated Article V (Safe Roadways) codifies a clear seasonal overnight parking ban (Nov. 15-Apr. 1, 1:00 a.m.-6:00 a.m., § 325-37) to support snow removal, plus a snow/ice deposit prohibition (§ 325-39)
Clear chain from enabling section to schedule for every regulation type, making the code's cross-reference structure easy to navigate despite its length
concerns: Schedules VI, XI, XII, XVIII, XIX, XX, and XXI (Through Highways, Lane Designations, No-Passing Zones, Loading Zones, Angle Parking, Bus Stops, Taxi Stands) are all marked "(Reserved)" with no locations ever entered, even though §§ 325-11, 325-17, 325-18, 325-28, 325-29, 325-30, and 325-31 all describe active regulatory authority for them
Schedule I (Traffic Control Signals, § 325-43) lists only one signalized intersection (Bedford Road and Maple Avenue) for the entire Town, which appears incomplete

Schedule XXII (Handicapped Parking, § 325-64) designates only one space (Kent Place) despite the Town Hall Complex, Community Center, and other municipal lots being referenced elsewhere in the chapter

Towing and storage fee caps have not been adjusted for inflation: § 325-38 caps towing charges at $50 and § 325-41 caps removal/storage at $50 plus $10/day, figures that are unlikely to cover actual contractor costs today

No provisions anywhere in the chapter for electric-vehicle charging spaces (designation, signage, or enforcement against ICE vehicles occupying them), a feature increasingly common in peer municipal codes
General penalty ceiling in § 325-4 (max $250 fine on a third conviction within 18 months) is modest by current standards and has not been revisited since the chapter's original adoption

recommendations.suggestion: Resolve the seven "(Reserved)" schedules (§§ 325-48, 325-53, 325-54, 325-60, 325-61, 325-62, 325-63) by either populating them with the Town's actual through-highways, loading zones, bus stops, and taxi stands, or repealing the corresponding enabling sections so the code does not imply regulations exist where none have been adopted.

Expand Schedule XXII (§ 325-64) beyond the single Kent Place space to cover ADA-compliant handicapped parking at the Town Hall Complex, Community Center, and other municipal lots already referenced in § 325-33, closing a compliance gap.

Add an EV charging space designation/enforcement provision (mirroring the handicapped-parking model in § 325-35 and Schedule XXII) since the chapter currently has no mechanism to reserve or protect EV charging spots.

Revisit the towing and storage fee caps in §§ 325-38 and 325-41 ($50 towing, $50 removal/$10 per day storage), which are likely below current market rates and may be shifting real costs onto the Town or the towing contractor.

Audit Schedule I (§ 325-43) against the Town's actual inventory of signalized intersections; a single-entry schedule for traffic control signals is a strong signal this table has not been updated alongside physical installations.

chapters.peerComparison: This is a general professional assessment based on familiarity with common Westchester/NY municipal traffic chapters, not a document-to-document comparison. The overall structure — a short set of enabling sections in the main chapter body paired with a lettered/numbered set of street-by-street schedules amended by individual local laws — is the standard General Code/ecode360 template used by most Westchester towns (including neighboring municipalities), and North Castle's pattern of frequent small amendments (multiple entries added in 2020, 2021, 2022, 2024, and 2025) is consistent with active, well-functioning schedule maintenance rather than neglect. Where this chapter lags typical current practice is in two areas increasingly seen in peer towns: (1) explicit EV charging space designation and enforcement language, which a growing number of NY municipalities have added in the last five years as EV adoption has risen; and (2) complete-streets/traffic-calming cross-references (e.g., speed humps, road diets, bicycle facilities) which some peer codes now fold into their traffic chapters — North Castle's chapter, like many older codes, still frames traffic control almost entirely around signs, signals, and vehicle-parking restrictions.

recordEvidence.verdict: Criticism concentrated in schedules and sight distance
recordEvidence.amendmentTraffic: Maintained almost entirely through its numbered schedules rather than its substantive 1987 text: §325-12 amended June 22 and July 27, 2022; a 2026 package amended §325-44 Schedule IIA (one-way streets), §325-55, and §325-33 (parking lots) together (May 13 and 27, 2026). The sole uncodified item in the eCode360 New Laws queue as of the code's current date — Local Law 3 of 2026, “Quarry Hts One Way and No Parking” — amends this chapter.

The only reason why you're asking for a variance is because your code doesn't allow for that.
findings.corroboration: Applicant testimony, discounted accordingly — but unusually specific: it names the governing national standard (AASHTO) and a measured figure, asserting the local rule exceeds what safety requires.

chapters.title: Water
chapters.summary: Chapter 336 governs the Town's seven public water districts (Nos. 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8 and 9), each with a nearly identical set of rules covering applications for service, tapping and connection specifications, meter installation and testing, service discontinuance, water rates (all deferred to the Master Fee Schedule), billing/collection and tax-lien enforcement, and district liability disclaimers. Article III sets out a detailed, chapter-wide cross-connection control program (backflow prevention devices, hazard-tiered protection, annual testing) that applies across all districts. Article VII establishes a capital-cost assessment formula specific to Water District No. 7, and Article X (added 2024) centralizes hydrant-fee billing for several districts. The chapter contains no water-conservation or drought-management framework beyond a generic reservation of rights to restrict outdoor sprinkling.
chapters.ratingRationale: The chapter is actively maintained (Districts 8 and 9 and the Hydrants article were all added or rewritten in 2024-2025) and sensibly defers all dollar figures to the Master Fee Schedule, but it still shows a drafting error carried into the newest article (§ 336-348 mis-cites District No. 8 instead of No. 9), no water-conservation/drought provisions anywhere, and inconsistent administrative deadlines and hydrant-fee coverage across the seven nearly-identical district articles.
strengths: Article III's cross-connection control program (§§ 336-110 through 336-123) gives detailed, hazard-tiered backflow-prevention requirements (air-gap separation, approved double check valve assemblies, reduced-pressure devices) with annual testing and recordkeeping duties — a technically thorough public-health safeguard for a chapter of this size.

Water rates and nearly all fees (tap charges, meter fees, turn-on/turn-off charges, final meter reading fee) are consistently pointed to the Master Fee Schedule (Ch. A370, e.g. § 336-47, § 336-101) rather than hard-coded in the law, so routine fee changes don't require chapter amendments.

The chapter shows active recent upkeep: a uniform 'final water meter reading fee' was added to five districts in 2024 (§§ 336-55.1, 336-109.1, 336-178.1, 336-233.1, 336-288.1), and two new districts (Article VIII, IX) and a consolidated Hydrants article (Article X) were adopted in 2024-2025.

The senior-citizen 50% water-rate discount tied to registration on the Town's age-exempt list and RPTL § 467 eligibility (e.g. § 336-47B, § 336-101B) is applied identically across every district, giving low-income seniors predictable relief.

Water District No. 2's rate section (§ 336-101A) includes an explicit fallback mechanism letting the district levy an additional assessment, after notice and public hearing, if rate revenue falls short of budgeted needs — a fiscal safety valve most of the other districts lack.
concerns: § 336-348, the opening compliance section of the brand-new Article IX (Water District No. 9, adopted 3-12-2025 by L.L. No. 2-2025), states that acceptance of a permit signifies assent to the rules of 'North Castle Water District No. 8' rather than No. 9 — an uncorrected cross-reference error in the chapter's newest article.

No district contains a water-conservation, drought-stage, or outdoor-watering-restriction framework; liability sections in every article (e.g. § 336-43, § 336-165, § 336-220, § 336-389) only vaguely reserve 'the right ... to prohibit the use of water for sprinkling of lawns or gardens' with no defined trigger, stages, or enforcement procedure.

Article X (§ 336-404, added 2024) authorizes hydrant-fee billing only for Water District Nos. 1, 2, 4, 5 and 8 — Districts 7 and 9 are left out with no stated reason, leaving those districts' hydrant cost recovery unaddressed in the chapter.

The annual cutoff date for transferring unpaid water rents to the tax roll is inconsistent across districts for no explained reason: District 1 (§ 336-50) uses 'February 1 of the following year' while Districts 2, 4, 5, 7, 8 and 9 (e.g. § 336-103, § 336-171, § 336-226, § 336-281, § 336-339, § 336-395) all use 'October 31 of each year.'

The chapter duplicates roughly 50 nearly identical administrative/technical sections (tap specs, meter rules, billing/collection procedures) across seven separate district articles, producing 400+ numbered sections and 240,000+ characters; any substantive change (like the 2024 final-meter-reading fee) has to be manually copied into each article, creating real drafting-drift risk.

Water Districts No. 3 and No. 6 do not exist in the current chapter (the Derivation Table shows the corresponding 1987 Code article was 'Reserved/Omitted'), but the chapter itself gives residents no explanation or cross-reference for the missing numbers.

recommendations.suggestion: Correct § 336-348's reference to 'North Castle Water District No. 8' so it properly reads 'No. 9' — a misdirected cross-reference in a district's foundational compliance clause is an unnecessary opening for a consumer to dispute that the rules validly bind District 9 service.

Replace the generic 'reserves the right to prohibit sprinkling' language repeated in every district's liability section (e.g. § 336-43, § 336-165) with a real water-conservation/drought-management article defining conservation stages, triggers, and enforceable outdoor-use restrictions, as many peer Westchester water districts have adopted.

Consolidate the ~50 duplicated tap, meter, and billing-procedure sections common to Districts 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8 and 9 into a single set of chapter-wide general provisions, leaving each article to cover only district-specific rates, boundaries, and history — reducing the 400+ section sprawl and the risk of the kind of copy-paste error found in § 336-348.

Standardize the delinquent-water-rent-to-tax-lien cutoff date, currently February 1 for District 1 (§ 336-50) but October 31 for every other district (e.g. § 336-103, § 336-226), so the Receiver of Taxes and residents aren't tracking two different annual deadlines for what is otherwise an identical collection program.

Extend the Article X hydrant-fee billing mechanism (§ 336-404) to Water Districts 7 and 9, or add language explaining why those two districts are excluded, so hydrant-maintenance cost recovery is transparent and consistent across all seven districts.

chapters.peerComparison: Based on general professional familiarity with Westchester and lower-Hudson-Valley town water codes rather than a document-to-document comparison, North Castle's Chapter 336 follows a common legacy pattern for small towns with multiple special-benefit water districts: near-verbatim rules replicated per district, rates deferred to a master fee schedule, and a 1970s-vintage cross-connection control article modeled on the standard state/EPA backflow-prevention template of that era — all fairly typical and, on the cross-connection side, appropriately detailed. Where this chapter lags many comparable Westchester water utilities is in modern drought/water-emergency provisions (stage-based outdoor-watering bans, mandatory-conservation triggers, and defined penalties), which a number of peer towns facing supply-stressed aquifers or shared-reservoir sourcing have adopted explicitly rather than relying on a bare reservation-of-rights clause. Its practice of pushing all rate and fee figures into a separately maintained Master Fee Schedule is a genuinely current best practice that avoids the stale-dollar-figure problem common in older ordinances, though the chapter's sheer structural redundancy (seven parallel district articles instead of one consolidated set of general provisions) is more duplicative than typical current drafting practice, which usually consolidates common provisions and reserves district-specific articles for boundaries, capital charges, and rates only.

recordEvidence.note: Amended September 11, 2024 to permit collection of hydrant fees in Water Districts 1, 2, 4, 5, and 8. No criticism retained.

chapters.title: Wetlands and Watercourse Protection
chapters.summary: Chapter 340 regulates all wetlands, watercourses, water bodies and their buffers in North Castle, defining 'wetland' to include any size wetland (including vernal pools) rather than only the 12.4-acre state-jurisdictional threshold under NYS Freshwater Wetlands Act § 24-0107 (§ 340-3). A 100-foot buffer applies around wetlands/watercourses, expanding to up to 150 feet where slopes over 25% drain toward the resource (§ 340-3). Most activities in a wetland or buffer require either a Planning Board wetland permit (§ 340-4B) or, for one- and two-family parcels with limited-impact work, an administrative permit issued by the Building Inspector in consultation with the Town Wetland Consultant (§ 340-4C), with the Residential Project Review Committee triaging which track applies (§ 340-5C). Unavoidable impacts require a mitigation plan compensating losses at a 2:1 ratio for both wetland and buffer, with an option for the applicant to pay into a Town wetland mitigation bank in lieu of on-site mitigation (§ 340-9). Enforcement includes civil penalties up to $1,000 per day, escalating criminal fines ($1,000-$2,000 first offense; $3,000-$25,000 or up to six months' imprisonment for repeat offenses), injunctive relief, and restoration orders, with appeals routed to the Zoning Board of Appeals and then Article 78 review (§§ 340-16 through 340-18).
chapters.ratingRationale: The chapter is detailed and internally coherent, with a technically grounded definitions section tied to the 1989 Federal wetland delineation manual and NYS ECL Article 24 (§ 340-3), a buffer standard that scales with slope, and a fully built-out mitigation/monitoring/enforcement scheme (§§ 340-9, 340-12, 340-16). It has also been kept current through five rounds of amendment from 2013 to 2021, most recently updating the administrative permit and Building Inspector procedures (§ 340-5, § 340-6D, L.L. No. 2-2021). It falls short of top marks because § 340-4B and § 340-4C list nearly identical activities for full Planning Board review versus administrative permit, with the dividing line left to a subjective 'limited in scope' determination (§ 340-3, ADMINISTRATIVE PERMIT), and because it leans on a 2012 Environmental Map that the definitions section itself says is 'not site-specific' (§ 340-3, ENVIRONMENTAL MAP OF NORTH CASTLE).
strengths: Defines 'wetland' to reach all wetlands regardless of size, including vernal/woodland pools, closing the gap left by NYS DEC's 12.4-acre jurisdictional minimum (§ 340-3, WETLAND definition).

Buffer width is slope-sensitive, expanding from 100 feet up to 150 feet where steep slopes over 25% drain toward the resource, rather than using a single flat setback (§ 340-3, WETLAND BUFFER definition).

Mitigation policy is specific and enforceable: 2:1 replacement ratios, a defined order of preference (avoidance, minimization, rectification, reduction), required monitoring of at least five years, and a fee-in-lieu wetland mitigation bank option added in 2018 (§§ 340-9, 340-12).

Layered enforcement combining civil penalties, escalating criminal fines and imprisonment, injunctive relief, and mandatory restoration orders, plus a clear appeal path to the ZBA and Article 78 judicial review (§§ 340-16, 340-17, 340-18).

Escrow and consultant-fee mechanism requires applicants to fund Town review costs and replenish the account when it drops to one-third of its initial balance, protecting the Town's budget from being on the hook for third-party review costs (§ 340-6D).
concerns: § 340-4B (Planning Board regulated activities) and § 340-4C (administrative permit activities) list nearly the same 12-13 activities verbatim; the only differentiator is the Building Inspector/Consultant's subjective judgment of what is 'limited in scope,' which could produce inconsistent outcomes for similarly situated applicants.

The chapter's own definition of the Environmental Map of North Castle (§ 340-3) concedes it is a 2012 map providing 'general guidance only' and 'not site-specific,' yet permit thresholds and review pathways can hinge on whether a property is mapped as wetland.

§ 340-8B(3) retains a denial ground tied to pending state/agency condemnation of a 'freshwater wetland,' language lifted from the NYS Freshwater Wetlands Act, that sits awkwardly next to the chapter's much broader local wetland definition and may rarely if ever be triggered in practice.

Application and mitigation-bank fee amounts are entirely deferred to the Master Fee Schedule (Ch. A370, referenced in § 340-6D(1) and § 340-9B) rather than stated in the chapter, making it impossible from this chapter alone to judge whether fees are adequate to cover review costs or mitigation-bank restoration goals.

Minimum monitoring period for mitigation is only five years post-construction (§ 340-12B(1)), which may be too short to confirm that a created or restored wetland has reached functional maturity, particularly for forested wetland types.

recommendations.suggestion: Replace the subjective 'limited in scope' standard in § 340-4C with objective numeric thresholds (e.g., square footage of buffer disturbance, distance from wetland edge) so applicants can predict up front whether a one- or two-family project qualifies for the administrative track versus full Planning Board review under § 340-4B.

Commission an updated GIS-based wetlands inventory to replace or supplement the 2012 Environmental Map of North Castle referenced in § 340-3, since the chapter itself flags that map as non-site-specific general guidance, which slows down preapplication scoping under § 340-5A.

Clarify or remove the state/agency condemnation denial ground in § 340-8B(3), which was drafted around the NYS Freshwater Wetlands Act's acquisition process and does not map cleanly onto this chapter's broader local wetland definition, to avoid ambiguity if ever invoked.

Extend the minimum mitigation monitoring period in § 340-12B(1) beyond five years for created or restored wetlands (particularly forested or scrub-shrub types) to better ensure long-term functional success before a bond is released under § 340-11.

Periodically reassess the wetland mitigation bank in-lieu fee (§ 340-9B) and administrative/Planning Board application fees (§ 340-6D, § 340-9B) in the Master Fee Schedule to confirm they still reflect current restoration and consultant-review costs, since the chapter itself does not state current dollar figures.

chapters.peerComparison: Based on general professional familiarity with Westchester County and comparable Hudson Valley wetlands ordinances, rather than a direct document-to-document comparison: North Castle's approach of regulating all wetlands regardless of size (including vernal pools) is a meaningfully stronger local overlay than towns that simply defer to the state's 12.4-acre Article 24 Freshwater Wetlands Act threshold, and its 100-foot base buffer (expanding to 150 feet on steep slopes) sits at or above the typical 50-100 foot range seen in many peer municipalities. The 2:1 mitigation replacement ratio and formal fee-in-lieu mitigation bank mirror best practices increasingly adopted in the region since the mid-2010s, though many towns still lack the mitigation-bank option entirely. Coordination with NYS DEC jurisdiction (via the Freshwater Wetlands Map and Article 24 cross-references in § 340-3) is handled about as well as is typical -- the local law supplements rather than conflicts with state jurisdiction -- though, as in many municipal codes of this vintage, the chapter would benefit from tighter integration with GIS-based wetland mapping rather than a static, admittedly non-site-specific reference map.

recordEvidence.note: The strongest-performing chapter in the record. Recent (adopted 2012) and cited operationally by section — §340-5/§340-5D as the governing wetland-permit procedure, §340-9's mitigation policy read into the record and applied — and repeatedly used to REFUSE development rather than accommodate it: e.g. Planning Board, June 13 and 21, 2022, on a motor court and curb cut — “… it's located in a wetland buffer and the town code does not permit that.” Never criticised by staff, board, or counsel across 263 meetings, making it the clearest internal benchmark this corpus provides for what a well-functioning chapter looks like — in direct contrast to Chapter 355.

chapters.title: Zoning
chapters.summary: Chapter 355 is North Castle's comprehensive zoning ordinance, organized into fourteen articles covering definitions, roughly 30 residential/business/office-industrial districts plus a Golf Course Community Floating Overlay District, dimensional/use schedules (attached as separate tables), special permit uses, site plan review, off-street parking, performance standards, nonconforming uses, administration/enforcement (including the Zoning Board of Appeals and variance standards), and amendment procedures. It regulates everything from base residential districts sized 4 acres down to 5,000 square feet, several multifamily and mixed-use hamlet districts in and around Armonk with mandatory 'AFFH' (affordable, affirmatively-furthering-fair-housing) set-asides, and specialized business/office/industrial zones including a density-transfer (TDR-like) program between office parcels. Supplementary articles address steep slopes/hilltops/ridgelines, scenic roadscape preservation, conservation subdivisions, short-term rentals, wireless facilities, and dozens of individualized special-permit use standards (day care, accessory apartments, asphalt plants, helistops, day camps, country inns, assisted living, etc.). The chapter has been amended dozens of times since 1988, most recently in 2025 and 2026, and reflects continuous, active maintenance rather than a static, seldom-revisited ordinance.
chapters.ratingRationale: The chapter is unusually well-maintained (amendments as recent as March 2026) and includes sophisticated, forward-looking features -- mandatory inclusionary AFFH housing set-asides (§355-24I), density-based-on-net-lot-area environmental integration (§355-14, §355-26F), a density-transfer program (§355-30A(7)), and detailed short-term-rental and battery-storage regulation. But it is held back from 'Good shape' by a genuinely dated accessory-apartment (ADU) framework (§355-40K) that requires owner-occupancy, a discretionary Town special permit, a four-year post-CO waiting period, and automatic termination on any change of ownership -- out of step with where many peer towns and state housing policy have moved -- plus at least one uncorrected stale cross-reference (the 'factory-manufactured home' definition in §355-4 still cites Executive Law Article 18-B, which the chapter's own editor's note says was repealed in 1984).
strengths: Mandatory inclusionary affordable housing built into multiple multifamily districts, requiring 10% AFFH units in developments of 10+ units and additional set-asides in the CB-A, R-MF-A, R-MF-DA and R-MF-SS Districts (§355-24I, §355-25, §355-28, §355-29B)

Density calculations in residential and business districts are tied to 'net lot area' that subtracts wetlands, watercourses and steep slopes, directly linking allowable development to environmental sensitivity (§355-4, §355-14, §355-18, §355-26F)

Actively amended through 2025-2026 and covers current topics most zoning codes still lack, including tiered battery energy storage system classifications, EV charging station standards, and a detailed short-term-rental regulatory scheme with occupancy caps, quiet hours and a 120-day annual rental limit (§355-4, §355-26J)

A rare transfer-of-development-rights/density-transfer mechanism between Office Business and DOB-20A parcels intended to preserve open space and scenic vistas -- a more advanced planning tool than found in most suburban zoning codes (§355-30A(7), §355-30J(5))

Highly individualized special-permit standards for niche and high-impact uses (asphalt/concrete plants, helistops, day camps, country inns, commercial dog care) that go well beyond generic boilerplate criteria (§355-40)
concerns: The accessory apartment (ADU) provision remains discretionary and restrictive: it requires a Town Planning Board special permit (not an as-of-right process), mandatory owner-occupancy, a four-year wait after the principal dwelling's certificate of occupancy, automatic termination on any change of ownership, and reinspection every three years (§355-40K)

The 'FACTORY-MANUFACTURED HOME' definition still cites Executive Law Article 18-B as its governing authority even though the chapter's own editor's note states that article was repealed effective 1984 -- an unresolved stale cross-reference (§355-4)

Definitions are duplicated rather than centralized -- day-care center, family day-care center and group family day-care center are defined verbatim in both §355-4 and again in §355-40P(2), creating a risk that a future amendment to one copy will not be mirrored in the other
Extremely deep nested subsection numbering (e.g., §355-40M(6)(a)[3][L]{1}) throughout a 100+ page chapter makes precise citation and navigation difficult for residents and practitioners alike

Many moderate-impact uses (e.g., asphalt/concrete plants) trigger heavy discretionary review layers -- escrowed consultant fees, environmental impairment insurance, and even a 51%-of-neighbors consent petition -- that add substantial cost and delay (§355-40M)

Traditional suburban minimum parking ratios (e.g., 2 spaces per dwelling unit, 1 per 200 square feet of retail) have not been revisited despite the CB-A Armonk hamlet district's own stated goal of a walkable, 'village-like' pedestrian character (§355-29B(6), §355-57)

recommendations.suggestion: Convert accessory apartments (§355-40K) from a discretionary Town special-permit use with mandatory owner-occupancy and multi-year waiting periods into a more streamlined administrative or as-of-right pathway (retaining basic dimensional and septic/parking safeguards), consistent with the direction of statewide and regional ADU policy aimed at expanding housing supply.

Correct the stale Executive Law citations in the 'FACTORY-MANUFACTURED HOME' and 'MOBILE HOME' definitions in §355-4, which still reference repealed articles, and replace them with the current Uniform Fire Prevention and Building Code / Real Property Law provisions that actually govern manufactured housing today.
Consolidate the duplicated day-care center definitions in §355-4 and §355-40P(2) into a single cross-referenced definition so future Social Services Law updates only need to be incorporated once.

Revisit the one-space-per-200-square-foot minimum parking standard applied in the CB-A Armonk hamlet district (§355-57) in light of that district's own 'village-like, pedestrian-scale' design guidelines (§355-29B(6)), which are otherwise undermined by conventional suburban parking minimums.

For lower-impact special-permit uses (e.g., day spas, fine arts instruction schools), consider a lighter administrative or Planning-Board-only review track rather than the same Town Board/escrowed-consultant process used for high-impact uses like asphalt plants (§355-40), to reduce carrying costs and timeline uncertainty for small businesses.

Add a dedicated solar/renewable-energy article with siting, screening and dimensional standards comparable in specificity to the chapter's tiered battery-energy-storage-system framework (§355-4), since ground-mounted solar is an emerging land-use pressure point not yet addressed with similar rigor.

chapters.peerComparison: Based on general professional familiarity with Westchester County and broader New York State zoning practice rather than a document-to-document comparison, North Castle's chapter sits above the median in sophistication and currency but is not clearly at the leading edge on housing flexibility. Its district structure (a long ladder of one-family districts from 4 acres down to 5,000 square feet, separate multifamily and hamlet-mixed-use districts, and a distinct floating overlay for an age-restricted golf course community) is more granular than many peer towns, and its mandatory AFFH inclusionary set-asides -- rooted in the Westchester County Fair and Affordable Housing settlement that many county municipalities share -- are a genuinely common regional feature rather than unique, though North Castle's version is unusually detailed (resale price formulas, affirmative marketing, fixed-improvement credit schedules). Conservation subdivision authority under Town Law §278 is now standard practice across NY towns, and North Castle's version is comparably thorough. Where North Castle likely lags many actively-reforming peer towns is accessory dwelling units: a growing number of NY municipalities have moved toward as-of-right or lightly-conditioned ADU approval to help address regional housing shortages, whereas North Castle still requires a discretionary special permit, owner-occupancy, and automatic termination on sale -- among the more restrictive ADU regimes still on the books regionally. Its short-term-rental ordinance and wireless-facilities framework (cross-referenced to a separate, FCC-shot-clock-compliant telecommunications law) are relatively current compared to many towns that still lack any STR regulation at all. Parking minimums, by contrast, remain conventional 1960s/1970s-style suburban ratios that many progressive Hudson Valley and Westchester municipalities have begun to relax near walkable centers, an area where North Castle has not modernized despite its own hamlet design guidelines calling for pedestrian-oriented development.

recordCorpus.pass1: Deficiency pass — code vocabulary paired with deficiency vocabulary across a rolling context window: 409 candidate passages, classified down to 59 retained passages across 34 distinct meeting-topic episodes.
recordCorpus.pass2: Provision-specific gap pass — targeted the provisions Pass 1 under-covered (trees, wetlands, steep slopes, setbacks/height, site-plan procedure, comprehensive plan, stormwater, subdivision, signs, accessory apartments, short-term rentals): 168 candidates, classified down to 3 additional retained findings.
recordCorpus.pass3: Citation pass — every spoken chapter, article, and section citation extracted from all 263 transcripts, filtered for false positives and validated against the authoritative chapter list: 342 verified citing utterances across 18 chapters.

crossCuttingFindings: Ambiguity as a general drafting property: “The current legislation … [and] code needs [to be] addressed. [It is] very ambiguous [and a] difficult code even to enforce.” — Unattributed public commenter, Town Board, November 8, 2023, 00:30:52.

Enforceability assessed prospectively, and accepted anyway: “It'll be a tougher thing to enforce. It'll be vague, perhaps.” — “Steve,” likely a Planning Board member, Planning Board, March 9, 2026, 01:42:26 — a board recognising in advance that language it is advancing will be hard to enforce.

Amendment by accretion around individual applicants: visible in the citation traffic rather than in any one quote — §355-27 across five meetings in 2023 for one airport-campus density question, §355-32B across three for one golf-course overlay, §355-28 across three for R-MF district additions, §355-21 across eight, and §355-40 grown to 28 lettered subsections, several written for a single site or use. Chapter 355 is being maintained by insertion, which is the predictable source of its internal-inconsistency findings.

Process criticism as a recurring theme, three separate years, same concern that amendments move faster than the Board can review them: “This is not the way to amend town code” (Sept. 14, 2022); “Either we change code or … not make [a] one-off exception because [it] is a de facto change” (July 12, 2023); a Board member asking whether a redline of Chapter 27 would be available before its public hearing (Aug. 10, 2022).

Identified gaps that remain open as of the March 11, 2026 code date: battery energy storage (no guidelines, flagged January 2024, still absent from §355-40 and the New Laws queue); short-term rentals (a conceded 19-year gap since 2007, still uncodified); the parking-in-lieu mechanism at §355-56.K (still a land-dedication provision, not the fee mechanism the Town has described wanting). The record therefore supports identified-and-unremedied defects, not merely defects — the more damaging finding for a chapter-strength assessment.
